note: English version of primitives.json (translated 2026-11-17 by a cheaper model, structure checked by script, wording not reviewed line by line). The Chinese file is the original; implementations live only there.

primitives.name: Minimal-contrast discrimination
primitives.oneLine: First hear which of a pair differing by one sound is which, then say the one that lets a listener tell them apart
primitives.difficulty: The learner's first language does not have this contrast, so the two sounds are heard as one. Chinese learners hear think as sink, and cannot tell ship from sheep or bad from bed. In Japanese they write か heard as が, hear きって as きて, and おばあさん as おばさん. English native speakers group bà with pà and xī with shī, and cannot tell front and back nasal finals apart. If you cannot hear it, you cannot say it. The word you say is taken for another word, and the learner does not notice.
primitives.object: A set of minimal-contrast cards on one contrast axis (6–10 pairs). Each card is two words differing by one sound, each with a picture or gloss and recordings by several speakers. The learner's own recording from Step 3 is attached to the same card, next to the original
primitives.requires: Needs media (at least two real speakers for each word; if only TTS is available, a person must check that the contrast is actually audible). Step 3 needs mic, or a partner to act as listener; with neither, do only Steps 1 and 2. The learner can match the two words on the card to their meanings or pictures
learnerAction: Step 1 Discriminate: hear one word and tap the picture it matches (two choices). Each round mixes in two trials that play the same word twice and ask "same or different?"

Step 2 Classify: hear one recording and choose A / B / neither (a third sound, such as /f/ standing in for /θ/) / the same word said differently. The last option is the reverse half: the recordings differ audibly, but it is still the same word

Step 3 Say it so someone can tell: the system shows the learner one randomly assigned target word only, and the learner says it. A listener (a partner, or the learner later) cannot see the target and taps which one they heard
systemResponse: After each choice, the pair of cards flips open with the two spellings side by side. The letter, kana or pinyin where they differ is colored, and the pair is played once in A-B-A order
The contrast matrix in the side panel accumulates "heard A, chose A" and "heard A, chose B", so the learner can see whether they tend to hear both as A or are really confusing them at random

After Step 3, the card records "target A, listener heard B". The learner's recording is kept next to the original and can be replayed either way. The system makes no judgment of pronunciation from the recording

ui.screen: Two large picture cards (A, B) left and right, with a play button between them. Small buttons below: "same / not sure". The narrow right panel shows the 2×2 matrix for this contrast axis and the number of times heard; no score is shown. Step 3 uses two screens: the speaker screen shows only the target, the listener screen shows only the two cards
interactions: Space replays (replay count is recorded)
F / J keys or touch to choose the left or right card
Step 3: the speaker holds the record key and speaks. On release the screen switches to the listener view, and is passed to the partner to tap
With no partner: the recording is stored first, then shown at least 3 items later as a blind listen, and the learner taps it themselves
ui.childVariant: Ages 5–7 starting English: only two pictures (ship / sheep, pen / pin, bag / back), no text, all instructions spoken. At most 6 items per round. After each item the animal on the card does an action instead of giving a right/wrong symbol. In Step 3 a parent is the listener: the tablet first lets the child see and hear the target picture, then covers it automatically, and the parent taps "which one I heard". Chinese heritage children generally have no trouble hearing tones and initials, so they do not use this primitive unless the teacher observes a specific confusion (such as n / l from a dialect background). Children who cannot yet split a word into sounds do prim:oral-sound-play first
ui.adultVariant: Can show the phonetic-symbol or pinyin layer and the name of the contrast axis (aspirated / unaspirated, long / short mora, /θ/-/s/). Word pairs come from scenes where a mix-up really causes misunderstanding (prices 13 / 30, びよういん / びょういん, 买 / 卖). Step 3 can use a voice assistant as the listener, but say that the assistant's recognition counts as one listener only
ui.accessibility: Every item can be done by keyboard alone. Picture cards also have text alternatives. Learners with a hearing impairment should not be assessed with this primitive; say so at the top of the page. Playback volume and speed are adjustable, but an answer given with slowed playback is recorded as after hint

kcSignals: component is phonological, and itemTypes include listen-discriminate

commonErrors contain a merger of a single segment, such as "hears X as Y / X and Y sound the same / uses X for Y", for example kt:en-phon-sound-inventory, pen/pin in kt:en-orth-cvc-decoding, kt:ja-sound-kg / td / pb, kt:ja-sound-sokuon, kt:ja-sound-long, kt:zh-pinyin-initials-finals
The KC description gives minimal-contrast word examples (sheep/ship, きて/きって, bà/pà)
learnerSignals: In dictation, always gets the same pair of letters or kana wrong in the same place
"These two sound the same"
The word they say is taken by the listener as another word, and the learner does not know why
contraindications: Do not set items when there are no real-speaker recordings and only unchecked synthetic speech
If the contrast already exists in the learner's first language (such as tones for Chinese heritage children, voicing for Japanese native speakers), do not use it as practice
If the difference is an allophonic variant that does not distinguish meaning, it can go only in the reverse half and cannot be a contrast item
Never give a pronunciation score or stars from Step 3

rules: Each contrast axis needs at least 12 discrimination trials, with A and B appearing equally often in random order, plus 2 "same" trials. It passes only if accuracy on both A and B is at least 75% (blocks an answer that is too weak, and this also blocks a bias of always choosing A)
If more than half of the "same" trials are answered "different", mark the whole round as "guessing a difference" and do not count it as a pass (blocks gaming)

In Step 3 the listener cannot see the target. The item is recorded as "can be told apart" only if the partner's identification matches the target at least 4 times out of 5. Self blind-listen identification is recorded separately and not merged with the partner result
check.independence: The first tap on each item is saved before any replay, slow playback or difference-amplifying hint. The number of replays before answering is recorded on the item. An answer given after slow playback or amplification is recorded as completed after hint. Step 3 distinguishes three sources: "partner identification", "assistant identification" and "self delayed blind listen"

evidence.retained: Kept for this set of contrast cards: first choice on each item, replays before answering, hint use, the contrast matrix, the Step 3 recording (kept only inside the page and lost on refresh, so the learner must be reminded), and the listener's identification result and its source

licensed.claim: can hear this contrast in isolated words
the learner's spoken version of this contrast can be told apart by others
the learner can hear which one they themselves said

prohibited: Inferring correct speaking from correct discrimination
Inferring that the learner can tell them apart in connected speech from isolated-word discrimination
Treating self blind-listen identification as acceptable pronunciation
Any automatic pronunciation score on a recording, or any judgment such as "X% like a native speaker"

hints: Only point out "pay attention to the beginning / middle / end of the word"
Play the two words A-B-A-B, then play the target
Slow down and lengthen the differing segment (only for recordings with segment time codes); the answer is recorded as after hint
scaffold.fade: When, for two rounds in a row, first-attempt accuracy on both sides of a contrast axis reaches 85% with no after-hint answers, that axis appears only occasionally in mixed rounds and no hint above level 2 is given

primitives.reverseHalf: Every round has "same word, different pronunciation" items: the Japanese ら-row [ɾ] and [l], the flap of t in English water versus a clear t, the full third tone versus the half third tone in Mandarin. The recordings sound different but are still the same word, and the learner must choose "the same word said differently". This tells the learner that not every audible difference needs to be taken seriously

failureModes.failure: The learner tells the items apart by the speaker's voice, recording noise or volume, rather than by the target sound
failureModes.mitigation: At least two speakers for each word, the recordings of A and B use speakers crosswise, and volume is normalized
failureModes.test: Build "same" trials from the same speaker's A and a different speaker's A, and check whether they are answered "different"

failureModes.failure: In Step 3 the partner sees the target or guesses from the mouth shape
failureModes.mitigation: The listener screen appears only after the speaking ends, and there is an option "listen to the recording without seeing the person"
failureModes.test: Check that the listener view is not visible before the recording is complete

failureModes.failure: Familiarity of the picture leaks the answer (the child always taps the more familiar one)
failureModes.mitigation: The left-right position of the two cards is random, and statistics are kept separately for A and B
failureModes.test: Check whether the tap rate for one picture in the contrast matrix is far above its rate of appearance

stacksWith.how: When the contrast card flips, the spelling appears. Changing one letter turns A into B, so discrimination and blending are practiced on the same pair of words
The Step 3 recording goes into self-transcription: the learner writes down which word they heard, then compares with the target
When the contrast axis is tone or length, a contour grid is overlaid on the same card, and the discrimination result is drawn at the same time as high-low or long-short

languages.en: Contrast axes: /θ/-/s/ (think/sink), /iː/-/ɪ/ (sheep/ship), /æ/-/e/ (bad/bed), /v/-/w/, presence or absence of a final consonant (bag/ba), presence or absence of -s (book/books), the three pronunciations of -ed. Material comes from kt:en-phon-sound-inventory, kt:en-orth-cvc-decoding, kt:en-phon-s-endings, kt:en-phon-ed-endings. Trap: when Chinese learners say /θ/, a partner often guesses right from context, so items must be isolated words or contexts where both words are plausible
languages.ja: Contrast axes: voicing か/が・た/だ・ぱ/ば (for Chinese learners the key is vocal-fold vibration, not aspiration), geminate きて/きって, long vowel おばさん/おばあさん・ここ/こうこう, contracted sound びよういん/びょういん, the one beat of ん. Material comes from kt:ja-sound-kg, kt:ja-sound-td, kt:ja-sound-pb, kt:ja-sound-sokuon, kt:ja-sound-long, kt:ja-sound-yoon. Trap: mora-length contrasts must be recorded at the same speaking rate, otherwise overall speed alone gives the answer away
languages.zh: Contrast axes: aspirated b/p・d/t・g/k, j q x versus zh ch sh, ü/u (lǜ/lù), front and back nasals an/ang・in/ing, n/l. Material comes from kt:zh-pinyin-initials-finals. The target is mainly adult English and Japanese native speakers. Chinese heritage children generally do not need it, and tone contrasts go to prim:contour-match

primitives.name: Pitch-contour matching
primitives.oneLine: Draw or choose the contour of the tone, stress or pitch you hear, then say it following the contour
primitives.difficulty: Pitch or stress works differently in the target language than in the learner's first language. The learner hears that there is movement but cannot grasp its shape and position. English native speakers let sentence intonation cover lexical tone: they raise the last syllable of every question, mix up tone 2 and tone 3, and cannot get tone 4 to fall. Chinese learners read Japanese pitch accent as the four Mandarin tones, give every syllable of an English word the same stress, and use rising intonation for every question. After tone sandhi, the written tone and the heard tone differ, and the learner does not know which to trust.
primitives.object: A contour grid: a word or short phrase divided by syllable (by mora in Japanese). Each cell holds a draggable point or contour block. Chinese uses the five-level vertical scale, Japanese uses two levels (high / low), and English uses large and small dots for stressed and unstressed plus an arrow for the rise or fall at the end of the sentence. The original recording, the learner's drawn contour and the learner's recording are all attached to this one grid
primitives.requires: Needs media (real-speaker recordings); Step 3 needs mic, and the partner discrimination items need a partner. The learner can already read out the segments of the word (pinyin, kana or spelling) and lacks only pitch and stress. If segments cannot yet be read, fall back to prim:sound-spelling-blend first
learnerAction: Step 1 Draw the contour: listen to the original (can replay), then in each cell drag out the pitch or choose a contour block, or place stress dots on an English word

Step 2 Classify: for each cell, decide which class the syllable belongs to. The locked options depend on the language. Chinese: tone 1 / tone 2 / full tone 3 / half tone 3 / neutral tone / tone 3 that is read as tone 2 after sandhi. Japanese: falls here / does not fall here. English: stressed / unstressed and reduced. The last class, "the written tone and the read tone differ", is the reverse half: 你好 is written nǐ hǎo but read ní hǎo, and 一 is written yī but read yí in 一个

Step 3 Say it following the contour: choose a contour for a new word or short phrase (such as mǎi / mài, はし 箸 / 橋, REcord / reCORD), and record yourself saying it. A partner first listens blind and taps which contour they heard. With no partner, the learner listens blind to their own recording a few items later, draws the contour they hear in an empty grid, and then compares it with the target
systemResponse: After submitting, the reference contour is overlaid as a semi-transparent line on the learner's drawn contour, and cells that do not match get a frame. The learner can tap "hum it once": the page hums the pitch of the reference contour with a pure tone (this is not speech synthesis, only pitch), helping the learner match shape and sound

On sandhi items the contour grid has two layers. The upper layer is the tone given in the dictionary, the lower layer is the tone actually read. Change arrows are drawn between the layers, with the name of the sandhi rule

After Step 3, the target contour, the contour drawn by the partner or by self blind-listening, and the recording are shown side by side. The system neither extracts nor displays the pitch curve of the learner's recording. The judgment comes only from the listener

ui.screen: At the top is the source text (characters plus pinyin, kana, or English word). In the middle is the contour grid, one column per cell. Below is the contour block palette (5 for Chinese, 2 for Japanese, 2 sizes for English). The right column records confusion pairs such as "tone 2 / tone 3 mixed up N times", with no total score
interactions: Tap a cell, then press 1–5 (Chinese), H / L (Japanese) or S / W (English) to set it
Drag the point up and down on a touch screen
Space replays the original; Shift+Space hums the reference contour (available only after submitting)
Step 3: hold the record key and speak
ui.childVariant: Ages 5–7: Chinese tones are drawn as the road a little car travels (flat road, uphill, a valley that goes down then up, downhill). The child drags a car sticker onto the matching road while making a gesture. English word stress uses elephant steps (strong) and mouse steps (weak): the child claps BA-na-na and ba-NA-na, then chooses which is right. Chinese heritage children (ages 6–12) already have stable spoken tones, so the aim here is to match what they can say to the tone marks in pinyin: they listen to words they know (妈妈, 苹果) and attach the tone marks to the pinyin. The sandhi layer is especially useful for them, because they say ní hǎo but do not know why it is written nǐ
ui.adultVariant: Can show the five-level numeric values and rule names (third-tone sandhi, 一 and 不 sandhi, 頭高型 / 平板型 / 中高型 / 尾高型). Short-sentence items add sentence intonation, so the learner can see that a question tone at the end does not change lexical tone. Japanese items must include the following particle (花が / 鼻が), otherwise 尾高型 and 平板型 cannot be told apart
ui.accessibility: Contours are shown by both position and shape blocks, not by color alone. All operations can be done by keyboard. The volume of the hum is adjustable on its own. Not suitable for learners with a hearing impairment

kcSignals: component is phonological and the description involves tone, pitch, stress or intonation: kt:zh-pinyin-tones, kt:zh-tone-sandhi, the neutral tone in kt:zh-pinyin-erhua, kt:ja-sound-pitch, kt:ja-sound-loan-accent, kt:ja-sound-compound-accent, kt:ja-sound-intonation, kt:en-phon-word-stress, kt:en-phon-sentence-stress, kt:en-phon-intonation-questions, kt:en-phon-number-discrimination (stress in 13 / 30)
commonErrors include "sentence intonation overrides lexical tone", "reads high and low pitch as the four tones", "every syllable equally stressed", "every question rises"
itemTypes include listen-discriminate and read-aloud
learnerSignals: The sounds are all right, but native speakers do not understand or hear another word
"I don't know which tone I'm saying"
When reading aloud, the whole sentence is flat, or every character rises and falls
contraindications: Do not add contours when the learner cannot yet read the segments

Dialect or personal variation is not right or wrong: Japanese takes the Tokyo pattern as reference, and the page must say so. For English British/American stress differences (such as adVERtisement / ADvertisement), accept both
Never compare the pitch curve of the learner's recording with the reference automatically and give a score

rules: In each round the two easily confused classes (such as tone 2 / tone 3, 頭高 / 平板) appear equally often, and accuracy on each class must reach 75% (blocks an answer that is too weak, and this also blocks marking everything the same)

At least one third of the items have sentence intonation and lexical tone in opposite directions (a declarative ends in tone 2, a question ends in tone 4). A learner who only draws along with the sentence intonation fails (blocks gaming)
Sandhi items must fill both layers: filling only the actual sound or only the written tone mark does not pass
In Step 3 the item is recorded as "can be told apart" only if the partner's blind listening picks the target contour at least 4 times out of 5
check.independence: The contour first drawn in Step 1 is saved before the reference is shown. A redraw after seeing "hum it once" or the reference overlay is recorded as after hint. Step 3 distinguishes partner identification from self blind-listening, and in self blind-listening the original cannot be heard again first

evidence.retained: Kept on each contour grid: the first drawn contour, redraws, the reference contour, what was filled in on both sandhi layers, the Step 3 recording (inside the page), and the contour drawn by the listener and its source

licensed.claim: can hear this set of contour types or stress positions in isolated words
knows where the written tone and the read tone differ and can mark them
the learner's spoken contour can be told apart by others

prohibited: Inferring correct tone or stress in connected speech from correct contours in isolated words
Inferring correct pronunciation from self blind-listening
Treating the result of a pitch-curve comparison as a pronunciation score
Judging Japanese pitch patterns other than the Tokyo pattern as wrong

hints: Only ask "which cell has the highest point?" or "which cell is strongest?"
Play only the syllable in this cell, and play it together with a character of known contour (such as mā and the target character)
Show the first cell of the reference contour
scaffold.fade: When first-attempt accuracy on both classes of the same confusable contour set reaches 85% for two rounds in a row, remove the level 2 and 3 hints. After 6 sandhi items in a row with both layers correct, the lower layer is left empty by default and the learner must fill it themselves

primitives.reverseHalf: Written is not read: third-tone sequences, 一 and 不 sandhi and the neutral tone in Chinese; 尾高型 in Japanese, which shows only when a particle follows; English homographs whose stress changes with part of speech (REcord noun / reCORD verb). There must also be items where sentence intonation and lexical tone go in opposite directions, showing that sentence intonation does not change lexical tone

failureModes.failure: The learner draws the contour by the rise or fall at the end of the sentence (a question rises), not by the lexical tone
failureModes.mitigation: Include many items where sentence intonation conflicts with lexical tone
failureModes.test: Adversarial examples: in 你是老师吗, shī must be marked tone 1; in 他去不去？, 去 must be marked tone 4

failureModes.failure: The learner has memorized the tone marks of common words and is not listening
failureModes.mitigation: Mix in characters outside the learner's word list that have the same syllable with a different tone, and nonsense syllables
failureModes.test: Accuracy on items outside the word list is counted separately from accuracy on items inside it

failureModes.failure: The child places the car stickers at random
failureModes.mitigation: Two opposing contours alternate, and every picture needs the child to make the gesture at the same time and the parent to confirm
failureModes.test: Check the proportion of consecutive stickers placed on the same kind of road

stacksWith.how: A contour grid is overlaid on the same minimal-contrast card for tone or length contrasts (mǎi / mài, きて / きって)
When phonetic annotation is removed, the tone mark is the last layer to go. For a character drawn correctly the first time on the contour grid, its pinyin tone mark is removed first
For sentence-level items, mark the contour first on the same original recording, then shadow it and compare pauses

languages.en: Targets: word stress (hoTEL, deVElop, PHOtograph / phoTOgraphy), stress in 13 / 30, sentence stress and information focus, question intonation (falling tone for wh-questions). Material comes from kt:en-phon-word-stress, kt:en-phon-sentence-stress, kt:en-phon-intonation-questions. Trap: Chinese learners draw stress as "tone", so for English the contour grid uses only two levels, strong and weak, and not the five-level scale
languages.ja: Targets: the four pitch-accent patterns, 花が / 鼻が, 雨 / 飴, pitch of loanwords and compounds. Material comes from kt:ja-sound-pitch, kt:ja-sound-loan-accent, kt:ja-sound-compound-accent. Trap: Chinese learners read 頭高型 as a fourth tone plus a neutral tone, so items must include 平板型 and a following particle
languages.zh: Targets: the four tones and the neutral tone, the 20 two-syllable combinations, third-tone sandhi, 一 and 不 sandhi, neutral-tone words (东西 dōngxi / dōngxī). Material comes from kt:zh-pinyin-tones, kt:zh-tone-sandhi, kt:zh-pinyin-erhua. Trap: some textbooks mark the original tone and some mark the actual sound, so the sandhi layer must state which one this page uses

primitives.name: Rhythm shadowing
primitives.oneLine: First mark the pauses and stresses of the original, then shadow it and compare your own pause curve
primitives.difficulty: Every sound is right, but the whole sentence is hard to understand. In English every word gets equal stress and no weak forms, so the sentence is laid out flat in one breath, or it breaks in the middle of a block such as isn't coming back. In Japanese, learners squash とうきょう into two beats as with Chinese syllables, and drop a beat from geminates, long vowels and the moraic nasal. English native speakers speaking Chinese say one character at a time, do not apply tone sandhi, and let sentence intonation override lexical tone. What is missing is not pronunciation but hearing where the original pauses, where it stresses, and which words join into one block, and then doing the same.
primitives.object: 3–5 sentences of real-speed original recording (3–8 seconds each, with time codes and marked pause positions). The learner's taps, pause classifications, shadowing duration and rewritten sentences are all overlaid on this one timeline
primitives.requires: The learner can read these sentences aloud from the text and understands the gist (a translation may help); has a microphone. If the learner cannot hear which words are in the original, fall back to prim:transcript-diff first
learnerAction: Step 1 Tap the beat: play a sentence and tap (space key or button) at each pause you hear. When it ends, "where the original paused" and "where you tapped" are overlaid on the same timeline

Step 2 Classify: for each pause in the original, decide where it comes from (locked options: a sense group has ended / to stress the next word / between list items / the speaker is thinking of a word — don't learn this / not actually a pause, one sound is stretched — there is no pause there). The last two classes are the reverse half

Step 3 Say it along: shadow the sentence following the original's chunking. The system compares only pause positions and total duration. If the learner cannot finish in time, they write or say a version that fits within the original's duration without losing the key points
systemResponse: Taps become points on the timeline: a tap that lands in the tolerance band is filled in, an extra tap is crossed out, and a missed pause shows as an empty box. No score appears

After classification, a pause mark ▎ appears at the matching position in the sentence text, and the words wrapped by a sense group join into one color block. For positions classed as "thinking of a word" or "stretched sound", the mark turns into a strikethrough

After shadowing, the learner's own pause curve is drawn below the original curve, and the two durations are shown side by side (original 8.0 s / you 12.6 s). The number of blocks in the rewritten sentence is shown beside the original's

ui.screen: At the top is a play bar and a horizontal timeline with two lanes: original and you. In the middle is the text of the current sentence, hidden or shown without punctuation in Step 1. Below is a row of classification buttons. The narrow right column lists hits, extra taps and missed taps for each sentence, with no total score
interactions: Space key or a large button to tap; R to replay; 0.75x slow-play toggle
Number keys 1–5 choose the pause class, Tab moves between pause marks
Step 3: hold the record key to shadow; the recording stays only inside the page and disappears on refresh
ui.childVariant: Each sentence is no longer than 4 seconds, tapping becomes beating a small drum, and pauses are shown as small animals jumping between squares. Do only Step 1 and clap along while saying it once; no classification or rewriting
ui.adultVariant: Material is taken from meeting speeches, podcasts and news interviews, and the class terms are shown (sense group, focus stress, weak form). Step 3 requires writing a shortened version and saying it again
ui.accessibility: Hits, extra taps and missed taps are distinguished by both shape and color. Tapping can use an external switch or anywhere on a touch screen. A text rhythm-annotation mode is provided for learners with a hearing impairment, but records produced in this mode do not count as listening evidence

kcSignals: component is phonological and the label involves sentence stress, weak forms, linking, shadowing, beat or sandhi (such as kt:en-phon-sentence-stress, kt:en-phon-weak-forms, kt:en-phon-linking, kt:en-phon-listen-repeat, kt:ja-sound-mora, kt:ja-sound-sokuon, kt:ja-sound-long, kt:zh-tone-sandhi)
itemTypes include read-aloud or listen-discriminate
commonErrors describe rhythm problems such as "every word equally stressed", "syllable-timed", "one character at a time", and not a single segment
learnerSignals: Speech is flat all the way, with no pauses
Says everything in one breath and runs out of air
Sounds like reading from a script
"Every sound of mine is right, and people still don't understand"
contraindications: If the problem is a single segment (θ/s, voicing, aspiration), use prim:sound-contrast first
The original is machine-synthesized or a deliberately slowed reading voice, with unnatural pauses
It cannot be used to evaluate pronunciation accuracy or as a speaking scoring tool

rules: Material check: the pause hit tolerance is ±0.8 seconds. Two pauses must be at least 1.6 seconds apart and farther than the tolerance from the start and end of the sentence, otherwise one tap would hit two pauses at once

Material check: exactly one original sentence has no pause at all. The pause classes must include "thinking of a word" and "stretched sound". The number of ▎ marks shown to the learner must equal the number of pauses used for judging
Step 1: a sentence with more than twice as many taps as original pauses is treated as random tapping and no hits are counted (blocks gaming)

Step 3: each rewritten sentence must not exceed the limit (English ≤12 words), which blocks submitting the original unchanged. It must also keep all the key points listed for the original, which blocks cutting it down to an empty sentence. The original sentence itself must fail the limit, otherwise "say it shorter" has no object
check.independence: The first round of taps on each sentence is recorded separately. Taps made after seeing the annotated version with ▎ or with slow-play on are recorded as completed after hint. Shadowing with text shown and without text shown are recorded separately

evidence.retained: The time points of the first taps on each sentence, the classification of each pause, shadowing duration and pause curve, and rewritten sentences are all kept on the same timeline

licensed.claim: can find the sense-group boundaries of this batch of recordings by ear
has started to chunk their own speech by sense group, not word by word or character by character at equal stress

prohibited: Judging from this whether pronunciation is accurate
Judging that the learner is fluent because the shadowing duration is close to the original
Inferring listening comprehension level from the tap hit rate
Taking the pauses at "thinking of a word" as a rhythm target to learn

hints: Replay this sentence at 0.75x speed
Show the chunk boundaries of the words in the text, but not where the pauses are
Show the original sentence with ▎
scaffold.fade: After three sentences in a row with first-round tap hits of 80% or more and no random tapping, stop providing the annotated version with ▎ and keep only slow-play

primitives.reverseHalf: One original sentence has no pause anywhere: saying it in one breath is itself a kind of emphasis, and a learner who forces a pause in this sentence must be told. Two pause classes should not be copied: the speaker thinking of a word (the rhythm can be learned, the stumbling need not be), and a stretched sound that is not a pause (pausing there would cut in half a block that must be said together).

failureModes.failure: The learner taps by the punctuation in the text, not by listening
failureModes.mitigation: Hide the text in the first round or give only the version without punctuation. Include sentences with a comma but no pause and a pause with no punctuation
failureModes.test: The adversarial examples include at least one comma with no pause and one place with no punctuation but a pause, so a tap sequence that follows punctuation alone loses points at both

failureModes.failure: The host plays back with a delay, and the learner taps correctly but is judged to have missed
failureModes.mitigation: A ±0.8 second tolerance band, plus constraints on the gap between pauses and their distance from the sentence start and end
failureModes.test: Shift all correct taps later by 0.5 seconds; they must still all hit

failureModes.failure: The learner thinks the faster the shadowing the better
failureModes.mitigation: Step 3 compares only duration, and asks the learner to say it shorter, not faster
failureModes.test: Submitting the original sentence unchanged is always blocked by the length limit

stacksWith.how: The shadowing recording is also an object for transcription: look at the pause curve of the same recording first, then transcribe it word by word yourself and see which block you get stuck on
For Japanese and Chinese, a pitch contour is overlaid under the same timeline, so pauses, アクセント and tones are compared together
The sense groups cut out by rhythm are chunks and can go straight into the chunk book

languages.en: The five pause classes sense/stress/list/think/none are locked (c56); the list pause must be marked at no fewer than two places. The focus is weak forms of function words (to/of/and/can), linking (pick it up), and sentence stress on the information focus. Step 3 is "say it shorter, not faster", at most 12 words per sentence. Existing implementation c56
languages.ja: The timeline unit changes to the mora first: in Step 1, tap each mora first, then tap the pauses. The contrast focus is long vowels (おばさん / おばあさん), geminates (きて / きって), contracted sounds (きょう is two moras, not three), and the moraic nasal ん as a mora of its own. The "thinking of a word" class corresponds to えーと and あのー. The "stretched sound" class becomes "the empty beat of a long vowel or geminate is not a pause". A particle joins the word before it (わたしは｜), and there is no pause before a particle. Material uses natural conversation, not news reading
languages.zh: The unit is the prosodic word and the sense group (我们｜明天｜去北京), not one character at a time. The timeline also marks sandhi (一, 不, third-tone sequences) and the neutral tone: a neutral-tone syllable is short and light but is not a pause. The typical problem of English native speakers is sentence intonation overriding lexical tone and every character being the same length. The "thinking of a word" class corresponds to 那个, 就是, 嗯. Step 3 does not ask for a shorter version; instead the learner re-says it chunk by chunk following the original's chunking, and compares the duration of each chunk

primitives.name: Record and self-transcribe
primitives.oneLine: After speaking, the learner first transcribes their own speech, then judges the problem type themselves and re-says one sentence
primitives.difficulty: After speaking, the learner does not know what they said. They think they used the phrases they learned, but used none of them. Restarts, fillers, getting stuck on one word and first-language word order carried over all blur together, and the learner is left with one vague feeling: "my speaking is bad". The layer in between is visible only when the learner types out their own words, one word at a time.
primitives.object: The learner's own recording of 30–60 seconds, and the transcript they type word by word. The chunk comparison, the type labels and the rewrite all happen on this transcript
primitives.requires: Can speak continuously for more than 30 seconds (broken speech is acceptable) and can type in the target language (kana input for Japanese, pinyin or character input for Chinese). If the learner cannot speak for 30 seconds, fall back to prim:picture-describe first, using the picture to support the content
learnerAction: Step 1 Speak and transcribe: look at the prompt and 4–6 prepared chunks, and record 30–60 seconds. The transcription box appears only after recording. The learner listens to the recording and types it out word by word. The page does no speech recognition

Step 2 Identify the type: first practice on several prepared sample excerpts, sorting each excerpt into a locked class (used the prepared phrase / restart / too many fillers / stuck on one word / first-language word order carried over), then go back to your own transcript and mark the same classes. "Restart" is the reverse half
Step 3 Re-say one sentence: pick the worst sentence in your own transcript, rewrite or re-record it, and pass the executable check
systemResponse: The transcript is compared with the chunks in the prompt: chunks that were used are highlighted in the transcript, and the top shows "used 2/5". This number is usually lower than the learner thinks
After each excerpt is classified, it is colored, with a way to fix this class attached. An excerpt classed as "restart" gets no fix, only an explanation of why it is not a fault
The rewritten sentence is shown beside the original, with changes colored. Recording length and transcript word count are shown side by side

ui.screen: At the top are the prompt and a row of chunks (folded away once recording starts). In the middle are the record key and a timer bar; after recording the transcription box appears below. To its right is a column of five class labels, and at the bottom is the rewrite area. No score appears at any time
interactions: Space starts or stops recording; left and right arrow keys replay in 5-second steps
Select a stretch of text in the transcript and press number keys 1–5 to classify it
The rewrite area accepts typing, or the learner can re-record one sentence
ui.childVariant: Record 20–30 seconds, telling one thing from a picture. Transcription becomes tapping which of three versions is "what I just said", and the teacher can type for the child. Only two classes are kept: "used those words" and "got stuck"
ui.adultVariant: Prompts come from work scenes (introducing a project, asking for leave, reporting progress), with 5–6 chunks. Step 3 requires rewriting one sentence and re-recording it
ui.accessibility: The recording is not uploaded or stored and disappears on refresh, and the page says this plainly. When the page is opened from a local file the browser cannot get the microphone, so detect this and tell the learner to open it with localhost or https. The transcription box lets learners with a speech impairment answer by typing directly, but records produced this way are marked as written output

kcSignals: component is strategic or activity, and involves spoken production, self-correction or gaining time (such as kt:en-str-self-correct, kt:en-str-gain-time, kt:ja-str-aizuchi, kt:zh-str-paraphrase)
itemTypes include situated-production-spoken
commonErrors describe production-process problems such as "carrying first-language fillers over", "long silences", "reading a script word for word"
learnerSignals: After speaking, does not know what they said
Gets stuck as soon as they open their mouth
"My speaking is bad"
contraindications: The learner cannot yet write or type in the target-language script
Do not use it when pronunciation or tone is to be evaluated: this primitive only records and compares, and gives no score
If the learner is clearly anxious about recording, use a written version without recording first

rules: The transcript must be at least 30 words (Japanese counted by mora, Chinese by character), or it is treated as not done (blocks an answer that is too weak)
Every prepared chunk needs a lenient matching regular expression, and the model answer given in the hint must pass it, otherwise using the chunk would not count

Rewritten sentence: it must change at least a set number of words, which blocks swapping three words and submitting; and the longest sentence must not exceed the limit and must not contain written-style connectives, which blocks turning speech into an essay
Warn when the transcript is too fluent: a 60-second recording with a transcript that has no repetition and no fillers prompts "what you typed may be what you meant to say, not what you said"
check.independence: The transcription box does not appear before recording ends. Before recording the chunks can be glanced at only once, and are folded away when recording starts. Opening the model answer before rewriting is recorded as completed after hint

evidence.retained: The learner's own transcript, chunk hits, the learner's self-judged class for each excerpt, and the rewritten sentence. The recording itself is not saved

licensed.claim: can recognize one class of problem in their own transcript (for example first-language word order carried over)
can use the prepared chunks in timed spoken production

prohibited: Any judgment of whether the pronunciation is good
Taking the learner's transcript as an accurate record of what was actually said (the learner may tidy it up)
Judging speaking level from one recording
Recording "restart" as an error

hints: Replay this stretch of the recording
Show the definitions of the five classes and a sample excerpt
Give the direction for fixing this class
scaffold.fade: After two recordings in a row in which the learner's self-judged classes match the reference labels, stop showing the class definitions

primitives.reverseHalf: A restart is not a fault: changing route halfway to get the meaning across is something only people who can hold up a real conversation do. If you teach "speak fluently", some people will memorize scripts, and a person who memorizes a script collapses as soon as they are interrupted. A "restart" excerpt gets no fix, and the explanation must be thorough. Also, not every filler should be cut: a moderate amount of well, えーと, 那个 is a normal part of conversation, and it is a problem only when it crowds out content.

failureModes.failure: The learner writes in the transcript what they meant to say, not what they said
failureModes.mitigation: The learner can replay segment by segment while transcribing, and is prompted to "type out the um too". Warn when the ratio of duration to word count is abnormal
failureModes.test: A transcript with no fillers and no repetition paired with a 60-second recording must trigger the warning

failureModes.failure: The implementer plugs in automatic speech recognition instead of self-transcription
failureModes.mitigation: The contract says no recognition is done; the value lies in the learner hearing themselves
failureModes.test: The page must not call any speech recognition interface

failureModes.failure: The rewrite turns into a long written-style sentence
failureModes.mitigation: A longest-sentence limit plus a blacklist of written-style connectives
failureModes.test: Build a 30-word rewrite containing moreover; it should be caught by these two rules only, and not wrongly caught by any other rule

failureModes.failure: Microphone permission is unavailable and the page is blank
failureModes.mitigation: Detect the permission and explain how to open the page
failureModes.test: When opened from a local file, show explanatory text and not a blank page

stacksWith.how: Look at the pause curve of the same recording on the timeline first, then transcribe it, and see whether the places where you got stuck are the places where the rhythm broke
The transcript is the learner's own draft: fix one of the five classes at a time
The prompt's chunks come from the chunk book, and whether they were used is written back to the chunk book's usage record

languages.en: The five classes chunk/restart/filler/stuck/zh are locked (c55). Filler means um/like/you know. First-language word order, such as *I every day at home study English. The rewritten sentence is ≤18 words and must not contain furthermore/moreover. Existing implementation c55
languages.ja: The transcript can use kana only, or mixed kana and kanji, with length counted in moras. Fillers are えーと, あのー, なんか. The typical "first-language word order" class is a particle put in front or dropped (*で駅待ちます, *友達映画を見ます). ja adds one more class, "register drift" (mixing です・ます and だ in one passage). Written-style blacklist: しかしながら, したがって, すなわち
languages.zh: English-speaking learners can transcribe with toned pinyin or characters. Whether tones are right is outside this primitive and goes to prim:contour-match. Fillers are 那个, 就是, 嗯. The typical "first-language word order" class is an adverbial put after the verb (*我学习汉语在家), a modifier put after its noun, or a time word placed at the end of the sentence. Written-style blacklist: 综上所述, 由此可见, 与此同时

primitives.name: Sound–spelling blending
primitives.oneLine: Map each letter, kana or pinyin unit to its sound, blend them into a word, then spell by sound in the other direction
primitives.difficulty: The learner can say the sound of each letter, kana or pinyin unit one at a time, but cannot join them into a word. They read cat as "ke-a-te", read words with letter names, read English letters by pinyin (c read as ci), and add a vowel after a consonant. They read si and tu as し and つ. English native speakers read pinyin x q c as English. Chinese heritage children can say "苹果", but when they see píngguǒ it does not match the word in their own mouth. In the other direction, they hear a word and cannot spell it.
primitives.object: A strip of sound cells: one word is cut into phoneme units, one block per cell (a letter or letter group, a kana, or the initial / final / tone of pinyin), with a blending slide below. The learner reads, swaps a cell, and then spells, all on the same strip
primitives.requires: Needs media (real-speaker recordings of each block's sound and of the whole word; an isolated sound must not carry an added vowel, for example /b/ must not be recorded as "buh"). The learner can already discriminate the contrasts involved in the cells (if not, adults fall back to prim:sound-contrast first; children who cannot yet split and blend phonemes without looking at the letters fall back to prim:oral-sound-play first). The read-aloud check needs a partner, which is optional
learnerAction: Step 1 Blend: tap each block to hear its sound, then slide a finger from left to right so the cells light up in turn and the sounds join; then tap which word it is from three pictures

Step 2 Swap a block: the system swaps one block (cat→cot→cut, か→が, mā→mǎ, bā→pā). The learner first decides what the new word is, with locked options: a real word (tap the picture) / can be read but is not a word (nonword) / after the swap it does not follow the rule. The last option is the reverse half, such as said, one, the particle は read as wa, and the u in ju being ü
Step 3 Spell in reverse: hear a word (including some nonwords) and drag blocks from the block bank to build it. Children can instead choose the missing block from three
systemResponse: As the learner slides, the cells light up in turn while a continuous, unbroken blended sound plays. A place where the learner paused too long gets a small gap marker on the cells, meaning the blend broke here
A wrong picture is not marked wrong. Instead the word for the chosen picture is played, and the two words' sound strips are lined up one above the other, with the differing block colored
After Step 3 is submitted, the strip the learner built is aligned block by block with the target strip. Extra, missing and swapped blocks are marked separately

ui.screen: In the middle is one large sound strip (3–6 blocks), with the blending slide below it, and three picture options below the slide. In Step 3 the area below becomes the block bank. The narrow right column is the word-card record for this round (one small card per word, marked "read right the first time / after hint / not read out")
interactions: Tap a cell to hear a single sound
Slide a finger or mouse along the slide, or hold the right arrow key to slide automatically
Number keys 1–3 choose a picture
Step 3: drag blocks or type with the keyboard (pinyin can use digits for tones)
ui.childVariant: Ages 5–7 starting English: the blocks are made as large building blocks, and only the sound of the letter is said, not its name. Each round has 5 CVC words, with pictures of familiar objects. No written instructions; use speech and animated demonstration. The blending slide is a snail crawling slowly. The read-aloud part uses a parent as listener: the screen shows the child the word, and the parent's side has only three pictures, tapping the one they heard. Chinese heritage children (ages 6–12): first play the recording or picture of a word the child can say, and have the child build the pinyin from initial, final and tone blocks, then in reverse read the pinyin and choose the picture, using speech to carry the written form. Do not teach the sounds they can already say
ui.adultVariant: When adults are catching up on blending, do not use children's pictures; take words from street signs, menus and people's names. Can show rule names (short-vowel CVC, silent e, contracted sounds, y/w spelling rules, iou→iu abbreviation). Japanese kana are used to break dependence on romaji, so the romaji layer is off by default
ui.accessibility: Blocks can be enlarged. Vowel and consonant blocks are distinguished by shape as well as color. All operations can be done by keyboard. Learners with a reading disorder can extend the sliding time, and nothing is timed

kcSignals: component is orthographic or phonological and involves the match between letters / kana / pinyin and sounds: kt:en-orth-letter-sounds, kt:en-orth-cvc-decoding, kt:en-orth-digraphs-blends, kt:en-orth-long-vowels, kt:en-orth-vowel-patterns, kt:en-orth-multisyllable, kt:en-phon-awareness, kt:ja-script-hiragana, kt:ja-script-katakana, kt:ja-script-small-kana, kt:zh-pinyin-initials-finals, kt:zh-pinyin-spelling
itemTypes include read-aloud, dictation, script-reading
commonErrors include "reads phonemes one by one and cannot join them", "spells by letter names", "reads letters by pinyin", "reads pinyin by English"
learnerSignals: Can read each sound one at a time, but gets stuck when joining them
Reads words they recognize, and guesses new words
In dictation cannot write the whole word, only the first letter
contraindications: Do not blend until the learner can discriminate the contrasts in the cells
High-frequency irregular words (said, the) cannot be used as forward blending items and can go only in the reverse half
Learners who can already read fluently do not need block-by-block blending and go straight to prim:reading-aid-fade

rules: Picture distractors differ from the target by only one block (cat / cot / cap), so someone who guesses from the first letter fails (blocks gaming)
In Step 3 at least one third are nonwords (blick, ぬて), so spellings memorized as whole words cannot pass (blocks gaming)
Step 3 is scored by block alignment, and a word passes only if the whole word is right; getting half the blocks right does not count (blocks an answer that is too weak)
Read-aloud items are blind-chosen by a parent or partner, and "read out" is recorded only if the target is chosen 3 times out of 3
check.independence: The first picture choice on each word is saved before any hint. The number of times a single block was tapped to hear it again before answering is recorded on the word card. An answer given after hearing the whole-word recording is recorded as after hint. A respelling in Step 3 after seeing the target strip is recorded as completed after hint

evidence.retained: Kept on each word card: the first picture choice, the number of single-block replays, where pauses occurred during the slide, the Step 2 classification, the first spelling in Step 3 and its alignment differences, and the listener's choice on read-aloud items

licensed.claim: can blend unseen real words by this set of mapping rules
can spell nonwords they hear by this set of rules
knows which common words do not follow this set of rules

prohibited: Inferring the ability to read aloud from correct picture choices
Inferring mastery of the blending rules from correct reading of familiar words
Treating the parent listener's judgment as a pronunciation score
Inferring the ability to understand sentences from the ability to blend

hints: Only let the learner tap the hardest block once more
Slow down the sliding speed and carry the learner through once automatically
Play the whole-word recording (answers after this are recorded as after hint)
scaffold.fade: When the picture is chosen right on the first try for 6 new words in a row under the same rule (such as short-a CVC), with no single-block replays, the lighting animation of the blocks on the slide is turned off and the whole word appears in complete form

primitives.reverseHalf: Every round has at least one word that "cannot be read by the rule": said, one, come; the particles は・へ・を; the u in pinyin ju / qu / xu read as ü, iu as the abbreviation of iou, and Xī'ān needing the separation mark. The learner must put these in "does not follow the rule" and not force a blend

failureModes.failure: An isolated sound recording carries an added vowel (/b/ recorded as buh), and what the child learns is a spelling with the added vowel
failureModes.mitigation: Isolated sound recordings keep only the consonant itself, or use a sustained sound (mmm, sss) in place of a stop said alone
failureModes.test: Material check: the duration of each consonant's isolated recording, and no vowel at the end

failureModes.failure: The child guesses from the picture and does not look at the letters
failureModes.mitigation: All three pictures are objects of the same kind, with words differing by one block
failureModes.test: Adversarial example: hat / hot / hut pictures appear in the same round

failureModes.failure: The learner has memorized the practice words and cannot do new ones
failureModes.mitigation: Step 3 mixes in nonwords, and nonwords are counted separately from real words
failureModes.test: Check whether nonword accuracy is far below real-word accuracy

stacksWith.how: When the swapped block is one of a confusable pair (pen / pin), discrimination is done on the same sound strip at the same time
When words that passed blending go into a short text, their blending block marks and phonetic annotations are removed according to the rules
For Chinese heritage children, put the pinyin sound strip below the character cell, so the same character shows its sound and its components together
Chinese heritage children first connect a word they can say to its characters, then hang a pinyin sound strip under the same word. Pinyin is a bridge, not the target

languages.en: Rule groups: single-letter sounds → short-vowel CVC → sh/ch/th/ck and st/bl clusters → silent e and ai/ee/oa → r-controlled vowels → multisyllable splitting. Material comes from kt:en-orth-letter-sounds, kt:en-orth-cvc-decoding, kt:en-orth-digraphs-blends, kt:en-orth-long-vowels, kt:en-orth-multisyllable. Trap: Chinese learners read letters by pinyin (c read as ci, e read as ê), and isolated sound recordings must avoid this
languages.ja: Rule groups: the basic gojūon → voiced and semi-voiced sounds → contracted sounds → geminate → long vowel → the katakana long-vowel mark and loanword sounds. Material comes from kt:ja-script-hiragana, kt:ja-script-dakuten, kt:ja-script-small-kana, kt:ja-script-katakana. Trap: Chinese learners read romaji by Hanyu Pinyin (si, tu), so romaji is not shown under the kana strip by default
languages.zh: Rule groups: the three blocks initial + final + tone, then y/w, dropping the dots on ü, the abbreviations iou/uei/uen, and the separation mark. Material comes from kt:zh-pinyin-initials-finals, kt:zh-pinyin-spelling. The trap for English-speaking adults is reading x q c z as English. For Chinese heritage children, all the words are taken from words they can already say, and the aim is to match the written form. For these children, the main line for recognizing characters is in prim:oral-to-print, and this primitive is responsible only for pinyin

primitives.name: Character anatomy
primitives.oneLine: Split a Chinese character, kana or Latin letter into components and strokes, use the components to guess meaning and sound, then write it by stroke order, direction and ruled lines
primitives.difficulty: The learner copies characters, kana or letters as whole pictures. Stroke order is arbitrary ("国" is closed off first), look-alike components are mixed up (氵/冫, 亻/彳, 己/已), and the phonetic component is taken to be the exact reading ("江" read as gōng). Chinese learners of Japanese write 東 as 东 and 気 as 气, and reverse the stroke direction of シ and ツ, ソ and ン. Japanese native speakers learning Chinese write Japanese forms such as 単 and 歩. English beginners aged 5–7 mirror b/d and p/q, make all lowercase letters the same height with no ascenders or descenders, and start strokes anywhere in any direction (o drawn clockwise from the bottom). They leave no space between words, or give each letter one square. Characters are learned one by one, so a new character cannot be guessed for either meaning or sound.
primitives.object: One enlarged writing cell (Chinese characters use a 米 grid or 田 grid, kana use a square grid, Latin letters use four-line ruled paper). The character is already split into colored blocks by component or stroke, and each block can be opened. The side panel is the "same-component family" (for letters, the "same-starting-stroke family": c-a-d-g-o-q all start from the "curl of c"). For this one character the learner first splits it, then reasons by analogy from the components, and finally writes it by stroke order, direction and ruled lines, leaving their own handwriting on the cell
primitives.requires: Needs stroke-order and component data for the writing system (for Chinese characters and kana use open data such as KanjiVG or Make Me a Hanzi, with each licence checked one by one; stroke orders must not be invented. For Latin letters follow the type specification of the teaching materials used: print or pre-cursive style must be chosen in advance, and the page states which). Handwriting needs a touch screen or mouse, or the learner can write on paper and check themselves. The learner already knows at least two characters in the side-panel family (for letters, already recognizes the shapes of these letters), otherwise there is no basis for analogy
learnerAction: Step 1 Split: draw frames around the components on the character and attach a role to each component: meaning class (semantic component) / sound clue (phonetic component) / just a mark. For Latin letters, split into basic strokes instead (vertical line, curl, arc, diagonal) and attach "is the vertical on the left or right" and "which zones it occupies: middle zone / ascends to the sky zone / descends to the underground zone"

Step 2 Reason by analogy from components: look at an unlearned character with the same component, first choose its approximate meaning class, then judge its sound, with locked options: same sound as the phonetic / differs only in tone / initial or final differs / the phonetic no longer hints at the sound. The last option is the reverse half (江, 特, 海). The same step also has discrimination of look-alike pairs (己/已, 冫/氵, シ/ツ). Step 2 for Latin letters is discrimination of mirror images and height: show four orientations of one letter (b d p q) or three height positions, and choose which one is the target letter. The reverse half is "looks like the same orientation but is not the same letter" (n/u is a flip, not a mirror; i/j differ only in the descender)

Step 3 Write from memory: in the blank cell write the character by stroke order (or a member of a learned family), and the system checks stroke order, starting point and direction stroke by stroke. For Latin letters it also checks whether the letter lands in the correct ruled zone. A learner writing on paper watches the stroke-order animation and ticks each stroke themselves
systemResponse: After the components are framed, the side-panel family immediately filters the learned characters by that component. Characters with the same meaning class or sound light up, and exceptions are shown with a dotted outline
After an answer in Step 2, the real sound and meaning of the new character are revealed, and the label on the component is updated to "this time the clue helped / partly helped / failed"

In Step 3, for each stroke whose direction, order or starting point differs from the data, the stroke turns gray and a small dot appears at the correct start. When a Latin letter goes outside its ruled zone, the part that goes beyond is colored on the four lines (for example, the vertical of b does not reach into the sky zone). After writing, the learner's handwriting is overlaid on the standard form, and differences in structure and proportion (left and right parts separated, top and bottom squeezed, letters all the same height) are marked with frames

ui.screen: On the left is a large writing cell (米 grid, 田 grid or four-line paper; the four lines are shown in three color zones: sky, grass, underground). In the middle is a row of component or stroke label buttons. On the right is the family column. In Step 3 the cell becomes a blank writing area, and the stroke-order animation button is available only after submitting or after requesting a hint
interactions: Drag a frame or tap to select components
Number keys choose the role label
Write with finger / stylus / mouse; Ctrl+Z undoes one stroke (undo count is recorded)
Paper mode: after each stroke animation, tap "I wrote this stroke right / wrong"
ui.childVariant: English ages 5–7 (main focus): the four-line paper is drawn as three layers, sky, grass and underground. Letters are sorted into three groups: "tall" (b d h k l t), "small" (a c e o …) and "sinking" (g j p q y), and the child sorts the letter into a group before writing it. Starting-stroke rules are taught by family: the "curl-c family" starts counterclockwise from the starting point of c (c a d g o q), and the "vertical-stick family" goes top to bottom (b h k l). b/d are told apart by "write the vertical stick first or the round belly first", helped by the left-and-right-hand "bed" gesture. Each letter has three levels of tracing, faded step by step (full shadow → only starting point and arrow → empty cell), and the child drops one level only after writing it right twice in a row at each level. When writing words, a finger width is left between words. Chinese heritage children (ages 6–12): radicals are made into "family" character cards (the three-dots-water family are all about water). First use spelling blocks to build 氵 + 每 into 海, then guess new characters of the same family. Writing uses the same three levels of tracing. Chinese ages 5–7: only 6–10 basic strokes and single-component characters, the finger writes in a large cell, and each stroke has a sound cue
ui.adultVariant: Chinese learners of Japanese: the focus is comparing the Chinese and Japanese forms of the same character (東/东, 気/气, 単/单) and the stroke direction of シ/ツ and ソ/ン. Can show the relation between on'yomi / kun'yomi and the phonetic component. English-speaking adults learning Chinese: components are memory hooks, with a reminder that the phonetic of a phono-semantic character is not always reliable. Adult English handwriting generally does not need this primitive, and it is used only when writing height and word spacing clearly affect legibility
ui.accessibility: Components are distinguished by color plus number. The writing cell can be enlarged. A learner who cannot write can do only Steps 1 and 2 and complete Step 3 by choosing stroke-order cards, recorded separately

kcSignals: component is orthographic and involves character shape or writing: kt:zh-hanzi-strokes, kt:zh-hanzi-components, kt:zh-hanzi-l1 to l7, kt:ja-kanji-system, kt:ja-kanji-n5 to n2, kt:ja-script-hiragana, kt:ja-script-katakana, the upper- and lowercase writing part of kt:en-orth-handwriting and kt:en-orth-alphabet
commonErrors include "confusing look-alike characters", "arbitrary stroke order", "writing simplified forms or Japanese forms", "treating the phonetic as the exact sound", "b/d written reversed"
itemTypes include script-writing, script-reading, match
learnerSignals: Memorizes characters one by one and has no way into a new character
Writes like tracing, with a different stroke order each time
Submitted work mixes Chinese and Japanese forms
contraindications: Without checked stroke-order data, do not do the stroke-by-stroke check in Step 3, and do only paper self-checking
For targets that need only recognition, not writing (most characters above level 3, recognition of common characters), Step 3 is not required
Component clues must not be treated as etymology, and folk etymology stories do not enter the page

Stroke order and starting-stroke rules for Latin letters vary by school and typeface, so another convention must not be marked wrong. Check only against the one chosen on the page, and let the teacher switch it

rules: In each round of Step 2 at least one third of the characters have a failed or only approximate phonetic, so always choosing "same sound as the phonetic" fails (blocks gaming)
The meaning-class judgment and the sound judgment are counted separately, and getting only one right does not count as a hit (blocks an answer that is too weak)

In Step 3, order, starting point and direction are checked stroke by stroke. A wrong stroke count, or two or more order errors, does not pass; but crooked stroke shapes and imperfect proportions are not marked wrong (the card is too strict otherwise)

Latin letters: b/d/p/q are each written at least twice in the same round, and all four must be right to pass the mirror stage (this catches memorizing only one orientation). The height check is judged by ruled zone, not by pixel
Look-alike pair discrimination must be right on both sides: at least two items each for 己/已 and b/d
check.independence: Step 3 is by default a blank cell written from memory, and the first handwriting is kept. Writing after watching the stroke-order animation or with tracing turned on is recorded as completed after hint. Undo counts and whether each stroke was corrected by system prompt are both recorded

evidence.retained: Kept on each cell: component frames and role labels, the guess and reveal result in Step 2, the first handwriting in Step 3, the position of each stroke correction, and the tracing level

licensed.claim: can match common semantic components to meaning classes
can write this set of characters independently by the standard stroke order
knows when the phonetic is unreliable
can write b/d/p/q independently with correct orientation

prohibited: Inferring that the learner can read or understand a character from the fact that they can write it
Inferring independent writing from correct tracing
Inferring that the learner knows the character from correct component guessing
Treating how attractive the handwriting is as the level of mastery

hints: Only ask "in which character have you seen the part on the left of this one?"
Highlight in the family column a learned character with the same phonetic and the same sound
Play the stroke-order animation or turn on tracing (recorded as after hint afterwards)
scaffold.fade: Tracing fades in three levels: when a character is written right twice in a row at the current level with no correction, drop one level. Once at the empty-cell level, the family column is no longer shown by default for new characters of the same family, and the learner must call it up themselves

primitives.reverseHalf: Component clues have limits: characters whose phonetic has failed (江, 特, 海), characters whose semantic class has blurred (the 牛 radical in 特), the same component written differently in Chinese and Japanese or in simplified and traditional forms (东/東, 单/単), and exceptions to the general stroke-order rules (必, 火). The learner must put these in "clue failed" and not apply the rule by force

failureModes.failure: The learner chooses "same sound" whenever they see a familiar component
failureModes.mitigation: Items with a failed phonetic make up more than one third, and are counted separately
failureModes.test: Adversarial example: 江, 红, 空, 功 mixed together with the same phonetic

failureModes.failure: Handwriting recognition is too strict, marks readable characters wrong and discourages children
failureModes.mitigation: Check only stroke order and direction, and be lenient on stroke shape
failureModes.test: Replay sample handwriting from different writers and check the false-judgment rate

failureModes.failure: The stroke-order data itself does not match the standard (Chinese and Japanese standards differ)
failureModes.mitigation: Chinese follows the Modern Chinese Common Characters Stroke Order Standard (《现代汉语通用字笔顺规范》), Japanese follows the stroke orders in common use in Japanese school teaching, and the data source and version are written on the page
failureModes.test: Spot-check characters whose stroke orders differ between Chinese and Japanese, such as 必, 右, 左

failureModes.failure: The child remembers the orientation of b, but d, p and q are still random
failureModes.mitigation: Mix the four letters, and tell them apart by the same starting-stroke rule (d belongs to the curl-c family, b belongs to the vertical-stick family)
failureModes.test: Adversarial example: the target letters in bed, dog, pig, queen appear one after another, and the mirror rate is counted for each letter separately

stacksWith.how: Chinese: the pinyin sound strip hangs below the character cell, so the same character is split by shape and blended by sound at the same time
For a character misread after annotation is removed in a short text, one tap expands it into a cell, and it is split directly at its place in the original
Component splitting at character level and morpheme splitting at word level are placed on the same word: first split "教室" into 教 + 室, then split the components of 室
After Chinese heritage children connect a word they can say to its characters, the same character is split into components and writing is practiced directly in the cell

languages.en: The object is Latin-letter handwriting: upper- and lowercase forms, basic strokes and starting directions (the c family starts counterclockwise, vertical sticks go top to bottom), the three heights in four-line paper (middle, ascender, descender), the b/d/p/q mirrors and the n/u flip, and spaces between words. Material comes from kt:en-orth-handwriting, kt:en-orth-alphabet. The main learners are children aged 5–7 and 8–12. Step 2 is not guessing meaning from components but discriminating mirror images and height. Trap: Chinese children, influenced by square-grid exercise books, give each letter one square and make letters the same height
languages.ja: Targets: look-alike kana (ぬ/め, ね/れ/わ, シ/ツ, ソ/ン), kanji radicals and phonetics in on'yomi, and Chinese-Japanese form differences (東/东, 気/气, 図/图). Material comes from kt:ja-script-hiragana, kt:ja-script-katakana, kt:ja-kanji-system, kt:ja-kanji-n5 to n2. Trap: recognition is not hard for Chinese learners, but writing most easily gets mixed with simplified forms, so Step 3 is the focus
languages.zh: Targets: basic strokes and stroke order, common radicals (氵亻口木讠), reliability of the phonetic in phono-semantic characters, look-alike characters (己/已, 日/目, 人/入). Material comes from kt:zh-hanzi-strokes, kt:zh-hanzi-components, kt:zh-hanzi-l1 to l7. For Japanese native speakers, check Japanese forms in particular (単, 歩, 対). Chinese heritage children are the main users

primitives.name: Reading-aid fading
primitives.oneLine: Remove the reading aid (kana / pinyin / phonetic symbols) from the same material character by character as the learner gains mastery, and tell apart reading right with the aid from reading right without it
primitives.difficulty: The learner reads smoothly with the aid and cannot read once it is removed, and neither the teacher nor the learner can tell whether a correct reading came from the character or from the aid. English native speakers who have long relied on pinyin cannot recognize characters shown without it. Chinese heritage children read only picture books with pinyin. Learners of Japanese cannot do without furigana. English beginners read by tapping pictures and phonetic symbols. Removing everything at once is too hard, and never removing it builds dependence.
primitives.object: A short passage (3–8 sentences, or one picture-book page), with a layer of reading aid above each target word (pinyin, kana, or for English beginners the sound-button dots and lines or pictures). At the level of each character this layer has three states: shown / shown after one tap / removed. The same passage comes back in later rounds with changed aid states
primitives.requires: The learner can read the aid itself (pinyin, kana and sound-button dots have passed prim:sound-spelling-blend). Most words in the material have been seen by the learner. The read-aloud check needs a partner, which is optional. Needs reliable per-character aid data, and polyphonic characters must be checked by hand
learnerAction: Step 1 Blind read first: the aid is hidden by default and the learner reads the whole passage. For a character they cannot read, they can tap to peek (peeks are recorded). After reading, the system picks a few target characters at random, and before seeing the aid the learner types the reading (pinyin can use digits for tones, kana typed directly) or chooses from three readings

Step 2 Classify the places read wrong: for each character peeked at or read wrong, the locked options are: do not know this character / know it but tone or long-short sound is wrong / chose the wrong reading of a polyphonic character / confused on'yomi and kun'yomi. The last class, "know the character, but the reading is special here", is the reverse half (还 in 还书, 大人 おとな, 一 in 一个)

Step 3 Read another passage: the system gives a new passage that reuses these characters but removes the aid according to state. After reading, the learner answers a meaning question that can be answered correctly only if these characters are understood, and types the readings of two or three of the characters
systemResponse: The aid state of each character changes with the learner's performance: read right without peeking in two different rounds → aid removed by default; peeked at or read wrong → aid shown again. Above the passage it shows "characters still with aid in this passage", and the number drops over rounds

After the spot-check answers, characters answered wrong are underlined in the original. When opened, a word that contains the same character and that the learner has already read right is shown beside the reading, for comparison

In Step 3, when a character whose aid was removed is read right, it moves in the personal character list from "read right with aid" to "read right without aid", and the two columns are shown separately

ui.screen: The passage is centered in large type. The aid layer is above the characters (on the right for vertical Japanese). A character with hidden aid has a very faint dot below it to show it can be tapped. At the top is a count such as "characters with aid: 12 → 7". The right column is the personal character list with two columns: read right with aid / read right without aid
interactions: Tap a character, or use the arrow keys plus Enter, to peek at the aid (recorded)
On a spot-check, type the reading directly and press Enter to submit
Long-press a character to open its character cell (links to prim:character-anatomy)
One-tap show of the whole passage's aid is for checking after reading only; once turned on, answers in this round no longer count as independent
ui.childVariant: Chinese heritage children (ages 6–12): a picture-book page. The pinyin on each character is like a sticker, and a character read right twice has its sticker "fly away" into a little notebook. Read-aloud uses a parent as listener: the parent's side shows only the characters and three reading options, and the parent taps which one the child read. English ages 5–7: the aid layer is sound-button dots and lines (one dot per sound, one line for a letter group) and pictures. Remove the dots and lines first and the pictures last. After reading, first say what the page is about, then turn over the pictures to check
ui.adultVariant: Japanese adults: furigana is shown only for kanji they have not mastered, and when news or manuals are imported, furigana is removed automatically from characters already mastered. Chinese adults: can choose an intermediate state that removes only tone marks and keeps the pinyin letters. The list "read right without aid" can be exported
ui.accessibility: The font size of the aid can be adjusted independently. State is not shown by color alone: a character that has been peeked at has a corner mark. Screen-reader users can read the material itself character by character, but no recognition evidence is recorded in that case

kcSignals: component is orthographic and itemTypes include script-reading, read-aloud: kt:zh-hanzi-l1 to l7, kt:ja-kanji-n5 to n2, kt:ja-kanji-joyo
commonErrors include "long-term dependence on pinyin, cannot recognize characters without pinyin", "misreading polyphonic characters", "reading jukujikun character by character"
English beginners: kt:en-orth-cvc-decoding and kt:en-orth-sight-words entering the short-text reading stage
learnerSignals: "Can read it with pinyin, don't know it without"
When reading the text, the eyes look only at the aid line
When the teacher asks to remove the aid, the learner is clearly anxious or refuses to read
contraindications: Do not remove the aid while the aid itself is still read inaccurately (go back to prim:sound-spelling-blend first)
Not suitable when more than 30% of the characters in the material are new; change to easier material
Names of people and places, low-frequency proper names and jukujikun may keep their aid permanently and do not count toward the removal target
Never judge the accuracy of reading aloud by machine

rules: Spot-check characters are drawn at random, including both characters peeked at and not peeked at, and must be answered before the aid is shown (blocks gaming)

Distractors in multiple-choice items are the readings of characters with the same phonetic and another reading of the same character, so the answer cannot be guessed roughly from the shape (blocks an answer that is too weak)
Removing the aid needs reading right without peeking in two different rounds (at least one day apart); one correct reading does not remove it
The Step 3 meaning question can be answered correctly only by understanding the characters whose aid was removed; answering the meaning right but typing the reading wrong is recorded separately
check.independence: Each answer for each character carries a marker: answered after peeking / answered while the aid was shown / answered with the aid hidden and no peek. Only the last counts as independent. If the whole-passage aid was turned on in a round, no answer in that round counts as independent

evidence.retained: Kept for each character on this passage: the history of aid-state changes, the aid state and peek marker at each answer, the first typed reading, and the error class. The personal character list is divided into two columns, "read right with aid" and "read right without aid"

licensed.claim: can recognize and read this word without aid
can understand the gist of this passage without aid
