the sentence becomes unnatural once the time word is removed; such a sentence cannot be used as an item

rules: Material check: sentences must not contain time words or frequency words (one word list per language). One occurrence voids the item, because the learner would use it to bypass the form

Material check: exactly two options per item. The pointer must not contain the correct option. Across all items, at least two shortcuts are covered. In Step 3 the two sentences are identical except for the target form, and both are grammatical
Spread the position of the correct option evenly. The same meaning must not be the correct answer for three items in a row

A two-way choice has a 50% guess rate. Only when there are at least 8 correct first judgments in total, and both the first and second halves are correct, can the result be recorded as "can judge meaning from form"
check.independence: Record the first judgment of each item separately. A change of answer made after seeing the pointer counts as completed after a hint. Step 2 has no right or wrong and is not counted in any judgment

evidence.retained: The first judgment and any changed answer for each item, the counts of shortcut categories taken, and the Step 3 judgments

licensed.claim: With no other cues, can use this form to tell two meanings apart (comprehension level)
Has a habit of bypassing this form when reading (a given shortcut)

prohibited: inferring that the learner can produce this form
treating a single correct answer on a two-way choice as evidence
using Step 2 "Same for me / Not the same for me" in any ability judgment
inferring that the learner will notice the form in real reading that has time words

hints: This sentence has no time word. Only this word itself can tell you
Mark where the target form is, without explaining it
Show a minimal pair (walk/walked, 行きます/行きました, 吃了/吃过)
scaffold.fade: After 4 items in a row where a given shortcut was not taken, stop marking the position of the form

primitives.reverseHalf: Sometimes the form alone does not decide the meaning. When one form has two readings (ている can be progressive or resultant state, 了 can be completion or change of state, the English present tense can be habit or a scheduled future), the verb type or context decides. Put at least one such item in each set and say plainly "this one cannot be judged from the form alone", so the learner does not learn "one form, one meaning".

failureModes.failure: A time word gets through as a variant (the other day, 先週, 上个星期)
failureModes.mitigation: A time-word list for each language, plus manual spot checks
failureModes.test: Adversarial examples: sentences containing the other day, 先週 and 上个星期 must be flagged by the check

failureModes.failure: The first-language description of an option gives away the form (the Chinese option contains "了")
failureModes.mitigation: Options describe the situation and do not translate word for word. Options for Chinese items are written in English
failureModes.test: The option text must not contain the target form itself

failureModes.failure: The guess rate of a two-way choice lets chance success be taken as mastery
failureModes.mitigation: At least 8 observations, with the first and second halves consistent
failureModes.test: In a simulation of 1000 random-answer runs, fewer than 5% are judged "can judge meaning from form"

stacksWith.how: After the same set of context cards is understood, switch directly to production items that choose the form by intent
Next to the meaning judgment on a tense-aspect form, show a timeline at the same time, with each of the two options matching one interval
Judgments on particles and case markers show on a scene picture who did what to whom

languages.en: Four locked shortcut categories: endings/timeword/firstnoun/chinese (c13). Target forms: -ed, third-person -s, present perfect, be + past participle passive, plural -s. For the time-word regex see check.mjs in c13. Existing implementation: c13
languages.ja: Target forms: ます/ました; ている (progressive and resultant state: 結婚している); た/る (来たとき/来るとき); passive れる・られる; causative させる; particles が・を・に・で・は. The shortcuts become: reading only the stem and not the ending; skipping the verb when a time word is present (delete 昨日, 毎日, もう, まだ); assigning roles by word order and ignoring the particles (猫を犬が追いかけた, 先生に褒められた); mapping onto Chinese (treating every ている as "in progress", and both あげる and くれる as "give")
languages.zh: The learner is a native English speaker, and the options describe the situation in English. Target forms: 了 (completion or change), 过 (experience), 着 (durative), 在/正在, 把/被, resultative complements (找了 vs 找到了), 是…的. The shortcuts become: skipping the particles (了, 过, 着); ignoring the verb when a time word is present (delete 昨天, 已经, 每天, 以前); taking the first noun as the agent (饭吃了, 我被他骗了, the 把 construction); mapping onto English (了 equals past tense, 在/正在 used with stative verbs)

primitives.name: Paradigm application
primitives.oneLine: The learner first induces the inflection rule, then applies it to words never seen before, and the system shows the rule derivation at every step
primitives.difficulty: The learner can recite the inflections of the few words in the textbook but cannot inflect a new word. Examples: treating 帰る as a Group 2 verb and producing *帰ます, *帰ない; applying the rule to 行く to get *行いて; mixing sound-change groups (*読って, *泳いて). In English: *goed, *buyed, and missed spelling rules (*makeing, *stoped, *studyed). The reverse also happens: forcing the rule onto an exception, or being able to recite the table without seeing the rule behind it.
primitives.object: A derivation card. On the left is the base form of a new word. In the middle is a row of rule-step slots (identify class → take the ending → transform → adjust spelling or sound change). On the right is the generated form. In later rounds the same word is inflected into other forms, and the card gradually grows into that word's own row of the inflection table
primitives.requires: The learner has studied at least 6 example words for this set of rules, with their forms (the ones in the textbook). Can read the word aloud (if not, go back to prim:sound-spelling-blend first). Written input only, no mic needed
learnerAction: Step 1 Induce: sort 6–8 studied "base form → inflected form" cards into groups by how they change, then choose a rule from the rule templates for each group (ending X → Y). The system does not show the rule table first

Step 2 Apply to new words: derive each word the learner has not seen. First choose the class in the class slot. The locked options are: rule class A / B / C … / whole-word exception (する, 来る, the て form of 行く, go-went) / looks like A but is actually B. The last option is the reverse half (帰る, 入る, 知る and 切る are Group 1 verbs ending in る; the past tense of read is spelled the same but pronounced differently). Then write the final form in the later slots
Step 3 Put it in a sentence: use the derived form in a sentence with a task (～てください to ask someone to do something, the past tense to tell about something yesterday). The learner types the sentence
systemResponse: As each step slot is filled, the slot shows the rule used. When the final form differs from the target, the system traces back along the derivation chain and points out the step where it went wrong: wrong class, wrong sound-change group, or a missed spelling adjustment

A derived form is written into that word's inflection row. When the next form of the same word appears, the forms already derived stay on the row, and the learner sees the sound change they share (the て form and the た form are the same)
A word judged an exception goes onto the "exception shelf" at the side of the card. Words on the exception shelf do not count as evidence of rule generalization

ui.screen: On the left, a pile of new-word cards to derive. In the middle, the derivation card (four step slots in a row). Below, the word's inflection row (dictionary form | ます form | て form | た form | ない form, or base | past | -ing | 3sg). A narrow column on the right holds the exception shelf and the rule cards the learner induced
interactions: Number keys choose the class, Tab moves to the next slot
The final form must be typed (Japanese with an input method, English typed directly)
Click a rule card to see the example words the learner used when inducing it
ui.childVariant: English, ages 5–7: an oral wug test. A new little monster appears on screen: "This is a wug. Now there are two …". The child says it, and a parent, as listener, taps which of wug / wugs / wuggies the child said. For the past tense: "Today he blicks. Yesterday he …". All new words are nonsense words, so they cannot be memorized. Ages 8–12 can do a written version (plural, -ing, -ed spelling). Chinese heritage children: reduplication of verbs and adjectives (看看, 看一看, 研究研究, 高高兴兴, 干干净净) applied to new words through picture situations
ui.adultVariant: Japanese adults: the full derivation chain, showing the verb class names and the sound-change group names. Can be split into "practise only the て form" or "practise only the ない form". English adults: irregular verbs grouped by vowel-change family (sing-sang, ring-rang; but bring-brought)
ui.accessibility: The step slots can be entered one by one with the keyboard. Japanese items can show kana or kanji plus kana. No timer is shown

kcSignals: the KC is a set of forms that change by class: kt:ja-verb-groups, kt:ja-te-form, kt:ja-plain-paradigm, kt:ja-plain-adjectives, kt:ja-potential-form, kt:ja-causative-form, kt:ja-passive-event, kt:en-irregular-past, kt:en-orth-inflection-spelling, kt:en-noun-plural, kt:en-comparatives, kt:zh-verb-reduplication
commonErrors contain regularization (*goed, *帰ます, *行いて) or class confusion (*読って)
itemTypes include transform or form-fill
learnerSignals: all the textbook example words are correct, but new words are wrong
"Which group is this verb?"
knows the inflection table very well but still gets stuck on inflection when speaking
contraindications: Do not ask for induction when the learner has not yet studied any example forms of the set

Highly irregular forms that can only be remembered one by one (the English irregular verbs that belong to no family) are not suited to derivation. Put them only on the exception shelf and switch to prim:recall-before-reveal
Choosing which form to use (when to use the て form and when the た form) is not handled here. Leave it to prim:choose-by-intent

rules: At least one third of the new words in Step 2 have not appeared in the materials at all, and the number of words per rule class is balanced (this blocks gaming: a learner who knows only one way of inflecting will fail)
Each round includes at least two words that "look like A but are actually B" (Group 1 verbs ending in る, read)
The final form must be typed and must match exactly to count as correct. Multiple choice does not count as evidence of generalization (blocks an answer that is too weak)
Record separately: class correct but final form wrong, and class wrong but final form right by chance. The latter does not count as a pass
check.independence: The final form the learner first types for each new word is saved before any traceback hint. A re-entry after seeing the derivation-chain traceback or the example words on a rule card is recorded as after a hint. A word on the exception shelf, even if written correctly, counts only as "remembered the exception", not as "generalized the rule"

evidence.retained: Kept on each word's derivation card: the first class choice, the first final form, the step where the traceback found the error, and any re-entry. Also kept: the word's inflection row, the rule cards the learner induced, and the exception shelf

licensed.claim: Can generalize this inflection rule to words never seen before
Can tell apart words that look like one class but belong to another
Can use the derived forms in a sentence

prohibited: inferring mastery of the rule from correct textbook example words
inferring the ability to inflect on the spot when speaking from correct derivation
inferring that the learner can use the rule from remembered exception words
inferring that the learner knows how the form is used from correct inflection

hints: Ask only "What is the last kana of its dictionary form?" or "Is the letter before its last letter a vowel or a consonant?"
Show the rule card the learner induced, with its example words
Show the correct class for the first step along the derivation chain (recorded afterwards as after a hint)
scaffold.fade: After 5 new words in a row of a given rule class are all correct on the first try, collapse the middle step slots of the derivation card so that only the base form and the final form remain. If the learner errs once more, restore the step slots

primitives.reverseHalf: Rules have limits. Not every verb ending in る is Group 2 (帰る, 入る). The て form of 行く is an exception, and 来る and する are whole-word exceptions. In English, read keeps its spelling but changes its pronunciation, and bring does not follow sing. Sometimes a regularized form exists in some dialects or in speech (dreamed and dreamt are both correct), and both must be accepted

failureModes.failure: The learner applies the rule mechanically by the final letters and treats every word ending in る as Group 2
failureModes.mitigation: Include Group 1 verbs ending in る in every round and count them separately
failureModes.test: Adversarial examples: mix 帰る, 切る, 走る, 知る with 食べる, 見る, 起きる

failureModes.failure: The learner has memorized the words in the item bank
failureModes.mitigation: Draw new words at random from a large word list. The English child version uses nonsense words
failureModes.test: Check the difference in accuracy between words outside the bank and words inside it

failureModes.failure: The traceback hint appears too early and the learner waits for it
failureModes.mitigation: The traceback appears only after the final form is submitted
failureModes.test: Check that a level-3 hint cannot be requested before submission

stacksWith.how: Words on the exception shelf become recall-then-check cards. The first recall is still recorded on the same word's inflection row
The derived form immediately appears in items where only the ending decides the meaning (て form request or た form past)
Once the inflection row is full, choosing which form to use for the same word is handed to choose-by-intent

languages.en: Rule groups: -s/-es and -ies, -ing (drop e, doubling), -ed (doubling, y→i), comparatives -er/-est vs more. Irregular past forms grouped by vowel family. Materials come from kt:en-orth-inflection-spelling, kt:en-irregular-past, kt:en-noun-plural, kt:en-comparatives. Trap: *more cheaper is two rules stacked, not a failure to learn the rule
languages.ja: Rule groups: verb class identification → ます form → て form / た form sound change (う・つ・る→って, む・ぶ・ぬ→んで, く→いて, ぐ→いで, す→して) → ない form (う→わない) → potential, passive and causative forms. Adjective conjugation. Materials come from kt:ja-verb-groups, kt:ja-te-form, kt:ja-plain-paradigm, kt:ja-plain-adjectives, kt:ja-potential-form, kt:ja-causative-form. Trap: when recovering the dictionary form from the ます form, the class cannot be determined from ～iます, so the dictionary form must be given
languages.zh: Chinese has little inflection, so this is used only for reduplication: verbs AA / A一A / ABAB, adjectives AABB. Materials come from kt:zh-verb-reduplication. Trap: stative and non-volitional verbs cannot be reduplicated (*是是, *知道知道); put them in the reverse half

primitives.name: Choosing between contrasting forms
primitives.oneLine: One situation offers a set of contrasting forms. The learner chooses by the meaning they want to express and sees what the other choice would change
primitives.difficulty: The learner can recite the rule but chooses the form by feel in a real context: mixing present perfect and simple past, choosing a/the by feel, remembering は and が only as "は for the subject", confusing 了 and 过. What the learner lacks is not the rule itself but the decision "which meaning do I want to express?".
primitives.object: A fixed small context (a two- or three-line dialogue or a short narration) in which one position can be filled by any form in the contrasting set
primitives.requires: Can already recognise the basic shape of every form in the contrasting set (see prim:form-for-meaning). If the learner cannot recognise the forms, go back first
learnerAction: Step 1 Choose one: read the context and one sentence, "What you want to express is …", and choose one form from the contrasting set to fill the gap

Step 2 Reverse it: keep the context, swap the chosen form for another, and judge what the meaning becomes (locked options: the time span changed / the old-new status of the information changed / the speaker's stance changed / nothing changed — the reverse half)
Step 3 Say your own: given a new situation about the learner, write or say one sentence that must use a specific item from the contrasting set
systemResponse: After the choice, highlight the affected part of the context (an interval on the timeline, a noun first mentioned earlier, the question word in a question) to show what decides the form
If the learner chose another grammatical form, do not mark it wrong. Show "Saying it this way means …", and the learner can choose again
After the form swap in Step 2, keep the original and new sentences side by side, with the changed part coloured

ui.screen: A context card on top, with the gap as a clickable slot. A row of buttons for the contrasting set below (2–4). A narrow column on the right records "which forms you chose in this set, and how many times each". No score is shown
interactions: Click or press number keys 1–4 to choose a form
Tab moves between context highlights
Step 3 can be typed or recorded (recording stays on the page)
ui.childVariant: The context becomes a picture with one sentence. The contrasting set has at most two items, marked with colours rather than terms
ui.adultVariant: Contexts come from work or daily life. Term names can be shown. Step 3 asks for two or three sentences
ui.accessibility: Highlights use both underline and colour. All buttons work from the keyboard. On phones the buttons of the contrasting set are fixed at the bottom

kcSignals: the KC is one of two or more contrasting forms (notions include aspect-*, reference-definiteness, emphasis-focus, etc.)
commonErrors contain mix-up errors of the type "used B where A is needed"
itemTypes include recognize-choice and situated-production-*
learnerSignals: knows the rule but chooses wrongly in a real situation
"Why X here and not Y?"
mixes up the same pair of forms throughout their writing
contraindications: the learner cannot yet recognise the forms in the contrasting set
when both forms are natural in the context and mean the same, it cannot be used as an item

rules: The sentence in Step 3 must use the target form (form match; blocks an answer that is too weak)

Also check that the context contains a cue that triggers the form (time word, already mentioned earlier, question word, etc.). Filling in the form when the context does not support it does not pass (blocks gaming)
When the learner chooses the same form on three items in a row and accuracy is below that form's share in the contrasting set, prompt "You may be choosing out of habit"
check.independence: The first choice in Step 1 is recorded separately. A changed choice after seeing the highlight or the "Saying it this way means …" prompt is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 shows no model sentence

evidence.retained: Each item's first choice, changed choices, trigger cues and the Step 3 self-made sentence are all kept on this set of context cards

licensed.claim: Can tell this pair of forms apart in a controlled context
Can choose the target form unprompted in the learner's own situation

prohibited: judging mastery from correct Step 1 choices alone
counting a correct change after a hint as independent mastery
treating a grammatically correct self-made sentence as proof that the right form was chosen

hints: Ask only an intent question such as "Do you mean it already happened, or that it still matters now?"
Highlight the deciding cue in the context
Show one minimal contrast example for each of the two forms
scaffold.fade: After 4 items in a row of the same contrasting set are chosen correctly on the first try, hints above level 2 no longer appear

primitives.reverseHalf: Each set has at least one item where both forms are possible and differ only in meaning. It also has one item where the cue seems to point to A but B is the right choice (for example, "已经" is present but the simple past is used; a first mention that takes the definite article because the reference is specific)

failureModes.failure: The learner chooses mechanically by marker words in the item (yesterday, もう, 已经)
failureModes.mitigation: Design items where the marker word and the correct form do not agree, and items with no marker word
failureModes.test: In the adversarial examples, one third of the items have the marker word removed or a misleading marker word inserted

failureModes.failure: The position of the options gives away the answer
failureModes.mitigation: Keep the order of the buttons in the contrasting set fixed and do not change it with the item
failureModes.test: Check that the answer positions are evenly distributed

stacksWith.how: For tense-aspect contrasts, put a timeline on the same context card. The timeline interval changes as the form is chosen
The self-made sentence from Step 3 is saved as a first draft, and is checked again later in writing by the same check

languages.en: Contrasting sets: present perfect / simple past, a / the / zero article, active / passive, will / be going to. Existing implementations: c14, c15, c20
languages.ja: Contrasting sets: は/が, ている/た, intransitive / transitive, あげる/くれる/もらう, から/ので. Note: the は/が items need two kinds of context, old-new information and contrast
languages.zh: Contrasting sets: 了/过/着, 把 construction / ordinary word order, 的/地/得, 还是/或者, 再/又. The 了 items must separate completion from change of state

primitives.name: Word-order slots
primitives.oneLine: Drag word chunks into named syntactic slots (time, place, manner, verb …). When the order is violated, point out which slot rule was broken
primitives.difficulty: The learner knows every word but arranges the sentence in first-language order. Chinese learners write *I every day at home study English, *I eat always breakfast, *I like very much music, *You are a student?, *Where you went?. English-speaking learners of Chinese write *我学习汉语每天, *我看书在家 and put modifiers after the noun. Chinese learners of Japanese put the verb in the middle or say 三つのりんご. The learner knows "it doesn't sound right" but cannot say which position rule was broken.
primitives.object: A named sentence track. The slots on the track (subject | time | place | manner | verb | object | question word | auxiliary …) are laid out in the normal word order of the language. The learner holds word-chunk cards cut from one sentence. The same track is reused across sentences, and a track in the learner's first language can be overlaid for comparison
primitives.requires: The learner knows every word in the sentence and can say roughly what each chunk means. The chunks are already cut (cutting is not the task here). No media or mic needed
learnerAction: Step 1 Order first: the track does not show slot names at first. The learner arranges the chunks into the sentence they think is correct and submits it (this ordering is saved as is). Then the slot names appear, and the learner labels each chunk with the slot it belongs to

Step 2 Judge sentences: judge the given sentences one by one. The locked options are: word order correct / violates a slot rule (choose which one) / correct in another position too but the emphasis or meaning changes — the last is the reverse half (Sometimes I walk vs I sometimes walk, 明天我去 vs 我明天去; in Japanese, with case particles the order is fairly free but the predicate must be sentence-final)
Step 3 Make your own: write one sentence about this week that includes at least three kinds of slot, then label the slots of your own sentence by hand
systemResponse: After the slot names are attached, a curved arrow appears between the two chunks that break the order, with the violated rule written on it ("time and place come before the verb", "frequency adverbs go before the main verb and after be", "in questions the auxiliary comes before the subject")

The first-language track can be expanded. The Chinese track and the English track sit one above the other, and lines connect the position of the same chunk on both tracks, so the learner sees which track they followed

When the learner picks "correct in another position too" in Step 2, the two versions of the sentence appear side by side with the changed part coloured, and the change in emphasis or meaning is shown, instead of marking right or wrong

ui.screen: A horizontal track in the middle, with slots as cells with different background colours. The word-chunk cards to arrange are above. The first-language comparison track can be expanded below. A narrow column on the right lists the rules violated this round and how many times. No score is shown
interactions: Drag chunks to slots, or select a chunk and move it with the left and right arrow keys
Number keys attach slot names to chunks
In Step 3, type the sentence, then use the mouse or Tab to select a part of your own sentence and attach a slot name
Space expands or collapses the first-language track
ui.childVariant: Ages 8–12, English: the track is a little train with fixed carriage colours (who | does what | what | where | when), and the chunks are passengers. Ages 5–7 do not do the written version. Use picture sentences instead: the child puts three pictures (girl / eat / apple) into the carriages in the order of the sentence they hear, and the parent says the sentence. Chinese heritage children already have mostly correct spoken word order and use this only for long written sentences (multiple layers of attributives or adverbials). The track becomes "attributives in a queue": 我们学校｜那两位｜从北京来的｜年轻｜汉语｜老师
ui.adultVariant: Sentences come from work email and reports. Slot names can use terms. English adults focus on question inversion, restoring statement order in indirect questions, and the order of frequency adverbs and adverbials. Japanese adults focus on the sentence-final predicate and the position of quantity words
ui.accessibility: Slots are marked by both text name and background colour. Drag and drop has a full keyboard alternative. Screen readers read each chunk by its slot name

kcSignals: notions include time-location, space-location, questioning, or the KC title contains word order or position: kt:zh-time-word-order, kt:zh-complex-attributives, kt:zh-phrase-types, kt:en-word-order-svo, kt:en-adverbial-phrases, kt:en-adverbs-frequency, kt:en-be-questions, kt:en-do-questions, kt:en-wh-questions, kt:en-past-questions, kt:en-subject-questions, kt:en-embedded-questions, quantity-word position in kt:ja-counters, kt:ja-relative-clause
commonErrors contain "follows Chinese word order", "put at the end of the sentence", "keeps statement order", "modifier placed after"
learnerSignals: the words are right but the order is wrong
"I feel something is wrong but can't say what"
the same kind of word-order error recurs in writing
contraindications: do not use when the sentence has words the learner does not know
where word order is truly free and only affects information structure, it cannot be made into a right/wrong item. It can only go into the "correct in another position too" option in Step 2
choosing which structure to use (the 把 construction or ordinary order) is not handled here. Leave it to prim:choose-by-intent

rules: In Step 1 the first ordering must be submitted before the slot names are shown, and only then are labels attached (blocks gaming if the learner can see the slot names before ordering)

In each round of Step 2, at least a quarter of the sentences are "correct in another position too", plus one sentence that looks like first-language order on the surface but is in fact correct (Sometimes I…). A learner who marks every such sentence wrong will fail

The learner's own labels in Step 3 are spot-checked. The time slot must contain a word from the time-word list or a number plus a time unit. The place slot must begin with at/in/在/で/に etc. A label that does not fit its content does not pass (blocks gaming). The sentence needs at least three kinds of slot (blocks an answer that is too weak)
check.independence: The first ordering in Step 1, made without slot names, is saved separately and is the most important evidence for this primitive. A reorder after seeing the arrow rule or the first-language track is recorded as after a hint. Step 3 shows no track, and shows it only after the learner has attached labels

evidence.retained: Kept on the track for each sentence: the first ordering without slot names, the slot labels attached, the violated rule, and the reordering process. Also kept: the Step 3 self-made sentence and self-attached labels, and the running count of rules violated this round

licensed.claim: Can order controlled chunks by this slot rule
Can tell a word-order error from an order change that only shifts emphasis
Orders words by this rule when making their own sentences

prohibited: inferring independent ordering from correct reordering after labels were attached
inferring correct word order in free writing or speaking from correct chunk dragging
judging an acceptable word-order variant as wrong

hints: Ask only "Does this chunk answer 'when', 'where' or 'how'?"
Show the slot names (after the first ordering is saved)
Expand the first-language comparison track and show which track the learner followed
scaffold.fade: After 5 sentences in a row of the same rule are ordered correctly on the first try without slot names, the slot names on the track are no longer shown by default and the first-language track is collapsed. After two consecutive passes of the label spot-check in Step 3, labels are no longer required

primitives.reverseHalf: There is more than one possible order. sometimes and 明天 can go at the start of the sentence with little change in meaning. In Japanese, once the case particles are in place the order is fairly flexible, but the predicate must be sentence-final. In English, a frequency phrase such as every day or twice a week goes at the end of the sentence, while a frequency adverb does not. In Chinese, an expression of duration goes after the verb (我学了两年)

failureModes.failure: The learner looks at the slot names before ordering, so the first ordering loses its meaning
failureModes.mitigation: Show the slot names only after the first submission
failureModes.test: Check that the interface before submission does not contain slot names

failureModes.failure: The learner learns "time always goes at the end of the sentence" and then errs the other way in Chinese
failureModes.mitigation: For multilingual learners, the track shows the name of the current language. Step 2 mixes in items contrasting duration complements with time adverbials
failureModes.test: Adversarial examples: 我每天学习两个小时 / 我学习两个小时每天

failureModes.failure: The learner attaches labels at random to pass the check
failureModes.mitigation: Spot-check labels against word lists
failureModes.test: Simulate labelling a place phrase as time, and check that it is blocked

stacksWith.how: Where a modifier attaches and the slot order are on the same track: move the same chunk to another slot and see how the meaning changes
Quantity chunks enter the track. The Japanese quantity position (りんごを三つ) and the Chinese one (三个苹果) are compared on the same sentence
Short sentences from a split long sentence are first ordered on the track and then combined, and the slots of the combined sentence are kept

languages.en: Rules: SVO, and the copula cannot be dropped; manner-place-time order of adverbials; frequency adverbs before the main verb and after be; auxiliary fronting in yes/no and wh-questions; no do in subject questions; statement order restored in indirect questions. Materials come from kt:en-word-order-svo, kt:en-adverbial-phrases, kt:en-adverbs-frequency, kt:en-be-questions, kt:en-do-questions, kt:en-past-questions, kt:en-subject-questions, kt:en-embedded-questions. Trap: You are a student? can be said in speech, so state that the written requirement applies
languages.ja: Rules: sentence-final predicate; modifiers (including prenominal clauses) before the noun; quantity word after the case particle and before the verb (りんごを三つ買う); with case particles the order is fairly free. Materials come from kt:ja-counters, kt:ja-relative-clause, kt:ja-te-sequence. Trap: Japanese word order is flexible, so the share of "correct in another position too" in Step 2 should be higher than for English and Chinese
languages.zh: Rules: time and place come before the verb, with time first and going from larger to smaller; order of multiple attributives and multiple adverbials; duration and frequency after the verb. Materials come from kt:zh-time-word-order, kt:zh-complex-attributives, kt:zh-phrase-types. Trap: the most common error for English speakers is putting time and place after the verb. Heritage children err only in long written sentences

primitives.name: Role marking
primitives.oneLine: In a scene picture, connect each noun to its role (agent, object, place, instrument, direction), then choose the right particle or preposition
primitives.difficulty: The learner marks the role of a noun by translating the first language's preposition or word order directly. Chinese speakers learning Japanese map "在" to に or で every time (*図書館に勉強します, *東京で住んでいます) and mark things like "take a vehicle" and "meet someone" with を (*電車を乗ります, *友達を会います). English speakers learning Chinese put the prepositional phrase at the end (*我看书在图书馆, *他很好对我, *我放书在桌子上). Chinese speakers learning English say *in the wall for "on the wall" and *walked in the shop for "walked into the shop". What is missing is not memorizing the particle table, but first judging "what role does this noun play in this event?" and then mapping the role to the target language's marker and position.
primitives.object: A scene picture plus one sentence that describes it. The verb is fixed, and three to five nouns in the sentence each leave one position to be marked. Connecting roles, choosing markers and making one's own sentence all happen on this picture and this sentence
primitives.requires: Knows the nouns and verb in the scene and can recognise the form of every particle or preposition in the marker set (see prim:form-for-meaning). If the nouns are unknown, go through prim:scene-walkthrough first
learnerAction: Step 1 Connect roles: drag each noun in the sentence onto the role ring around the verb (only the three to five roles relevant to this item are shown: doer, object of the action, receiver, place where the action happens, place of existence, arrival point, direction, tool or means, companion, starting point)

Step 2 Choose markers: for each noun with a connected role, choose a particle or preposition and put it in the correct position. For each item, the learner also judges what decides the marker at this point, with locked categories: the role decides / the verb requires it (会う・乗る→に, interested in …) / the first language uses one word here that must be split in the target language (Chinese "在" maps to で or に; "给" maps to に or ために). The last category is the reverse half: the roles look the same but the markers differ
Step 3 Say your own: a new scene picture with the same verb family. Write or say one sentence that contains at least three different roles
systemResponse: After the roles are connected, the people or things in the scene picture get a colour mark and arrow for the matching role. The action points from the doer to the object. Movement roles draw a path line, and static roles draw a range box

After the markers are chosen, the sentence is rearranged by the target-language rules: the Chinese prepositional phrase moves before the verb, and the Japanese particle attaches after the noun. The marker colour matches the role ring

When the role is connected correctly but the marker is wrong, the system does not just mark it wrong. It changes the scene picture according to the meaning of the chosen marker. If the learner chose 「図書館に勉強します」, the person in the picture "walks to the library entrance" and the studying does not happen there, and it shows "this marker shows an arrival point"
When a verb takes a fixed case frame (会う, 乗る, 住む, interested in …), the case-frame card of this verb pops up next to the verb

ui.screen: The scene picture is on the left, and the draggable nouns in it are numbered. On the right, the sentence is at the top, with the gaps as clickable slots. Below it are the role ring and a row of marker buttons (3–6 particles or prepositions, in fixed order). The bottom bar records what the learner first chose for each role in this set. No score is shown
interactions: Drag a noun to the role ring, or click the noun first and then the role
Number keys choose the marker, Tab moves between the gaps in the sentence
Step 3 can be typed or built from word cards
ui.childVariant: Use only two or three spatial roles (where, go where, with whom). Roles use icons (footprints = go, house = at, two little people = together) and no terms. Sentences are built from word cards, and writing is not required
ui.adultVariant: Scenes come from commuting, errands and work. Role names and verb case-frame cards are shown. Step 3 requires one sentence with four roles, or two sentences that contrast two roles of the same noun
ui.accessibility: Roles are marked by icon, text and colour at once. Every drag and drop has a keyboard alternative of selecting first and then placing. The scene picture has a text description for screen readers

kcSignals: notions include space-location, space-motion, reference-person

the KC is a particle or preposition system (kt:ja-case-particles, kt:ja-ni-goal, kt:ja-de-place, kt:ja-de-means, kt:ja-direction-e, kt:ja-to-companion, kt:ja-kara-made, kt:zh-dui-gei-gen, kt:zh-zai-location, kt:zh-v-zai-dao-gei, kt:zh-ba-placement, kt:en-prepositions-place, kt:en-prepositions-movement)
commonErrors contain "used B where A should mark the position" or "prepositional phrase placed at the end of the sentence"
itemTypes include form-fill, error-correct, translate-zh-target
learnerSignals: keeps mixing に and で, 在 and 给
puts the prepositional phrase at the end by first-language word order
"Why に here and not で?"
contraindications: the nouns in the scene are not yet known
fixed collocations with no role-based reason (at home, *in school) belong to prim:usage-boundary and are not set as items here
information-structure contrasts such as は/が are not role marking. Use prim:choose-by-intent

rules: The Step 3 sentence has at least three different roles, and every marker agrees with the role the learner connected (blocks an answer that is too weak)

The roles must match the actual relations in the picture. If one marker accounts for more than 70% of a set, or the learner makes only single-role sentences such as "我在 X", mark it not passed (blocks gaming: coping with one safest marker)
Count connecting roles and choosing markers separately: a wrong role and "role right, marker wrong" are two kinds of problem and are not merged into one right/wrong
check.independence: The first connection in Step 1 and the first choice in Step 2 are recorded separately. A changed choice after seeing the scene change of "this marker shows …" or the verb case-frame card is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 shows no case-frame card, and any the learner opens is recorded

evidence.retained: The first and final role connections on the scene picture, the first marker and any changed choice for each noun, which case-frame cards were viewed, and the Step 3 self-made sentence with its role annotations

licensed.claim: Can tell this set of roles apart (e.g. place where the action happens vs place of existence, arrival point vs direction)
Can choose the right marker and position for a recognised role
Can mark several roles correctly in the learner's own sentence

prohibited: inferring the ability to use the marker from correct role connections
counting a correct choice made while the case-frame card was displayed as mastery of that verb's case frame
inferring performance in one language from role-marking performance in another

hints: Ask only "Does this action happen there, or does a person or thing go there / stay there?"
Play the action animation of this noun on the scene picture (moving or still)
Show the verb case-frame card and a minimal contrast pair (図書館で勉強する／図書館に行く; 在桌子上写字／写在桌子上)
scaffold.fade: After 4 items in a row of the same pair of roles are chosen correctly on the first try, stop playing the animation. After a verb is chosen correctly and independently twice in a row, its case-frame card no longer pops up automatically

primitives.reverseHalf: Each set has at least one item where the role is the same but the marker differs (existence uses に, action uses で: 部屋に猫がいる／部屋で遊ぶ; Chinese "在" means different things before and after the verb: 在桌子上写／写在桌子上). It also has one item where the marker is decided by the verb and cannot be derived from the role (友達に会う, 电车に乗る, 对中国文化感兴趣). State that "the role is the starting point, not the whole rule"

failureModes.failure: The learner chooses mechanically by noun type (a place noun gets で / 在)
failureModes.mitigation: The same place noun appears in two roles within one set
failureModes.test: In the adversarial examples, one third of the items give the same noun different roles. Check whether accuracy drops to chance

failureModes.failure: The scene picture is ambiguous and the role is not unique
failureModes.mitigation: Two authors label the roles of each picture independently, and pictures where they disagree are not used. When a picture must be kept, accept both and note it
failureModes.test: A record of the authors' agreement check

failureModes.failure: The learner only drags on the picture without reading the sentence and guesses the marker from the arrows
failureModes.mitigation: Do not show the arrow animation before the first choice in Step 2
failureModes.test: Compare first-try accuracy between animation-off and animation-on groups

stacksWith.how: For Chinese items, overlay slots on the same sentence: after the preposition is chosen, the prepositional phrase must be dragged into the adverbial slot before the verb, and a violation points out which slot rule was broken
Share the same scene picture: connect the roles first, then use those roles to describe the whole picture
In the same scene, listen to instructions that contain locations and objects and place things accordingly. The placement result is shown directly as role connections

languages.en: Contrasting sets: in/on/at (position), into/onto/across/through (path), to/for (receiver / beneficiary), with/by (companion / instrument / transport). Traps for Chinese speakers: *in the wall, *walked in the shop, *walk through the road, *go to home. Fixed expressions such as at home / at school go in the reverse half
languages.ja: Contrasting sets: が・を・に・で・へ・と・から・まで. Key contrasts: で (place of action) / に (existence, residence, arrival), に / へ, で (means) / を, と / に (会う, 言う). Verb case frames: 乗る・会う→に, 住む→に. Location nouns need の (机の上に, *かばん中に). Trap for Chinese speakers: treating particles as prepositions and putting them first (*で駅待ちます)
languages.zh: Contrasting sets: 在 (before the verb = place of action; after the verb = attached end point: 住在, 放在), 给/对/跟/为, 到, 把 (object of disposal), 被 (agent). In word order the prepositional phrase goes before the verb, and a place noun needs a locative word (桌子上). Traps for English speakers: *我看书在图书馆, *他很好对我, *我放书在桌子上. Trap for Japanese speakers: *我被雨下了

primitives.name: Aspect on a timeline
primitives.oneLine: Place an event on a timeline (start, in progress, completed, experience, resulting state), then choose the matching tense-aspect form
primitives.difficulty: The learner treats aspect as tense, or treats time words as the only cue. English speakers learning Chinese take "了" as past tense (*昨天很冷了, *我以前常常去了公园) and use "着" for progressive (*他跑着步). Chinese speakers learning English pair the present perfect with a specific past time (*I have seen him yesterday) and treat the past perfect as "a long time ago" (*I had visited Paris in 2015). Learners of Japanese read every ている as "in progress" (結婚しています = a wedding is going on) and always say たところ for "just" (*先週日本に来たところです). What is missing is a picture: where the event starts, where it ends, whether the result still holds, and how all this relates to the moment of speaking or a reference time.
primitives.object: A timeline marked "now" (the moment of speaking), plus one event or a short narrative of three to five events. Each event is an interval block that can be dragged and stretched, with a start point, an end point, and a "result still holds" tail that can be switched on and off
primitives.requires: Can recognise and form the target forms (see prim:form-for-meaning, prim:paradigm-apply). If the learner cannot yet form them, go back first
learnerAction: Step 1 Place events: read or listen to one sentence, drag the event block onto the timeline, stretch it to show how long it lasts, set the reference point (now / a moment in the past), and decide "does the result still hold at the reference point?"

Step 2 Choose the form: from the contrasting set, choose the form that fits the timeline the learner placed. For each item the learner also judges what decides it, with locked categories: in progress / completed with the result still holding / happened before, result no longer holds / state has changed / about to happen. The last category is the reverse half: the timeline shape is the same but the verb type decides the form (a stative verb cannot take the progressive; ている on an instantaneous verb is a resulting state)

Step 3 Place and write your own: given something about the learner (how long they have studied this language, where they have been, what they are doing now), place the timeline first and then write the sentence
systemResponse: As the event block is dragged or stretched, the form buttons below that match the current timeline shape light up and the ones that do not match are dimmed, but can still be chosen

Once a form is chosen, the sentence is bound to the timeline. If the learner then changes the timeline (for example, stretches the end point past "now"), the form in the sentence is flagged "the timeline changed and this form no longer fits"

If the learner chose another grammatical form, the system does not mark it wrong. It automatically redraws the timeline as that form describes it and shows the two side by side (choosing 过 instead of 了 removes the result tail; choosing was doing turns the event block into a long background bar)
In a narrative of several events, where the order of telling and the order of happening differ, the two lines cross on the timeline and are marked

ui.screen: The sentence or short narrative is on top. In the middle is a horizontal timeline, past on the left and future on the right, with a vertical line marked "now" and the reference point as a draggable dashed line. Event blocks sit on the timeline. Below is a row of form buttons (2–4, in fixed order). A narrow column on the right records the timeline shapes the learner placed and the forms chosen in this set
interactions: Drag an event block to move it, drag the two ends to stretch it, click the tail to switch "result still holds"
Keyboard: after selecting an event block, ←/→ moves it, Shift+←/→ stretches it, R toggles the result tail, number keys choose the form
Touch: long-press to drag, two fingers to stretch
ui.childVariant: No abstract timeline. Use a three-panel comic strip instead (starting to do / doing / finished), and the learner puts a picture in one panel. The contrasting set has at most two items (在/了; -ing/-ed), shown by colour rather than terms
ui.adultVariant: Show two lines for speech time S and reference time R, and allow two events at once (past perfect, たところ vs ていたところ). Terms can be shown. Step 3 asks for a three- or four-sentence self-description that uses at least two different timeline shapes
ui.accessibility: Each time the timeline changes, a text description is generated at the same time ("the event started two years ago, lasts until now, and is still going") for screen readers. Timeline states do not rely on colour alone. Everything works from the keyboard

kcSignals: notions include aspect-progress, aspect-completion, change-of-state, time-duration, sequence

the KC is a tense-aspect contrast (kt:zh-le-perfective, kt:zh-le-modal-basic, kt:zh-guo-experience, kt:zh-zhengzai, kt:zh-zhe-durative, kt:zh-le-double, kt:zh-yao-le, kt:ja-progressive-teiru, kt:ja-result-state-teiru, kt:ja-teshimau, kt:ja-tokoro-aspect, kt:en-present-perfect, kt:en-present-perfect-vs-past, kt:en-past-perfect, kt:en-present-perfect-continuous, kt:en-future-perfect)
commonErrors contain "treats an aspect marker as past tense", "uses the progressive with a stative verb", "uses it with a specific past time"
learnerSignals: "了 is just the past tense, right?" "ている means 'in progress'"
reading a narrative, takes had done in the order of reading and gets the sequence backwards
in self-descriptions, tense stays flat throughout, or the past is expressed only by time words
contraindications: the learner cannot yet form the target forms
when the difference between forms is mainly mood or attitude (the regret of てしまう, the modal uses of 了), the timeline can express only half. Overlay prim:choose-by-intent or prim:register-calibrate
when both forms are natural in the context and mean the same, it cannot be used as an item

rules: The form in the Step 3 sentence matches the timeline the learner placed (blocks an answer that is too weak)

The timeline must not contradict the time words and content of the sentence. If the timeline is placed as "lasting until now" but the sentence is "我小时候在上海住了五年了", mark it not passed. The learner's own sentences must use at least two different timeline shapes and cannot keep placing the easiest single-point event (blocks gaming)

Count placing the timeline in Step 1 and choosing the form in Step 2 separately: "wrong timeline" and "timeline right, form wrong" are two kinds of problem. The timeline is judged by topology only (before now / across now / after now, with or without a result tail, whether it lasts), not by pixel position
check.independence: The first timeline placed and the first form chosen for each item are recorded separately. A change made after seeing the "timeline changed" prompt or the timeline template is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 shows no timeline template

evidence.retained: For each item, the first timeline shape, the first form chosen, later changes and the comparison picture. For Step 3, the self-made sentence and the timeline the learner placed for it

licensed.claim: Can represent this set of tense-aspect meanings as a time structure
Can choose the right form by time structure in a controlled context
Can use this set of tense-aspect contrasts unprompted in a self-description or narrative

prohibited: inferring the ability to produce the form from correct timeline placement
inferring understanding of the English present perfect from telling 了 and 过 apart (the aspect systems of different languages do not map one to one)
giving feedback as if forms and timeline shapes were a one-to-one lookup table, ignoring restrictions by verb type

hints: Ask only "When you say this sentence, is the event still going on? Does the result still hold?"
Show the reference-time line on the timeline and pin the time words in the sentence to the timeline
Show the timeline template of this form and a minimal contrast example
scaffold.fade: After 4 items in a row of the same contrasting set are correct on the first try for both timeline and form, hints above level 2 no longer appear. The timeline template is always hidden in Step 3

primitives.reverseHalf: Each set has at least one item where the same timeline shape matches two natural forms that differ in meaning or pragmatics (I've lived here / I've been living here; 我学了两年汉语 / 我学了两年汉语了). It also has one item where the verb type blocks the timeline (*我正在知道, *知っているところです; 死んでいる is a resulting state, not "dying"; *他跑着步 should be 他在跑步). It also has one item with "昨天" that nevertheless needs had done, to show that time words do not decide the form

failureModes.failure: The learner places the timeline and chooses the form by time words (yesterday, 已经, もう)
failureModes.mitigation: Design items with no time word and items with misleading time words
failureModes.test: In the adversarial examples, one third have the time word removed or a misleading time word inserted

failureModes.failure: Imprecise dragging is misjudged
failureModes.mitigation: Judge only topological relations, not pixel positions
failureModes.test: The same topology gives the same result under ±10% position jitter

failureModes.failure: The learner treats the timeline as a translation table (了 = have done)
failureModes.mitigation: Cross-language comparison appears only in after-lesson notes, and items contain no first-language equivalents
failureModes.test: Check that the item text and hints contain no one-to-one first-language equivalents

stacksWith.how: Overlay the timeline on the same context card: the timeline reshapes as the form is chosen, and when the timeline is changed the sentence marks the form that no longer matches
The same set of event cards used for retelling goes directly onto the timeline. Where the order of telling differs from the order of happening, require the past perfect, 之前已经……了 or ていた to mark it
When describing a picture, for each action or state in it first judge on the timeline whether it is in progress or a resulting state, then choose 着/在, ている, or -ing

languages.en: Contrasting sets: simple past / present perfect, progressive / simple, past perfect / simple past, present perfect continuous, future perfect. Traps for Chinese speakers: *I have gone to Shanghai last year, *When have you arrived?, taking had done as "a long time ago". The existing c35-tense-shifts covers only narrative register shifting in the reading direction (background / event / looking back to an earlier time / comment). It has no timeline operation and can serve as reading material for Step 1. For the choosing direction, see c14
languages.ja: Contrasting sets: ている (progressive) / ている (resulting state: 結婚している, 住んでいる) / た, てしまう (completion plus regret), るところ・ているところ・たところ, たばかり. ている on an instantaneous verb is a resulting state. *来たところ (a week ago) should be 来たばかり. Half of the regret of てしまう cannot be expressed on the timeline and needs a separate mood dimension
languages.zh: Contrasting sets: 了₁ (completion) / 了₂ (change) / 过 (experience) / 着 (durative state) / 在, 正在 (progressive) / 了……了 (lasting until now) / 要……了. Traps for English speakers: *昨天很冷了, *他跑着步, *我正在学汉语两年了, *我没买了书. Negation uses 没 and drops 了

primitives.name: Modifier attachment
primitives.oneLine: Move a modifier or a coordinated item to different positions, see how the meaning changes, then put it back in the right place
primitives.difficulty: The sentence is grammatical but the meaning is wrong. The modifier is attached to the wrong element (only misplaced, a dangling participle, whether a relative clause needs commas), or the items in a coordinated list do not match in shape (I like reading, to swim and music). Chinese learners writing English rely on feel and do not notice that "a modifier attaches to whatever is right next to it". English speakers learning Chinese put the modifier after the noun (*那个人站在门口是我们的老师) and put 只, 也 and 都 where English would put them. In Japanese, modifiers always come before the noun, so the difficulty becomes "which noun does this long string in front modify?", and how far だけ and も reach.
primitives.object: A set of 4–8 sentence frames in which the meaning changes with the position. Each sentence has one element that can be moved and several slots. The two misattached places in the learner's own draft are corrected on the same interface
primitives.requires: Can understand the meaning of every element in the sentence. If the learner cannot even find the main clause, first use prim:strip-skeleton to find the skeleton
learnerAction: Step 1 Move it around: the top states the meaning the author wants to say. Click the movable element into different slots. Each move re-lays out the sentence and shows "Now this sentence says …". When the learner has seen enough, they click "Put it here"

Step 2 Flip a switch: for the same sentence, flip one switch (in English, with or without commas; for coordination, same shape or not), and see what the reader will think. Choose one for the given occasion, and assign it to a locked attachment category (attaches to a certain noun / attaches to the whole event / an added aside / limits the word right after it)
Step 3 Fix it: a draft that is fully grammatical but has two misattached or lopsided coordinated places. Rewrite those two sentences
systemResponse: After a move, the sentence is re-laid out immediately. An arrow points from the modifier to what it modifies in that position, with the meaning of this position written below. The right side records how many moves were made in all (moving is encouraged)

When the switch is flipped, the sentence changes live, and below it is shown how the reader will understand it (no comma: only the 6 who did not pass have to come back; with comma: the whole class did not pass, and the whole class has to come back)
Coordinated items are drawn as bars. Colour shows shape and length shows word count. Once aligned, the bars turn the same colour

ui.screen: On top, "What the author wants to say is …" and the movable element. In the middle, the sentence with round slots. Below, the "Now this sentence says …" note. Step 2 swaps this for a switch or a bar chart. On the right, a column of move counts and attachment categories
interactions: Click a slot or choose it with the arrow keys, Enter to put it down. Drag is also supported
Space flips the switch
Step 3 edits directly on the draft
ui.childVariant: Only two kinds: "limits the word right after it" and "attaches to which noun". Sentences come with pictures (Only I ate the apple / I only ate the apple, with the difference drawn in the picture). No comma switch and no draft fixing
ui.adultVariant: Drafts come from academic writing, CVs and notice emails. Terms are shown (restrictive / non-restrictive, dangling modifier, parallel structure). Step 3 rewrites two places and explains why
ui.accessibility: Moving does not depend on dragging, and both click and keyboard work. The arrow relations are also written in text. The bar chart has a text version (shape, word count)

kcSignals: component is grammatical and involves modifier position, scope adverbs, relative clauses or coordination (e.g. kt:en-orth-punctuation-advanced, kt:en-adverbs-degree-probability, kt:ja-noun-modification, kt:ja-focus-dake, kt:zh-de-relative, kt:zh-complex-attributives, kt:zh-adverbs-basic, kt:zh-he-conjunction)
commonErrors contain modifiers placed after the noun, wrong adverb position, inconsistent coordinated forms
itemTypes include order-words or error-correct
learnerSignals: puts only and also anywhere
does not know that a modifier is attached in the wrong place
writes sentences that are ambiguous
the two sides of and do not match in shape
contraindications: the learner still cannot find the main clause of the sentence
an element whose meaning does not change when moved (a time adverbial at the start or end of the sentence) cannot be used in items about "the meaning will change"
when what is to be taught is a fixed word-order rule and not a meaning difference, use prim:slot-order

rules: Material check: each sentence has at least two positions that are grammatical, and exactly one that matches the author's intent. Every position must have a note "Now it says what". Each of the four attachment categories appears in at least one sentence. The two versions of the switch are identical except for the switched element

Step 3: both places must be fixed (one check for each place: the target element appears in the correct position), and both sentences must be written (blocks an answer that is too weak). Ambiguity cannot be "removed" by deleting the modifier. The modifier must still be in the sentence (blocks gaming)

Coordination: after the fix, all items have the same shape, and the ratio of the word counts of the longest and shortest item is within a threshold. A case such as "wrong order" cannot be judged by shape alone, because aligned bars do not mean the sentence is right
check.independence: Moves made before clicking "Put it here" are exploration and are not counted as errors. The first choice for the final placement is recorded separately. Placement after seeing the explanation is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 shows no reference revision

evidence.retained: For each sentence, the path of moves (which positions were tried, how many times), the final placement, the switch choices, and the Step 3 rewrites

licensed.claim: Can judge what a modifier attaches to when it is in different positions
Can put a modifier in the position that matches the intent in their own writing

prohibited: judging that the learner cannot do it because they made many moves (moving is encouraged exploration)
inferring other structures from performance on one kind of attachment
inferring that the learner will not misattach again in later writing because Step 3 was fixed correctly

hints: A modifier attaches to whatever is right next to it
Draw the pointing arrow for the current position
Show the complete sentence for the position that matches the author's intent
scaffold.fade: After three sentences in a row are placed correctly on the first try, stop drawing arrows and show only the meaning note

primitives.reverseHalf: Most positions are not "wrong" but mean something else. Each position tells the learner what it says, rather than being marked with a cross. There are also cases where moving does not change the meaning (a time adverbial at the start or end of the sentence). Put at least one in each set, so the learner does not think "moving always changes the meaning". For coordination, aligned bars do not mean the sentence is right: in the sentence with the wrong order, the colour and length are aligned and the problem lies only in the sequence.

failureModes.failure: The learner reads "only one matches the intent" as meaning that every other position is a grammar error
failureModes.mitigation: Every position gets "Now it says …", with no right/wrong marks
failureModes.test: The interface must not show an error mark on a position that is grammatical

failureModes.failure: In rewriting, the learner tears the whole sentence down and starts again, sidestepping the attachment problem
failureModes.mitigation: Check that the modifier is still in the sentence and in the position that matches the intent
failureModes.test: A rewrite that deletes with the telescope cannot pass

failureModes.failure: The word count of a bar is mislabelled, so the bars mislead
failureModes.mitigation: Automatically count the words and compare with the labels
failureModes.test: Material that labels 2 words where there are 3 must be reported as an error

stacksWith.how: First fold the modifiers away to find the skeleton, then unfold them one by one and decide where each attaches
In Chinese and Japanese, modifiers coming first is a slot rule. Show the slot names and the attachment arrows on the same screen
When the Step 3 draft is replaced by the learner's own essay, attachment is revised separately as one kind of problem

languages.en: The four attachment categories noun/verb/extra/scope are locked (c18), and the switch is the comma in restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses. The four coordination categories form/weight/order/pair are locked (c21), and the clamps include not only…but also…, both…and…, either…or…. Typical: three positions of only are three different things; dangling participles Running, I caught the bus / I caught the bus running. Existing implementations: c18, c21
languages.ja: All modifiers come first, so the item becomes "which noun does this long string modify?": 昨日買った友達の本 (is it the friend or the book that was bought yesterday?), 黒い目のきれいな女の子. For scope, use the focus particles instead: the position of だけ, しか, も, さえ (私だけ／コーヒーだけ). The switch becomes the position of the reading comma 「、」. Coordination shape: with 〜たり〜たりする both sides need たり, and the connective forms of AくてB and NAで must agree. Typical errors: *だけ飲みますコーヒー, and stacking は and も
languages.zh: The learner is a native English speaker. The modifier must come before the head (*那个人站在门口是我们的老师 should be 站在门口的那个人), the order of multiple attributives is possessor, demonstrative-measure, descriptive, head, and adverbials come before the verb (*我学汉语在家). The scope adverbs 只, 也, 都 and 就 control the element after them (只他去 / 他只去), and "都" sums up the plural element to its left. The switch becomes the presence or absence of "的" (学习文件 is verb-object, 学习的文件 is modifier-head). Coordination: "和" cannot join predicates (*我吃饭和看电视), the two sides of 不但…而且… must have the same shape, and whether the subjects are the same decides the position of "不但"

primitives.name: Combine & unpack
primitives.oneLine: Join short sentences into one according to the point to be stressed, or take a long sentence apart and see what is lost
primitives.difficulty: Either everything the learner writes is short sentences strung along with and/then, それから, 然后; or the reverse, a comma all the way, three things stuck into one sentence until the writer gets lost. When reading a packed long sentence (nominalization, participial phrases, multi-layer compound sentences), the learner cannot tell which thing is background and which is the point. What the learner lacks is not connectives but two decisions: "how many things does this sentence really say?" and "which one do I want in the foreground, and which do I demote to background?".
primitives.object: A set of short sentences about the same event (3–5 sentences, preferably from the learner's own draft) and the one long sentence made by joining them. The whole primitive works back and forth between this set of short sentences and this one long sentence
primitives.requires: Can write a complete simple sentence with subject and predicate, and recognises at least one coordinating device and one subordinating device (and/because, て/から, 和/因为). If simple sentences are still incomplete, go back to prim:slot-order
learnerAction: Step 1 Join them: read a few short-sentence cards and one line, "What you really want to say is …". From the locked ways of joining, choose one to join them into a sentence (side by side / demote one level as background / compress into a phrase / attach to a noun), and see where the point lands

Step 2 Take it apart: given one long sentence, first count "how many things this sentence says", then split it and judge what was lost by splitting (locked options: the cause is gone / the concession is gone / the sequence is gone / the "which one" limiting is gone / nothing was lost — the reverse half)
Step 3 Fix your own: join three run-on sentences from the learner's own draft into one. One of the things must actually be demoted. Using only coordinating devices is not allowed
systemResponse: After a way of joining is chosen, the short-sentence cards above shrink and fade, and the joined sentence grows below. The joining device is highlighted, and the thing placed in the foreground is in bold
If the learner chose a way of joining that is grammatical but puts the point in the wrong place, it is not marked wrong. It shows "Joined this way, the point has moved to …" and allows another choice

After the right count of things is given in Step 2, the long sentence splits itself at the subject-predicate boundaries. A relation lost by the split is shown as a broken line between two cards, with its original marker word
After Step 3 is submitted, the three original sentences and the new sentence are kept side by side, and the thing that was demoted is shown in the background colour

ui.screen: The short-sentence card area is on top. In the middle is a row with the intent bar "What you really want to say is …". Below it is a row of join buttons (3–4, each with a one-line note on "weight"). At the very bottom is the sentence that grows. In Step 2 the long sentence is on top and the count buttons are below
interactions: Click or press number keys 1–4 to choose how to join
In Step 2, left and right arrow keys move the cursor, and Enter cuts at the subject-predicate boundary
Step 3 is typed, and the learner can undo back to the previous version
ui.childVariant: Only two sentences joined into one: picture cards show the two things, and there are only two ways of joining, "and / because" (ja: て／から; zh: 和、然后／因为). Colour marks which one is the "why". No count of things and no terms
ui.adultVariant: Material comes from work email, reports and academic paragraphs. Step 1 adds compression by nominalization (en nominalization, ja こと／の, zh 进行研究-style written register). Step 2 asks the learner to say what occasion the loose and the tight version each suit
ui.accessibility: The way of joining and the point are marked by both bold and underline, not colour alone. The cut points can be used from the keyboard. Screen readers read the split cards as "thing n"

kcSignals: notions include cause-reason, contrast-concession, condition, sequence, discourse-organisation, in KCs for compound sentences and connectives (e.g. kt:en-complex-sentences, kt:en-participle-clauses, kt:ja-conjunctive-particles, kt:ja-kara-node, kt:ja-noni, kt:zh-yinwei-suoyi, kt:zh-suiran-danshi, kt:zh-complex-written)
itemTypes include transform and situated-production-written
commonErrors contain marking both clauses (*雨だから、だから行きません) or sentence-building errors such as "then / それから all the way"
learnerSignals: the essay is all short sentences, popping out one at a time
a comma all the way, run-on
"How do I write a long sentence?" "This sentence is too long to understand"
contraindications: the learner cannot yet write a complete simple sentence
when the sentences in the material are truly coordinate and of equal weight, with no one to demote, it cannot be used for Step 1 items
tasks of spoken, immediate communication do not require compressing sentences

rules: The result of Step 3 must be one sentence (en: one end punctuation mark; ja: one 「。」; zh: one full stop, and a run-on joined by commas does not count as joined; a clause connective, a 的 attributive or a subordinate structure must appear)

It must contain at least one demoting device (en: because/although/when/-ing/which; ja: ので/のに/てから/たら/連体修飾; zh: 因为/虽然/如果/以后/的字定语). Using only and/but/so, て, 然后/和 does not count (blocks an answer that is too weak)

Each sentence of the draft must keep at least one content word. Dropping a thing to make it fit into one sentence is not passed. More than 70% literal overlap with the model sentence is judged as copying (blocks gaming)

Hard checks specific to a language: in ja, a noun or na-adjective before ので・のに must take な, and the clause after のに cannot be a request; in zh, when connectives come in pairs neither part may be missing, and what follows "因为" must be a clause, not just a noun
check.independence: The first choice in Step 1 and the first count in Step 2 are recorded separately. A changed choice after seeing "the point has moved to …" or the model split is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 shows no model sentence. "Show me a way to split it" appears only after the learner fails to split twice in Step 2

evidence.retained: Kept on each set of short-sentence cards: the first way of joining, changed choices, the count judgment and the lost relations marked after splitting. The Step 3 draft and the rewrite are archived side by side

licensed.claim: Can choose the way of joining that puts the point in the right place for a given intent
Can count how many things a long sentence contains and say what relation is lost by splitting
Demotes clauses by subordination on their own initiative in their own draft

prohibited: treating longer sentences as writing improvement
judging that the learner can build sentences in writing from correct Step 1 choices alone
treating the use of a connective as the relation being used correctly
counting a correct change after a hint as independent completion

hints: Ask only "Of these things, which one do you most want people to remember?"
Mark in a light colour the one that can be background
Show two ways of joining the same set of short sentences side by side, each with one line on where the point is
scaffold.fade: After 4 sets in a row where the way of joining is chosen correctly on the first try and the Step 2 count is correct on the first try, remove hints above level 2. Step 3 never has a model

primitives.reverseHalf: When taking apart, at least one item has the answer "nothing was lost" — a longer sentence is not always better. When counting things, the longest sentence has only one thing (and, と, 和 join two nouns, not two sets of subject-predicate). In ja, a string of て-linked actions is a deliberate telling in sequence, and forcing it into から creates a cause out of nowhere. In zh, a run-on that relies on meaning (下雨了，不去了) is already fine, and forcing "因为……所以……" onto it makes it stiff

failureModes.failure: The learner decides "the longer the better" and stuffs everything into one sentence
failureModes.mitigation: Step 2 has items where "nothing was lost". Step 3 sets a sentence-length limit and checks the number of subject-predicate sets
failureModes.test: Adversarial example: include a draft that is already too long, where the right fix is to split it

failureModes.failure: The demotion is assembled from a list of connectives alone, and the relation itself is wrong (cause reversed, or cause used where concession is needed)
failureModes.mitigation: In Step 1 each item has an intent bar, and the check confirms that the demoting device matches the relation family declared in the intent bar
failureModes.test: Build a submission with "every connective present but the relation family does not match the intent bar". It must be blocked

failureModes.failure: Things are counted by commas, not by subject-predicates
failureModes.mitigation: Include sentences with many commas but only one thing, and sentences with no commas but two things
failureModes.test: In the adversarial examples, one third of the sentences have a comma count that does not match the thing count

stacksWith.how: In Step 2, first strip the long sentence to its skeleton on the same card, then count the things by the skeleton and split
The relation family of the join buttons and the prediction direction share the same set of locked categories, and a joined sentence can be used directly to bet on the next sentence
Step 3 is done on the learner's own draft, as the kind of problem "this round only fixes how sentences are joined"

languages.en: Locked ways of joining: equal/sub/phrase/relative (c16). The four ways of compressing in the loose-tight contrast: link/count/fit/name (c19). Run-on signals splice/and_two/chain/nest/none and the five ways of rejoining because/although/which/after/stop (c44). Existing implementations: c16, c19, c44. Traps: Chinese speakers join sentences with commas; which referring to a whole sentence is unclear
languages.ja: Locked ways of joining: て (coordination or sequence, equal weight) / から・ので (demote to a reason) / のに・けど・が (adversative) / 連体修飾 (attach to a noun) / こと・の nominalization (compression). The splitting direction is counting how many predicates are in a long string of て forms or continuative forms. Traps: influenced by "because … therefore", marking both clauses (～から、だから). When apologizing, から sounds like an excuse, and ～て／ので should be used. のに is followed by a request. When the subjects differ, use ながら
languages.zh: Locked ways of joining: coordination (又……又, 而且; "和" cannot join predicates) / demotion by clause connectives (因为, 虽然, 如果, 既然, 只要, 即使) / 的 attributives attached to a noun / written-style compression (进行研究, 从而, 以便, 以免). Count things by the number of predicate cores, not commas. Traps: English speakers treat so as a degree adverb (*他所以高兴), reverse cause and effect, follow "因为" with only a noun, and use "和" to join two predicates

primitives.name: Strip to skeleton
primitives.oneLine: Fold the modifiers away to find the skeleton, then judge which blocks can be skipped on the next reading
primitives.difficulty: Halfway through a long sentence the learner forgets the beginning, and at the full stop still does not know who is doing what. The learner is led off by the noun nearest the verb (a subject-verb agreement error). In Japanese, a very long prenominal modifying clause sits between the topic and the predicate, so the learner cannot find the noun being modified and cannot tell the が inside the clause from the は of the main clause. In Chinese, multiple layers of "的" attributives push the head noun far back, and the learner mistakes a verb inside the attributive for the main predicate. The error at the other end is stripping off every modifier as decoration, and losing even "which one is meant".
primitives.object: One long sentence of 15–45 words (30–80 characters for ja/zh), with each layer of modification marked as a foldable block. The whole primitive strips, judges and reassembles on this one sentence
primitives.requires: Can read the subject-verb-object of basic sentence patterns, and recognises the modifier markers of the target language (en: who/which/of phrases; ja: the attributive form before a noun; zh: 的, 地). If basic word order is still unstable, go back to prim:slot-order first
learnerAction: Step 1 Strip: click to fold the modifier blocks layer by layer until only the skeleton remains (subject head + predicate core + necessary object). The follow-up questions appear only after the skeleton is exposed (should the predicate be singular or plural, which noun is being modified, which verb is the main-clause predicate)

Step 2 Judge: classify each layer of modification (locked: sentence-initial adverbial / inserted addition, can be skipped / sentence-final addition, can be skipped / limiting that decides "which one", cannot be stripped — the reverse half), and judge which blocks can be skipped first on the next reading
Step 3 Put back: given the skeleton and the scrambled modifier blocks, put them back into one complete sentence in the word order of the target language
systemResponse: Click a layer and it collapses to ⟨…⟩ and fades, the word-count bar beside it drops (e.g. 37→9), and the skeleton gradually lights up
Clicking a layer that cannot be stripped is blocked, with "After stripping, only X is left — which one?", and that layer is relabelled in the limiting colour
When the subject-verb agreement or predicate judgment is wrong, point out which word led the learner astray (the noun nearest the verb, a verb inside a clause)
