When a block is put in the wrong place in Step 3, point out which word-order rule was violated (modifier before / after the noun, order of multiple attributives)

ui.screen: The long sentence runs horizontally on top, with modifier layers dotted-underlined. On the right is the falling word-count bar. Below are the current question and its options. In Step 2 a classification label appears beside each layer
interactions: Click, or Tab to select a layer and press Space to fold or unfold it
Number keys choose the classification and options
In Step 3, drag, or move the modifier block to the insertion point with the arrow keys
ui.childVariant: Sentences are at most 12 words / 20 characters. Two big cards, "Who? Does what?", are used to find the skeleton, and modifier layers are shown as picture bubbles ("What kind?" "Where?"). No terms for restrictive and non-restrictive. Ask only "If you remove this block, do you still know which one?"
ui.adultVariant: Material comes from news, manuals and paper abstracts. Layer names are shown. Step 2 asks the learner to write a "sign for scanning next time" for each skippable block (a comma, a long clause before の, several 的)
ui.accessibility: The folded state also has the text "folded". Layers are not told apart by colour alone. All blocks work from the keyboard, and word-count changes have a spoken prompt

kcSignals: KCs on modification and clauses (kt:en-relative-defining, kt:en-relative-nondefining, kt:en-participle-clauses, kt:ja-relative-clause, kt:ja-noun-modification, kt:zh-de-relative, kt:zh-complex-attributives, kt:zh-phrase-types)
notions include quality-description and itemTypes include order-words or read-comprehend
commonErrors contain transfer of modifier position (*那个人站在门口是我们的老师, *昨日買ったの本) or subject-verb agreement led astray by a neighbouring noun
learnerSignals: forgets the beginning halfway through a long sentence
"What is this sentence actually saying?"
reads word by word, and when reading aloud breaks the sentence in the wrong places
contraindications: the sentence is short and has no modifier layers to strip
the learner cannot yet recognise the modifier markers of the target language (learn the form first)
in literary text, where the modification itself is the point to read, do not lead the learner to skip

rules: The stripped skeleton must stand as a sentence by itself (with a subject and a predicate core), and its word or character count must be no more than half of the original sentence (card not stripped enough)
Stripping a limiting layer is not passed. Stripping down to a bare noun that cannot say "which one" is also not passed (card stripped too far)

Data level: each set has at least one sentence that can be stripped all the way, and at least one with a layer that cannot be stripped. For subject-verb agreement items, correct singular and plural answers are balanced, and option positions are scattered

Step 3 word-order check: en relative clause after the noun, non-restrictive clause with commas; ja modifier before the noun, clause predicate in plain form, clause subject marked with が and not は, attributive modification without の; zh attributive before 的, multiple attributives in the order possessive > demonstrative-measure > verbal > adjectival > noun, no relative pronoun
check.independence: The first folding path and the first predicate judgment in Step 1 are recorded separately. Continuing after being blocked by "cannot be stripped" is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 does not show the original sentence

evidence.retained: Kept on each sentence: the order of folding, the layers that were blocked, the first predicate judgment and the result of putting back. The word-count drop curve is saved too

licensed.claim: Can find the skeleton (subject head and predicate core) in controlled long sentences
Can tell limiting modification that decides "which one" from supplementary modification that can be skipped
Can put modifiers back before / after the noun in the word order of the target language

prohibited: inferring from this that reading speed or overall reading comprehension has improved
treating "stripping quickly" as having understood what the modification means
counting a skeleton found after a hint as independent completion

hints: Ask only "In the end, who did what in this sentence?"
Mark the predicate core first (en finite verb, ja sentence-final predicate, zh main-clause verb)
Pre-fold the first foldable modifier block as a demonstration
scaffold.fade: After 4 sentences in a row where the correct skeleton is found on the first try, stop marking the predicate in advance. Step 3 never shows the original sentence

primitives.reverseHalf: There is always a layer that cannot be stripped: in en, a who/that clause that sits right against the noun with no comma; in ja, a prenominal modifying clause that answers "which one" (昨日兄がくれたお守り: after stripping only お守り is left and you do not know which one); in zh, a 的 attributive that distinguishes the object (我昨天买的书 vs 书). Also include one sentence where all three layers can be stripped, to keep the learner from going to the other extreme of "no modification can be stripped". When a zh 的 structure omits the head (我买的), the skeleton is not missing anything

failureModes.failure: The learner strips off all modification and loses the reference
failureModes.mitigation: Every set must contain a layer that cannot be stripped. When it is stripped, block it and ask "which one?"
failureModes.test: Adversarial example: a sentence whose subject can be identified only through a limiting clause

failureModes.failure: In en the learner judges skippability mechanically by "with or without a comma", and in ja/zh the learner copies this rule although there is no reliable comma marker
failureModes.mitigation: For ja/zh the criterion becomes "after removing it, can you still answer which one?", with no punctuation shortcut
failureModes.test: In the ja/zh adversarial examples, include sentences where the position of the reading comma (、) does not match restrictiveness

failureModes.failure: The verb inside an attributive or clause is taken as the main-clause predicate
failureModes.mitigation: In Step 1 the predicate core must be confirmed before the learner can continue
failureModes.test: Include sentences where the clause verb is closer to the start and the main-clause predicate is at the very end (always present in ja; in zh use multiple layers of attributives)

stacksWith.how: On the same sentence, move one layer of modification next to another noun, see how the meaning changes, then judge what it originally attached to
The skeleton and modifier blocks that were stripped out are the source of the short sentences when splitting. The same long sentence then goes on to counting things and splitting
A pronoun or omitted subject in the skeleton is then connected back to its antecedent in the same passage

languages.en: Four layers front/on/after/tail, and the mark of the limiting layer is no comma before or after (c29). The four kinds of material that stand between subject and verb: of/clause/phrase/special (c22). Sense-group chunking (c30). Existing implementations: c22, c29, c30. Traps: a number of / the number of; resumptive pronouns like the man who I met him
languages.ja: Layers: sentence-initial circumstance (～とき, ～ので clause, ～によると) / prenominal modifying clause (judge whether it decides "which one") / N の N の N chains / parentheticals. Skeleton = topic (は) or subject (が) + sentence-final predicate. Traps: the が inside a clause is not the main-clause subject, and the scope of は extends to the end of the sentence; using は for a clause subject (*兄はくれたお守り), using the ます form in the clause predicate, Chinese "的" transfer as *買ったの本; the reading comma cannot serve as a criterion of restrictiveness
languages.zh: Layers: sentence-initial adverbial (time, place, according to …, as …) / multiple layers of 的 attributives / 地 adverbials / complements. Skeleton = subject head + predicate center + object head. Traps: English speakers put modifiers after the noun (*老师从北京来很受欢迎), add relative pronouns (*那个人谁站在门口), and overuse 的 (*我的中国的朋友); the topic of a topic sentence is not necessarily the agent; a 的 structure can omit its head

primitives.name: Reference chains
primitives.oneLine: Connect pronouns, omissions and rewordings back to what they refer to, and fill in what was omitted
primitives.difficulty: Every sentence is understood, but the passage does not hold together. The learner does not know what it, this, それ or 这 refers to. The same thing reworded is not recognised, so a summary counts one thing as three. In Japanese and Chinese the subject and object are often omitted, and the learner misjudges who did it (the direction of くれた / もらった, the subject carried over in Chinese run-on clauses). In production the reverse happens: Chinese speakers writing English drop objects and subjects, and English speakers writing Chinese add "他/它" in every sentence and even repeat the object with a pronoun in the object position.
primitives.object: A coherent short text of 100–400 words (200–600 characters for ja/zh), in which pronouns, rewordings and omission sites are marked as linkable anchors. The whole primitive grows a coreference arc diagram on this passage step by step
primitives.requires: Can understand this material at sentence level. If the learner cannot yet find the skeleton of a sentence, go back to prim:strip-skeleton first
learnerAction: Step 1 Connect back: for each highlighted pronoun, rewording or omission site (shown as ∅), click the piece it refers to. For an omission site, first fill in who was omitted, then connect the line

Step 2 Group: sort the scattered expressions into several buckets of "actually the same thing", and mark which way of referring is used at each place (locked: pronoun / demonstrative + noun / a different noun / a general noun referring to a whole event / zero-form omission / not the same thing as the above — the reverse half)

Step 3 Write on: continue the passage with three sentences, or revise a draft where the same name is repeated again and again. Use at least two different ways of referring, one of which is a general noun or an omission
systemResponse: After a correct connection, an arc rises from the reference point back to the antecedent, with colour showing the way of referring. At the same time a chain grows in the right column, listing all the names of the same referent in one column
When a connection is wrong, say what led the learner astray (the nearest noun, an object that semantically cannot do this action)
After an omission site in ja/zh is filled in, the added element appears in grey and can be hidden with one click, so the learner sees why the original does not need it
When grouping, the matching places in the passage light up in the bucket's colour

ui.screen: The passage takes most of the left of the screen. Anchors have dashed boxes, and blocks that can be referred to are dotted-underlined. Arcs are drawn above the text. The right column is the coreference chain that grows. In Step 2, below are the tray of expressions and the buckets
interactions: Click an anchor and then the antecedent to make a connection, Esc cancels
Tab moves between anchors, Enter confirms
On touch screens, long-press an anchor and drag it to the antecedent
ui.childVariant: Picture-book style, two or three sentences with pictures. References are only he/she/it (ja: この人／それ; zh: 他、她、它), and the learner drags the pronoun to the person or thing in the picture. Omission appears only as filling in the subject in a one-question, one-answer form such as "Who ate?"
ui.adultVariant: Material comes from news and commentary, with general nouns added (this move, この措置, 此举) and written-style reference (en former/latter, ja 同社・前者, zh 该、其、此). Step 3 rewrites a paragraph of the learner's own report
ui.accessibility: The arcs also have a text-list version (the chain in the right column). Ways of referring are told apart by shape as well as colour. All connection operations can be done from the keyboard

kcSignals: KCs whose notions include reference-person, reference-deixis, reference-definiteness (kt:en-personal-pronouns, kt:en-substitution-ellipsis, kt:ja-demonstrative-things, kt:ja-giving-receiving, kt:ja-tekureru, kt:zh-demonstratives, kt:zh-topic-comment)
commonErrors of reading and listening activity KCs mention misjudging an omitted subject (kt:ja-skill-listen-bridge, kt:ja-str-implicature)
commonErrors contain resumptive pronouns or dropped objects (*这本书我看过它, *I think yes)
learnerSignals: understands every sentence but cannot hold the passage together
later in the passage does not know whom it / それ / 这 refers to
keeps dropping the subject in English; every clause is "他……他……" in Chinese
contraindications: all references in the passage are in adjacent sentences and there is no chain to connect
the learner has not yet understood the sentences
texts that create ambiguity on purpose, such as poems, are not suited to items with a single answer

rules: Each arc must connect to a real antecedent. The head of a chain cannot be a pronoun or an omission
Step 3 must use at least two different ways of referring, and must not repeat the same name in three sentences in a row (blocks an answer that is too weak)

Step 3 must not create ambiguity. When a sentence has two possible antecedents, a pronoun or omission does not count as a valid way of referring. A general noun must match the type of event it refers to (a decision cannot be called trend / 傾向 / 趋势) (blocks gaming)

Language specific: in en the object of a transitive verb cannot be left empty; in ja, 彼は／あなたは appearing repeatedly and unnecessarily is marked as over-explicit, and an omitted subject must agree with the direction of the giving-receiving verb; in zh, the object position of a topic sentence cannot take a resumptive pronoun (*看过它), and the subject carried over in run-on clauses must agree with the previous sentence's subject
check.independence: The first connection of each arc in Step 1 is recorded separately. A changed connection after seeing the explanation "what led you astray" is recorded as completed after a hint. The Step 2 grouping result does not show right or wrong until all the items are placed. Step 3 shows no model

evidence.retained: Kept on this passage: all arcs (including records of wrong first connections), the omitted elements the learner filled in, the grouping result, and the three sentences written or revised in Step 3

licensed.claim: Can connect pronouns, demonstratives and omissions back to what they refer to in a given passage
Can recognise different expressions for the same referent
Controls reference in their own writing (no dropping, no ambiguity, no excess repetition)

prohibited: inferring understanding of the whole text from correct connections
treating the ability to fill in an omitted subject as appropriate omission when producing
counting a correct connection after a hint as independent completion

hints: Ask only "Who can do this action?" or "Which thing earlier could …?"
Narrow the candidate antecedents to two or three and highlight them
Show the type of reference (this is a general noun, and it refers to a whole event)
scaffold.fade: After two passages in a row where the first-connection accuracy reaches 80%, stop narrowing the candidates. Step 3 never has a model

primitives.reverseHalf: en: this often refers to a whole earlier event, not the nearest noun. There are false friends — things that look the same but are not. In slots where Chinese can omit but English cannot, "filling in nothing" is always wrong. The reverse for ja/zh is the opposite: supplying 私は／彼は or 他 in every sentence is what is unnatural, and the learner has to judge where omission should be kept. Include also one omitted subject that is not the previous sentence's subject (the subject has changed, and it is judged by くれる／もらう or by context)

failureModes.failure: The learner always connects to the nearest noun
failureModes.mitigation: Design anchors whose antecedent is not in the nearest position, at least one third
failureModes.test: In the adversarial examples, the nearest noun is one that semantically cannot do the action of the predicate

failureModes.failure: ja/zh learners assume by default that an omitted subject continues the previous sentence's subject
failureModes.mitigation: Each passage has at least one omission with a change of subject, decided by a giving-receiving verb, honorifics or context
failureModes.test: Build omission sites that are half "subject carried over" and half "subject changed"

failureModes.failure: In Step 3 the learner writes an ambiguous sentence just to get enough kinds of reference
failureModes.mitigation: Ambiguity check: when there are two candidate antecedents, the pronoun scores nothing
failureModes.test: Build a continuation with two antecedents of the same kind. It must be blocked

stacksWith.how: First strip out the skeleton on the same sentence, then connect the pronoun or omitted subject in the skeleton back to the earlier text
After the coreference chains are drawn, overlay paragraph functions on the same text and see which chain runs through the whole piece
In listening material, after the transcript is aligned, fill in the omitted subjects on the same transcript and check whether the giving-receiving direction was heard correctly

languages.en: Ways of referring pro/thisn/def/cmp (c23). Coreference grouping syn/hyper/gen/pro, including one false friend; each general noun such as move/trend/claim/issue must have been the correct answer at least once (c24). Existing implementations: c23, c24. Traps: transfer of Chinese omission leads to dropped objects (used ___ twice), *I think yes
languages.ja: Ways of referring: contextual demonstratives こ／そ／あ (そ points to what was just mentioned, あ to what both sides know) / rewording with a noun (同社, この措置) / zero pronoun / implied subject inferred from giving-receiving verbs, honorifics, and emotion adjective + がる. Traps: reading every そ-series as "that" and using あ; misjudging the actor of ～てくれた／～てもらった when the subject is omitted; Chinese "他／她" transferring into too many 彼／彼女
languages.zh: Ways of referring: 他／她／它／这／那 + measure word + noun / rewording / zero form (forward-omission, backward-omission) / written 此, 该, 其. Traps: English speakers repeat the object with a pronoun (*这本书我看过它), put a subject in every clause, and use "它" for people or for a whole event; the use of "这" for a whole earlier event; subject agreement in serial-verb and run-on sentences

primitives.name: Discourse mapping
primitives.oneLine: Label each paragraph or sentence with its function in the text, recognise the overall shape, then write a missing paragraph to fit that shape
primitives.difficulty: The learner understands every paragraph but cannot say what the whole text argues or how it gets there. They read with no expectations, from start to end. When writing, they have no skeleton: unrelated content gets stuffed into a paragraph, or after finishing one sentence they do not know how to connect the next. What the learner lacks is the judgment "what is this paragraph doing in the whole text?" and a sense of what a few common text shapes look like.
primitives.object: A short text of 4–6 paragraphs (or only the topic sentences), with a function colour band beside each paragraph and a skeleton diagram on the right that grows as the learner labels. The paragraph the learner writes in Step 3 is inserted back into this same text
primitives.requires: Can read the main idea of each paragraph and recognise the basic connectives between paragraphs. If the learner cannot yet read the relations between sentences inside a paragraph, go back to prim:grow-text, from one sentence to one paragraph
learnerAction: Step 1 Label functions: choose for each paragraph what it is doing (locked: set the background / state the claim / give evidence / concede a point / close). The skeleton diagram grows at the same time, and in the end the learner sees which link is missing

Step 2 Recognise the shape, and see whether details attach: from the topic sentences alone, recognise the shape of the whole text, or judge whether each detail sentence attaches under its topic sentence (locked: attaches / changed topic / went beyond the scope / only repeats / actually argues against — the last two are the reverse half)
Step 3 Write a paragraph: write a paragraph for the empty link on the skeleton. Begin with the signal for that function, and insert it back into its place in the text
systemResponse: As each paragraph is labelled, a colour appears at the left of the paragraph and a section grows on the skeleton at the right. When all are labelled, the empty row in the "five functions" table lights up
A wrong function choice is not simply called wrong. It tells the learner what this paragraph actually does (for example, "This is a close. It is shrinking everything before it")

After an attachment judgment, the detail card flies up and attaches under the topic sentence, or falls below with a reason label. After the scope of the topic sentence is changed, a card previously marked "went beyond the scope" attaches again
The paragraph written in Step 3 is inserted back into the text, and on the skeleton diagram that link goes from dashed line to solid line

ui.screen: On the left is the text, arranged by paragraph, with a function colour band at the left edge of each paragraph. On the right are the vertical skeleton diagram and the "five functions" count table. Step 2 switches to shape-diagram options (bar sketches, not text)
interactions: Click a paragraph or choose it with the up and down arrow keys, number keys choose the function
In Step 2, drag detail cards to the "attach / fall off" areas, or press Y/N
In Step 3, type directly at the insertion point
ui.childVariant: Use a three-panel story (beginning, middle, end) instead of argument functions. The learner puts three picture cards into the skeleton and says what each panel is "about". The attachment judgment becomes "Is this sentence about the same thing?"
ui.adultVariant: Material comes from commentary, reports and proposals. Add comparison and problem-solution shapes. Step 3 asks for a concession paragraph with a sentence that turns back
ui.accessibility: Functions are marked with both a text label and colour. The skeleton diagram has an equivalent text list. Drag and drop has a keyboard alternative

kcSignals: KCs on text and writing whose notions include discourse-organisation (kt:en-fn-systematic-argument, kt:en-skill-read-argument, kt:en-formal-signposting, kt:ja-skill-write-paragraph, kt:ja-written-connectives, kt:zh-discourse-connectives, kt:zh-skill-write-l5)
itemTypes include read-comprehend and situated-production-written
commonErrors contain text-connection errors such as "然后／それから in every sentence" or "treating つまり as 总之"
learnerSignals: after reading, does not know what the text argues
understands every paragraph but cannot describe the structure of the whole
"going off topic", "after finishing one sentence I don't know what to write next"
contraindications: the material has only one or two paragraphs and no text structure to divide
the learner still cannot understand single sentences within a paragraph
literary narrative should not be forced into argument functions

rules: The first sentence of the paragraph written in Step 3 must contain the signal of that function (concession paragraph: en Granted／Admittedly, ja 確かに～が・もちろん～しかし, zh 诚然、固然……但、当然……不过), and a concession paragraph must be followed by a sentence that turns back (blocks an answer that is too weak: concede without turning back)
The written paragraph must not share more than half of its content words with the existing paragraphs, and a paragraph that restates the original text does not pass (blocks gaming)
Data level: the order of function options is fixed. At least one text has two shapes nested together. Each of the five kinds of attachment item appears at least once
In Step 2, "went beyond the scope" must be solved by changing the topic sentence. Deleting the detail does not count as correct
check.independence: The first label of each paragraph in Step 1 is recorded separately. A changed choice after seeing the explanation "what this paragraph actually does" is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 shows no model paragraph

evidence.retained: Kept on this text: each paragraph's first function label, changed choices, attachment judgments, revised topic sentences and the inserted paragraph

licensed.claim: Can mark the text function of each paragraph in a short text and point out the missing link
Can judge whether a detail supports the topic sentence
Can write a paragraph of a specified function and connect it into the whole text

prohibited: judging from this that the learner can independently write a structurally complete argumentative essay
treating recognising signal words as understanding text structure
using one text shape as the only correct way of writing when evaluating the learner's draft

hints: Ask only "If this paragraph were deleted, what would the text be missing?"
Highlight the topic sentence and the signal words inside the paragraph
Show a typical opening sentence for each function
scaffold.fade: After two texts in a row where the first-label accuracy reaches 80%, remove the signal-word highlighting. Step 3 never has a model paragraph

primitives.reverseHalf: There is always a row empty on the skeleton table (the text never concedes). When two shapes are nested, both ways of recognising are right. A detail that "went beyond the scope" is not deleted but fixed by changing the topic sentence. The last sentence does not connect back but takes a step outward. In ja kishōtenketsu, "ten" is a change of viewpoint, not a rebuttal, and applying an English argumentative frame to it gives a wrong judgment. In zh, a paragraph can lay out first and state the point later, with the topic sentence at the end of the paragraph, so "the topic sentence must be at the start of the paragraph" cannot be taken as a rule

failureModes.failure: The learner labels by signal words alone (sees however and marks a concession)
failureModes.mitigation: Include paragraphs whose signal word does not match the actual function, and paragraphs with no signal word
failureModes.test: In the adversarial examples, one third of the paragraphs have the signal word removed or a misleading signal word inserted

failureModes.failure: The Step 3 paragraph is all concession and does not turn back
failureModes.mitigation: Check that a concession paragraph contains a turning-back sentence
failureModes.test: Build a paragraph that only grants the other side's view. It must be blocked

failureModes.failure: The text habits of one language are taken as universal rules
failureModes.mitigation: ja and zh each have at least one text in a shape native to that language (起承転結, general-specific-general, point at the end of the paragraph)
failureModes.test: Test with a 起承転結 text. When the "転" paragraph is labelled as a rebuttal, give an explanation and do not simply mark it wrong

stacksWith.how: After recognising the shape, at the junction between paragraphs of the same text, bet on the function of the next paragraph and then open it to check
Overlay coreference chains on the same text and see which referent runs through the whole piece and in which paragraph it is reworded
The paragraph written in Step 3 is saved first as a draft, then compared side by side with the original author's paragraph of the same function

languages.en: Functions bg/claim/concede/evidence/close (c25). Shapes problem/compare/cause/claim (c32). Attachment fit/offtopic/toobig/echo/against and topic-sentence scope narrow/wide/right/shifted (c39). Relay writing word/pron/general/link/close (c45). Existing implementations: c25, c32, c39, c45
languages.ja: Functions: 問題提起 / 主張 / 具体例・根拠 / 反論の受容 (確かに～。しかし～) / 結論. Shapes: two sets, 序論・本論・結論 and 起承転結. Signals: まず・次に・一方・つまり・したがって・ただし・なお. Traps: influenced by "然后", using それから in every sentence; treating つまり as "in sum"; mixing だから・でも into written prose; using なお for contrast or cause
languages.zh: Functions: state the thesis / give an example / quote / concede (诚然……但是) / sum up (由此可见、总之). Shapes: general-specific-general, specific-general, parallel, progressive, problem-solution. Signals: 首先、其次、另外、总之、后来、结果. Traps: English speakers always say "然后" for and then; "后来" used for the future; first of all translated literally as "第一个"

primitives.name: Predict the next move
primitives.oneLine: At a connective or a pause, bet first on the direction of the next sentence, then read or listen to the actual content and check
primitives.difficulty: The learner knows the connectives but does not use them when reading and listening. They do not react to however, でも or 可是. In listening they are completely passive and lose the thread the moment attention drifts. They are fooled by signal words (and it is followed by but; the second half of ～んですけど is left unsaid; "本来……结果" and "其实" bring a reversal). In production they do not mark the relation between two sentences, or mark every one as so / 所以, carrying meaning-based juxtaposition straight into the target language.
primitives.object: A coherent piece of material: adjacent sentences in writing, or a recording with time codes. The next sentence is covered at every connection point. The direction the learner bets at each turning point and the result of the check stay on this material
primitives.requires: Can understand single sentences (read or heard) and knows the meaning of the common connectives. If the learner cannot grasp single-sentence structure, go back to prim:strip-skeleton first. For the listening version, if the words in the speech stream cannot yet be made out, do prim:transcript-diff first
learnerAction: Step 1 Bet on a direction: after reading or hearing sentence A (and the connective, if there is one), bet one card from the locked directions (continue in the same direction / turn around / draw a result / give an example and expand / it does not continue from this sentence — the reverse half). Only after betting is the next sentence turned over or can it be played

Step 2 Check and tell apart: pick the original from three continuations that all read smoothly. Or judge which family of relation holds between the two sentences (cause-effect / concession / just sequence / two sentences side by side that need no marking), then choose the right one among several markers of the same family by weight and position
Step 3 You continue: given one sentence (in the listening version, play one sentence and stop), write or say the next sentence. The learner decides the direction and marks it with a marker
systemResponse: The next sentence is unlocked only after the bet. In the listening version, the "Reveal" button stays grey until the next sentence has actually finished playing
On reveal, show side by side: the direction you bet / the direction it actually turned / the original next sentence / why
A turning point that was bet wrongly leaves a mark on the material, so that when the learner looks back they see "you bet wrong here" — exactly where attention should be pinned
When a marker of the same family is chosen wrongly, explain the difference in weight or position (therefore carries a flavour of inference, だから sounds forceful to a superior, "因此" leans written)

ui.screen: On top are the sentences already read or heard. In the middle is a bet bar (3–5 direction cards). Below is the covered next-sentence card or a play button. A narrow column on the right records what was bet at each turning point and whether it was right. No score is shown
interactions: Number keys or click to choose a direction card
Space plays or stops the current segment (listening version)
Step 3 is typed or recorded (recording stays on the page)
ui.childVariant: Use a three-panel comic: look at the first two panels and guess whether the third is "happy goes on" or "something unexpected happens". There are only two direction cards (還有 / 可是; ja: それから／でも; zh: 还有／可是). In the listening version the teacher reads the story and stops, and the child holds up a card
ui.adultVariant: Material comes from lectures, podcasts and commentary. The direction cards add "it does not continue from this sentence". Step 2 adds weight comparison of markers in the same family. Step 3 asks the learner to continue a remark in a meeting or report context
ui.accessibility: Direction cards use text and an arrow graphic, not colour alone. Betting and revealing can both be done from the keyboard. The listening version offers 0.85× / 0.7× speed, but its use is recorded

kcSignals: KCs on connection and relation (kt:en-however, kt:en-because-so, kt:en-logical-markers, kt:ja-discourse-connectives, kt:ja-written-connectives, kt:ja-noni, kt:zh-erqie-faner, kt:zh-discourse-connectives)
KCs for listening activities (kt:en-skill-listen-lectures, kt:ja-skill-listen-bridge, kt:zh-skill-listen-l4), especially where commonErrors contain "ignores the reversal brought by 其实, 本来……结果"
notions include contrast-concession, cause-reason, result, addition, sequence
learnerSignals: knows the connectives but does not use them when reading
completely passive when listening, loses the thread when attention drifts
uses and / so, 然后 / 所以 between every two sentences
contraindications: the relation between sentences in the material is carried by vocabulary the learner does not know (add the vocabulary first)
the learner cannot yet read or hear single sentences
when the next sentence is entirely unpredictable (a news-flash style list), it is not suited to betting items

rules: The bet must be submitted before the next sentence is revealed or played, otherwise it does not count as betting evidence (judged by the order of event timestamps)

Step 3 must contain a direction marker (has_any) and at least 3 content words not in the previous sentence (new_content). The two cheats "add a So and say it again" and "mark no direction" are each caught by only the matching one check
If Step 3 asks for three relations, the three cannot all be from the same family (variety). The given pair of "two sentences side by side" must not be given a relation marker (no_overlink)
Data level: each set has at least one item whose answer is "it does not continue from this sentence", at least one item with a misleading signal word, and the last item has no connective
check.independence: The first bet at each turning point in Step 1 is recorded separately. The listening version records the number of replays and whether the speed was slowed. Later items in the same set after seeing "why" are still recorded as independent, but redoing the same turning point is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 does not show the original text

evidence.retained: At each turning point of the material: the first bet, the actual direction, whether the learner was fooled by a signal word, and the number of replays. Also the continuation sentence the learner made in Step 3

licensed.claim: Can use connective signals in given material to predict the direction of the next sentence
Listens with expectations (bet comes before playback and the hit rate is above chance)
Can use a suitable marker to express the relation between sentences explicitly

prohibited: inferring overall listening or reading level from this
treating a correct direction as having understood the content of the next sentence
counting a choice made after the reveal as a prediction

hints: Ask only "After sentence A, does the speaker want to go further, turn back, or give an example?"
Highlight the signal word in sentence A (and where it may mislead)
Show a minimal example pair for each direction
scaffold.fade: After 6 turning points in a row are bet correctly on the first try (including one trap item), remove the signal-word highlighting. The listening version removes the text version of sentence A

primitives.reverseHalf: The next sentence does not always continue the previous one. One item has the answer "it does not continue from this sentence" (returns to an earlier point or sets this line aside). One item has a signal word that misleads (en: and it is followed by but; ja: ～けど used as a lead-in and not as contrast, すみませんが; zh: "而" can be contrast or coordination). Two kinds of relation should not be marked as cause-effect: simple sequence (time) and two sentences side by side (none). In Chinese meaning-based juxtaposition one "就" or "而且" is enough, but in the target language marking it announces a relation that does not exist

failureModes.failure: The learner only classifies and does not listen with expectations
failureModes.mitigation: In the listening version the Reveal button stays grey until the next sentence has finished, and the bet must come before playback
failureModes.test: Build a session where the bet timestamp is later than the start of playback, and confirm it does not count as betting evidence

failureModes.failure: The learner bets mechanically on connectives without reading the content
failureModes.mitigation: Design items with misleading signal words and items with none
failureModes.test: In the adversarial examples, one third have no connective, and at least one item has a signal word opposite to the actual direction

failureModes.failure: A sentence unrelated to the previous one can pass in Step 3
failureModes.mitigation: Check has_any and new_content together, and check that it shares at least one referent with the previous sentence
failureModes.test: Remove the direction word from the model opening, and rephrase the previous sentence. Both must be blocked

stacksWith.how: In the listening version with the same recording: bet on the direction first, then dictate the next sentence and align it, and see whether what was missed is the words at the turning point
The relation bet correctly is used directly to join two sentences into one. The direction cards and the join buttons share one set of relation families
Scale the bet up from between sentences to between paragraphs: in the same text, bet on the function of the next paragraph

languages.en: Reading directions same/turn/eg/close (c33). Listening directions on/turn/so/eg/aside, including a trap (c49, needs media). Relation families cause/concede/mind/time/none (c59). Existing implementations: c33, c49, c59. Trap: Chinese meaning-based juxtaposition transfers as and/so all the way
languages.ja: Direction cards: それに・しかも (go on saying) / でも・しかし・ところが (turn around) / だから・それで・そのため (result) / たとえば (example) / ところで・さて (does not continue from this sentence). The Japanese predicate is at the end of the sentence, and negation, conjecture and wish are revealed only at ～ない・～かもしれない・～たい. In the listening version the betting point can be placed before the predicate arrives, to bet "affirmative or negative". Traps: それで followed by a command or intention; the second half of ～んですけど omitted to signal a request or refusal; hearing 「行きたいんだけど……」 as agreement
languages.zh: Direction cards: 而且、并且 (go on saying) / 但是、可是、不过、却 (turn around) / 所以、因此、于是 (result) / 比如 (example) / 对了、话说回来 (does not continue from this sentence). Traps: catching only individual words and missing the reversal of "其实" and "本来……结果"; taking a rhetorical question as a real question; "而" is both contrast and coordination; English speakers always say "然后" for and then

primitives.name: Source & stance
primitives.oneLine: Tell the author's own words from reported ones, judge how certain the speaker is, and point to the evidence at its place in the text
primitives.difficulty: The learner takes a view the author is reporting as the author's own. They cannot read which reporting verb shows whom the author trusts and whom not. They read a guess as a conclusion. After listening they cannot say which things the other person said and which they inferred themselves, so when relaying it comes out as "he said …". In production they either speak too absolutely or pile up softening words.
primitives.object: An argumentative passage (or a spoken contribution with time codes) with reported speech and different degrees of certainty. Each sentence has a position on two tracks, "author's own words / reporting someone", and on one certainty ladder. The evidence (a position in the text or a time code) is pinned to the text
primitives.requires: Can understand the gist of the material (read or heard) and recognises basic "say, think" verbs and modal words. If the learner cannot even grasp the paragraph structure, go back to prim:discourse-map first
learnerAction: Step 1 Sort to tracks and rank: judge for each sentence whether it is the author's own words or reported, and when it is reported, where the author stands (locked: neutral report / on his side / keeps distance / concedes a point). Or rank five ways of saying the same thing by certainty, from the boldest to the least bold

Step 2 Point to evidence: for a report or a conclusion, make a judgment (locked: he said exactly that / reworded but the meaning is the same / only half right / can be inferred but he did not say it — the reverse half / he said the opposite), and point to the position in the text or the time code

Step 3 Write it twice: report the same statement twice (once keeping distance, once standing with the speaker, changing only the verb or the source marker), or correct a report that treats an inference as the speaker's words
systemResponse: As each sentence is judged, it falls onto the matching track, and the reporting verb is underlined and coloured by stance. After sorting, the system spreads out "how few sentences are the author's own words, and where they are"
After ranking, each sentence gets the softening device it uses (degree adverb, modal, attributing to a source, condition)

When the evidence point is a hit, the matching place in the text is highlighted. When the judgment is "can be inferred but he did not say it", the page shows the closest passage and explains why it cannot support this sentence
In Step 3 the two versions are shown side by side, with the differences coloured

ui.screen: Two tracks one above the other (author's words / reported), with the reported track coloured by stance. The Step 1 ranking version is a column of draggable sentence cards. In Step 2, below is a timeline or a text-locator bar. The right column shows the number of sentences judged. No score is shown
interactions: Number keys choose the track and stance
Ranking can be dragged, or moved with the up and down arrow keys
The timeline uses a range control, the left and right arrow keys fine-tune it, and Enter confirms "right here"
ui.childVariant: Becomes "Who said it?": several characters in a story speak, the child drags the speech bubbles onto the speakers, then sorts into "he really saw it" and "he guessed". No certainty ladder
ui.adultVariant: Material comes from news, research abstracts and meeting remarks. Add academic reporting verbs and multi-level reporting. Step 3 rewrites a distorted set of meeting minutes
ui.accessibility: Tracks and stances use text labels plus colour. Ranking has a keyboard alternative. The timeline control is natively keyboard-operable and reads out the current time

kcSignals: KCs whose notions include reported-speech, possibility-probability, evaluation-attitude (kt:en-reporting-verbs, kt:en-fn-hedging, kt:en-certainty-scale, kt:ja-sou-hearsay, kt:ja-evidentials, kt:ja-quotation, kt:zh-keneng-dagai, kt:zh-stance-markers)
activity KCs that require relaying or mediating (kt:en-skill-relay-information, kt:ja-skill-mediate-ja, kt:zh-skill-translate-mid)
commonErrors contain mixing appearance with hearsay, stacked softening words, over-assertion
learnerSignals: takes a quoted view as the author's own
does not know which side the author is on
"Did he say it or not?" chooses the "not stated in the text" option on listening questions
contraindications: the material has no reporting and no change in certainty
the learner cannot yet recognise the forms of reporting and modality (do prim:form-for-meaning first)
in everyday greetings and dialogue dominated by politeness softening, do not test politeness softening as uncertainty

rules: In Step 3 the keep-distance version must contain a source marker or a distancing verb, and the stand-with version must contain an affirming verb. The two versions must share basically the same content words except for the verb or source marker (blocks an answer that is too weak)

When correcting a distorted report, the learner must both mark the source (has_any) and keep at least one concrete fact (variety). Empty text made all of hedges and a copy of the original report are each caught by only the matching one check (blocks gaming)

The version of "not a single softening word allowed" is checked for no softening device. Within one clause there may be no more than two softening devices (en might possibly perhaps, ja ～かもしれないらしい, zh 可能大概也许 stacked do not pass)
The hit windows of evidence points must not overlap, and a window must be no narrower than ±2 seconds and no wider than ±10 seconds. The category "can be inferred but he did not say it" must appear
check.independence: The first track assignment of each sentence in Step 1, and the first judgment and first location for each item in Step 2, are recorded separately. The listening version records the number of replays. A changed judgment after seeing "the closest passage" is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 shows no model

evidence.retained: Kept on the text: each sentence's track, stance, position on the certainty ladder, first judgment and evidence point. Also the two versions of the report or the corrected report from Step 3

licensed.claim: Can tell the author's own words from reported ones, and read the stance that a reporting verb expresses
Can judge the higher or lower certainty of the same statement
Can tell what the text said from what they inferred themselves, and point to the evidence position
Controls source and certainty appropriately in reporting and writing

prohibited: judging the learner's level of critical thinking from this
treating being able to use softening words as judging accurately
counting evidence found after a hint as independent completion

hints: Ask only "Whose sentence is this? Does the author believe it?"
Highlight the reporting verb, source marker and modal words
Show a comparison of how the stance changes when the same sentence takes a different verb
scaffold.fade: After two passages in a row where the first track accuracy reaches 80%, stop highlighting reporting verbs. After 4 evidence points in a row are hit on the first try, stop showing "the closest passage"

primitives.reverseHalf: There is always one item that is "can be inferred but he did not say it", and the inference may well be right. "Some researchers believe…" looks better supported, but the author is actually stepping back. ja: 思います is often only politeness softening and does not necessarily show uncertainty; ～そうだ has two readings, appearance and hearsay, and ～らしい has two, inference and hearsay (same form, different source). zh: in speech "我觉得" is mostly politeness and does not mean the speaker is unsure; "据说" keeps distance and "研究表明" stands with the claim

failureModes.failure: The learner uses quotation marks or the presence of a reporting verb as the only criterion
failureModes.mitigation: Include sentences that have no reporting verb but are in fact reports (reportedly, ～とのことだ, 据悉)
failureModes.test: In the adversarial examples, at least one sentence is a distance report with no reporting verb

failureModes.failure: The learner is too cautious and writes empty text made all of hedges
failureModes.mitigation: The variety rule requires at least one concrete fact to be kept
failureModes.test: Build a submission with only the sentence "he didn't commit". It must be blocked

failureModes.failure: Politeness softening is taken as uncertainty
failureModes.mitigation: In ja/zh material, include polite 思います／我觉得 and set items that tell them apart
failureModes.test: In the adversarial examples, half of the sentences are politeness softening and half are real conjecture

stacksWith.how: Overlay paragraph functions on the same text and see that the author's own words concentrate in the paragraphs that state the claim and close
In the listening version, first align the transcript on the same recording, then point to the evidence time codes on the aligned transcript
The two reported versions from Step 3 are then adjusted for formality by the relationship with the reader, stacking two layers of judgment on the same sentence

languages.en: Stances neutral/back/distance/concede (c31). Softening devices degree/modal/attrib/cond (c34). Evidence judgments said/same/part/infer/no (c53, needs media). Existing implementations: c31, c34, c53. Traps: suggest sb to do, *It might possibly perhaps…, translating "可能" literally as Maybe it can
languages.ja: Reporting markers: ～と言う・～によると・～そうだ (hearsay)・～とのことだ・～と言われている. Stance verbs: 認める・指摘する・主張する・強調する. Certainty ladder: だ > はずだ > だろう > ようだ・らしい > かもしれない. Traps: taking appearance for hearsay (meaning to say "I hear it's delicious" but saying *おいしそうです); dropping だ after a noun (*休みそうです); using らしい for one's own bodily feelings
languages.zh: Reporting verbs: 指出、认为、声称、承认、强调、表示. Source markers: 据……、根据……、……说、据悉. Certainty ladder: 一定、肯定 > 应该 > 大概、可能 > 也许、说不定. Traps: stacking "在我看来" and "我觉得"; misusing "显然的"; treating "毕竟" as "终于"; "一定" covers both conjecture and necessity

primitives.name: Transcript diff
primitives.oneLine: Write down what you heard first, then align it word by word with the transcript, and see where the sound changed and what was missed
primitives.difficulty: The learner knows every word but cannot understand them strung together. Familiar words change shape in the speech stream (linking, weak forms, dropped sounds, merged sounds), and the learner has stored only the dictionary shape. Japanese adds contractions (てる・ちゃう・なきゃ), vowel devoicing, and missing the mora count of long vowels and geminate consonants. Chinese adds tone sandhi (不, 一, third-tone sequences), neutral tone, erhua and sound merging. Another kind of failure is missing one sentence, getting stuck going back over it, and so losing the next ten seconds too.
primitives.object: A recording with time codes (each segment 6–14 words or 10–25 characters, several segments) and the learner's own dictation. The word-by-word (ja mora by mora, zh syllable by syllable) alignment bar stays on this same recording
primitives.requires: Most words in the recording are familiar words the learner can read. If the learner cannot yet tell single phonemes or tones apart, go back to prim:sound-contrast first
learnerAction: Step 1 Dictate and align: listen as many times as wanted, write down what you heard, and after submitting, align it word by word (mora by mora, syllable by syllable) with the transcript

Step 2 Find the change: given the text, point to the seam between two words where the change happens, and classify it (locked: linked / weakened / swallowed / merged into one sound / nothing changed — the reverse half). Or, in a three-slot strip where the middle sentence is blanked out, judge what it is doing and what to do (it can be inferred / a new fact, mark it and keep listening / it carries nothing, ignore it)
Step 3 A long passage with no comparison: only a play bar. Write down everything heard in the whole passage, and type ___ where it was not clear
systemResponse: After alignment the top row is what you wrote and the bottom row is the transcript, one word per column. Matching columns fade, substitutions, omissions and additions are highlighted, and columns the author marked as traps get a border

Spelling differences that do not affect meaning (en any more / anymore; ja 今日 / きょう; zh homophones other than 的/得 are recorded separately) are stated plainly in the header as "this one does not count"

After a correct seam is clicked in Step 2, a diagram of the change is drawn between the two words (a linking arc, a greyed weak-form word, a struck-out swallowed consonant), and that short stretch can be played alone
In Step 3, two gauges show live: coverage (how many words of the transcript you wrote down) and accuracy (how many words you wrote are really in the transcript)

ui.screen: At the top is a play bar (can slow to 0.85× / 0.7× and loop the current segment). In the middle is the input box. After submission, a two-row alignment table opens below the input box. In Step 3, the right side has two gauges and the prompt "type ___ if you did not catch it"
interactions: Space plays / pauses, R replays the current segment
Tab moves between alignment columns to view the explanation of the difference in each column
In Step 2, left and right arrow keys move between word seams, Enter selects, number keys choose the category
ui.childVariant: No writing required: after hearing one sentence, tap the one heard from three pictures or word cards, or arrange word cards in the order heard. Of the change categories only "linked" is taught, shown by two blocks joined together
ui.adultVariant: Material comes from film dialogue, podcasts and news. All five kinds of change, with different accents added. Step 3 uses longer passages and requires coverage and accuracy to meet the bar at the same time
ui.accessibility: Differences are marked with colour and symbol (substitution ≠, omission −, addition ＋). The alignment table can be read column by column by screen readers. All playback controls have keyboard shortcuts. When no usable media is available, the page says plainly that it falls back to machine speech, which contains no real speech-stream changes

kcSignals: component is phonological and the KC involves the speech stream (kt:en-phon-linking, kt:en-phon-weak-forms, kt:en-phon-word-boundaries, kt:ja-soc-casual-contractions, kt:ja-sound-devoice, kt:ja-sound-sokuon, kt:ja-sound-long, kt:zh-tone-sandhi, kt:zh-pinyin-erhua)
itemTypes include dictation or listen-discriminate
commonErrors of listening activity KCs mention contracted forms not heard, numbers and times misheard, catching only individual words
learnerSignals: knows every word but cannot understand them strung together
"They speak too fast"
missing one sentence throws the whole passage off, and gets stuck when something is unclear
contraindications: the recording has too many new words (the problem is vocabulary, not perception)
material with only machine speech and no real speech stream cannot be used to teach the changes
when the learner cannot yet write the target script, use the child version's tap-to-select form

rules: In Step 3, coverage and accuracy must both reach the threshold. Writing only the few content words understood (low coverage) and filling every blank with plausible words (low accuracy) are each caught by only one of the two checks
___ is filtered out in the calculation, so typing ___ as prompted does not lower accuracy
Step 2 passes only when both the position and the category of the seam are right, and the two kinds of error get different feedback. Each set has exactly one sentence with "nothing changed"

Triage of blanked-out parts: a number, month or name that is not in the context must be marked as not heard and not made up (making up a number does not pass). The slot that can be inferred must be filled in with its meaning (marking everything with a question mark does not pass)

In ja the alignment unit is the mora, and a missed mora in a geminate or long vowel is recorded separately. In zh alignment has two layers, pinyin and characters. "Sound right, character wrong" and "sound wrong" are recorded separately, and tone errors are marked on their own
check.independence: In Step 1 record the number of plays for each segment and whether it was slowed, and save the first submission separately. In Step 2 the first seam click is recorded separately. Redoing the same segment after seeing the alignment result is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 has no comparison of any kind

evidence.retained: Kept on each recording: the first dictation, the number of plays, the alignment differences (sorted by change category), the seam results of Step 2 and the two gauge values of Step 3

licensed.claim: Can recognise one kind of speech-stream change in controlled segments
Dictation errors concentrate mainly in one kind of change
When something is missed, can tell what to infer, what to mark, and what gap can be ignored

prohibited: giving an overall listening level from this
treating a fully correct dictation as being able to understand at real speed
counting dictation done after slowing down or replaying many times as performance at normal speed

hints: Say only "In this segment there is one place where two words run together"
Play the two words near the wrong column alone, at slow speed
Play the dictionary form and the speech-stream form side by side
scaffold.fade: After 3 items in a row of the same kind of change are correct on the first try, stop hinting that kind. Slowed playback is not available in Step 3

primitives.reverseHalf: "Nothing changed": when the speaker is stressing, every word is said in full, and being unusually clear is itself information. A place that is "written wrongly but means the same" does not count as an error, to keep the learner from fussing over spelling and missing the real listening failure. If the missed sentence is a new fact not in the context, the right action is to mark it and keep listening, and making it up is not allowed. If it carries nothing, ignore it. ja: the full form that is not contracted in formal settings must also be recognised. zh: "一" as an ordinal (第一) keeps its original tone, since not every "一" changes tone

failureModes.failure: The learner attributes all "couldn't hear it" to linking
failureModes.mitigation: Each set must have a sentence where "nothing changed", and the learner has to press it themselves
failureModes.test: Adversarial example: include a sentence with stressed emphasis and no change at all

failureModes.failure: The learner fills every blank with plausible words to raise coverage
failureModes.mitigation: Check coverage and accuracy together
failureModes.test: Build a submission that fills all blanks with common words. Its accuracy must be below the threshold

failureModes.failure: A zh learner hears the sound right but writes the wrong character, and is judged as a listening failure
failureModes.mitigation: Align and record the pinyin layer and the character layer separately
failureModes.test: Submit a dictation with homophone characters. It must be recorded as "sound right, character wrong" and not as missed

stacksWith.how: On the same segment where the changes were aligned, go on to mark pauses and stress and shadow it, and compare with your own speech stream
Pause the same recording between sentences and bet on the direction first, then dictate the next sentence and align it, and see whether what was missed is the turning point
In the long passage of Step 3, look only at the alignment results of the number and date cells, and review by error type

languages.en: Five kinds of change link/weak/drop/merge/full (c47, needs media). Triage of blanked-out parts reason/contrast/feeling/fact/nothing (c50, needs media). Existing implementations: c47, c50. Trap: Chinese speakers pronounce word by word and add a vowel after consonants, and when listening also look for the dictionary form
languages.ja: Kinds of change: contraction (ている→てる, てしまう→ちゃう, なければ→なきゃ, では→じゃ) / vowel devoicing (です, した) / missed moras (long vowel, geminate, moraic nasal) / rendaku and sound changes (a change in form, where the original word must be recognised) / no change (a polite, carefully read-out form). Alignment is by kana mora, and differences in how kanji and kana are written do not count. Traps: hearing 「終わってない」 as 「終わった」; not knowing that 「なきゃ」 expresses obligation
languages.zh: Kinds of change: tone sandhi (不, 一, third-tone sequences) / neutral tone / erhua / merging and weakening (我们→m'men, 这样→zhèiyàng, weakened 不知道) / no change (stressed emphasis). Alignment has two layers, pinyin syllables and characters. Homophone character errors are recorded separately, and tone errors are marked on their own. Traps: mishearing a changed number or time (recording "moved to 2 p.m." as the original time); catching only individual words and missing the reversal brought by "其实"

primitives.name: Listening for data
primitives.oneLine: Record only the key information that fits the allowed cells (numbers, dates, times, prices), then review by error type
primitives.difficulty: Numbers are words you cannot guess back, but the more common failure is that the number is remembered and attached to the wrong thing: the learner hears four hundred thousand but misses over three years; cannot tell teens from tens; records the speaker's approximation as an exact figure; or tries to note everything while listening and ends up retaining nothing. In Japanese the learner also has to get through counter sound changes (いっぽん／さんぼん／ろっぽん) and special readings of dates and clock times (ついたち, はつか, 四時よじ, 九時くじ). In Chinese the hurdles are 二/两, 一百零五 vs 一百五, 块/毛, dates running from large to small, and years read digit by digit.
primitives.object: A number-dense recording (with time codes) and a table the project has already provided: on each row the "number" and the "unit / time / range" go into two separate cells, and the number of cells is capped. The learner fills in, revises and reviews on this one table from start to finish.
primitives.requires: Without the recording, the learner can already read aloud and write the basic numbers, clock times, dates and prices of the language (see KCs such as kt:*-numerals and kt:*-time-expressions). If the learner cannot read the numbers, fall back to sound discrimination first.
learnerAction: Step 1 Fill only the cells: listen row by row, each row played once (one replay may be requested), and put the number and its unit / time range in two separate cells. For a row where the speaker did not give an exact number, press "He didn't give an exact number" and do not fill in a number.

Step 2 Classify someone else's record: look at a table that someone else filled in wrongly and decide, row by row, which type of error it contains (locked options: similar-sounding numbers confused / number right but unit wrong / place value or order wrong / a period recorded as a point in time / approximate number recorded as exact, where the last one runs the opposite way and means "recorded too precisely").
Step 3 Say something with these numbers: listen to a new recording, then write or say one complete sentence that states the numbers heard together with their respective qualifiers.
systemResponse: After each row is filled in, the system puts the learner's "number + unit" back together as a sentence of meaning ("What you recorded: 400,000 a year") and shows it next to the original sentence. The error is pinned to the specific cell, rather than the whole row being marked wrong.

After "He didn't give an exact number" is pressed, the approximation markers in the original speech (roughly / くらい・ほど / 左右・来) are highlighted. If the button is pressed on an exact-number row, the exact number in the original speech is highlighted.
After classification in Step 2, the matching segment on the recording timeline is marked with the colour and name of that error type, and the learner can click back to listen to that spot.
After Step 3 is submitted, each number in the sentence is labelled with the qualifier it is attached to, and bare numbers with no qualifier are marked separately.

ui.screen: The top is a playback bar (time code, one ▶ per row). The middle is a three-column table (item already given / number / unit · time · range), with a "He didn't give an exact number" button at the end of each row. The narrow right-hand column counts the five error types and shows no total score.
interactions: Space plays / pauses; R replays this row (counted)
Tab moves between the number cell and the unit cell
Numbers may be written as Arabic numerals, target-language number words, or Chinese; full-width characters are folded to half-width automatically
Step 3 can be typed or recorded in the page
ui.childVariant: The table is replaced by picture cards (a number of apples, a clock face, a calendar square), and the learner taps or drags number cards instead of typing. Numbers are limited to 1–20, o'clock and half past; only two error types are kept, "number heard wrongly" and "the thing does not match"; the approximate row becomes "He said 'lots', not a number".
ui.adultVariant: Materials are real scenes: airport rebooking announcements, meeting budgets, courier delivery windows, medication doses. Each row is played once, and the cell limit (for example five cells) forces the learner to record only what should be recorded. Error types are shown with their technical names.
ui.accessibility: Playback speed can be lowered to 0.75×, but changing speed and replaying both count as assisted. A reading version that replaces the audio with a transcript is provided for learners with hearing impairment (the evidence is labelled separately as reading). Error types use both text and icons, not colour alone.

kcSignals: notions include quantity or time-location
the label involves numbers, clock times, dates, prices, counters / measure words (such as kt:ja-counters, kt:ja-calendar-dates, kt:zh-money-prices, kt:en-numbers-ordinal-dates)
itemTypes include listen-comprehend, dictation or form-fill
commonErrors include pronunciation-type errors (*よんじ, *さんひゃく, *二块, *一百五 meaning 105)
learnerSignals: "I heard the number but what I wrote down is wrong"
cannot tell thirteen / thirty, or 四 / 十
cannot remember the time and platform when listening to an announcement
notes become a running account, and nothing can be found later
contraindications: the learner cannot read these numbers even without listening (practise sound discrimination and the number words themselves first)
the numbers in the material carry no task meaning (a number mentioned in passing should not go into the table)
when the goal is word-by-word dictation, use prim:transcript-diff instead

rules: The number cell and the unit cell are judged separately. Normalisation keeps Chinese characters and kana and folds full-width to half-width; 14 / fourteen / 十四 / じゅうよん are all accepted (blocks false rejection).
An empty unit cell or a wrongly attached unit fails even if the number is right (blocks an answer that is too weak: recording only the number).

An approximate row must be marked "He didn't give an exact number", and filling in an exact number is wrong. Pressing the button on an exact-number row is also wrong, and the button usage rate is counted; a learner who presses it on every row fails the whole set (blocks gaming).

Step 3: at least two different numbers, and each number must be followed by a unit or range. Writing only a description (very expensive / 高い) or only a string of bare numbers fails (blocks both ends at once).

Every number required in Step 3 must be findable in the original speech. For an item marked as approximate / range, the original speech must really contain an approximation or range marker (checks the item itself in reverse).
check.independence: The first fill-in of each row is recorded separately. Replaying, changing speed and viewing the transcript are each recorded as assisted completion. Step 3 does not show the table or the original speech.

evidence.retained: For each row, the first fill-in, the number of replays, the changes, and the error type assigned are all kept on this table, along with the Step 3 sentences.

licensed.claim: Can record a number and its qualifier when the recording is played only once
Can tell the speaker's approximate numbers from exact ones
Can diagnose which type a number-listening error belongs to

prohibited: Inferring overall listening level from an all-correct table
Counting a correct fill-in after replay or speed change as independent completion
Treating being able to read numbers as the same as being able to hear them
Inferring from correct Step 2 classification alone that the learner will not make this kind of error when listening

hints: Ask only: "Does this row want the total or the amount per year? A point in time or a period?"
Replay this row and mark on the timeline the short stretch where the unit or range is
Show this row's transcript with the number and unit covered
scaffold.fade: After 3 consecutive rows of the same number type are filled in correctly on the first attempt, remove level 2 and 3 hints and withdraw the "one replay" option.

primitives.reverseHalf: Each set of material has at least one row where the speaker gave no exact number at all, and the right action is to mark "no exact number given" rather than record a number. This teaches "record numbers accurately" with the boundary that "an approximation must not be recorded as an exact number". There is also a kind of information that need not be recorded (modifiers that do not fit in the limited cells), and recording it only crowds out what should be recorded.

failureModes.failure: The table checks only the number, and the learner learns to record only the number and not the unit
failureModes.mitigation: The number and the unit are in two cells judged separately, and a wrong unit fails the whole row
failureModes.test: A simulated answer with the right number and the wrong unit must be judged as failed

failureModes.failure: Normalisation erases Chinese characters and kana, so valid spellings can never match
failureModes.mitigation: Normalise only by folding full-width and removing spaces, keeping Chinese and Japanese script
failureModes.test: 四月／4月／しがつ and 两点／2点 all match

failureModes.failure: The learner presses "He didn't give an exact number" on every row they are unsure of
failureModes.mitigation: Pressing it on an exact-number row counts as wrong, and the usage rate is counted
failureModes.test: A simulated answer that presses the button on every row has a pass rate of 0

failureModes.failure: Japanese / Chinese learners write Arabic numerals to avoid the reading, so sound-change problems never show up
failureModes.mitigation: Step 2 has a dedicated sound-change or 二/两 category, and the spoken version of Step 3 requires reading aloud
failureModes.test: Adversarial examples: さんぼん read as *さんほん and *二块 must appear in Step 2 and be classifiable

stacksWith.how: On the same recording, after the table is filled in, expand the wrongly answered row into a word-by-word alignment to see which sound change swallowed the unit
In Japanese and Chinese, the table's "unit" cell is the counter / measure word, so filling it in also checks the classifier and its sound change
When the gaps on the information cards are numbers, times and prices, the answers asked for go into the same two-cell table and are checked with a confirmation question

languages.en: Five locked types: teen (SIX-ty / six-TEEN stress position), unit (number right, unit wrong), order (place value and decimals, two point three), range (ten till one), approx (roughly / a couple of / around). Common for Chinese native speakers: errors converting by 万 (fifteen ten thousand), adding -s to hundreds, using cardinal numbers for dates. Existing implementations: c51, c48
languages.ja: Types change to: sound change (いっぽん・さんぼん・ろっぽん, さんぜん・はっせん・ろっぴゃく), special readings (ついたち・ふつか…とおか・はつか, 四時よじ・七時しちじ・九時くじ, 四月しがつ, ひとり・ふたり), 万 carry (一万＝いちまん, place value of 十万 / 百万), range (～から～まで, までに), approximation (くらい・ほど・約・～前後; ～ごろ for points in time, ぐらい for quantities). The unit cell is the counter, and days of the week cannot be derived from Chinese numerals.
languages.zh: Types change to: 二/两 (两点, 两块 vs 二十, 二号), zero (一百零五 vs 一百五＝150), money (块/毛/元角分; "八块五" is 8.5), dates from large to small and years read digit by digit (二〇二五年), clock times (两点一刻, 差五分三点, 半), approximation (左右, 大概, 来, 多, adjacent numbers used together as in "三四个"), range (从……到……). For English native speakers, the place value of 万 is a core order-type issue, and 四/十 sì/shí belong to the similar-sound type.

primitives.name: Listen and do
primitives.oneLine: Hear one instruction and make one move on the screen (tap, drag, place); the move itself is the evidence of understanding
primitives.difficulty: When listening to instructions, learners catch only the verb or the first noun and miss modifiers and positions: for Colour the small ball red they colour the ball without noticing the size; they confuse on/under, left/right, 上/下 and 前/後ろ; in class they wait for others to act and then imitate, which looks like understanding but is not. Adults, in directions and operating instructions, remember only the first step and miss negations (～ないでください, 不要……) and conditions.
primitives.object: An operable scene (classroom, desktop, room, street map, device panel) with objects that can be tapped, dragged or coloured, plus a series of pre-recorded instruction audios. The whole primitive is done on this one scene, and the scene state is kept throughout.
primitives.requires: The learner knows the names of the objects in the scene (can be taught first with prim:recall-before-reveal or prim:scene-walkthrough). Do not start while the object names are still unknown.
learnerAction: Step 1 Hear one, do one: listen without looking at text, and after each instruction make one move in the scene. The move is not judged right or wrong immediately; the object stays where the learner put it.

Step 2 Compare what differs: replay the instruction, and the learner compares it with the scene and judges for themselves which type of difference there is: wrong object / wrong attribute (size, colour, number) / wrong position / wrong order / no difference. The last is the reverse half: part of the instruction is not to be done or cannot be done (a negative instruction, or an "if … then …" whose condition is not met).

Step 3 Give the instruction the other way round: given a target scene state, the learner builds or types an instruction with word cards, and the system executes it literally to see whether the target state can be reproduced. The learner can also say it to a real partner outside the page, who carries it out.
systemResponse: After each move the scene records the new position and state of the object. It shows no right or wrong until Step 2.
In the Step 2 replay, the instruction is divided into phrases. As each phrase is heard, the matching object or position in the scene flashes, so the learner sees for themselves which part was missed.

In Step 3 the system parses the learner's written instruction deterministically against a controlled word list and executes it literally. When an attribute is missing, it picks at random one object that fits the literal wording, so the learner sees the consequence of an ambiguous instruction. It does no open-ended understanding and no automatic scoring of spoken instructions.

ui.screen: The whole screen is the scene. At the top are a large play button and the replay count. Text subtitles are off by default. In Step 2 a row of difference-type buttons appears under the scene. In Step 3 the bottom has a word-card bar or input box and a "Run literally" button.
interactions: Tap an object to select it, then tap the target position to put it down (an alternative to drag and drop)
Space plays or replays; number keys choose the difference type
On touch screens objects have large snap areas, suited to fingers
ui.childVariant: Each instruction has only one action plus one attribute or position; objects are large and few (4–6); at most two replays; no text; no demonstration animation is played, to avoid imitation. Step 3 builds the instruction with picture word cards, and an adult may read it aloud with the child.
ui.adultVariant: The scene is a street map, station, device panel or table. Instructions run two or three steps in sequence and include negation and conditions; speech rate can be adjusted. Step 3 is writing operating instructions for a colleague.
ui.accessibility: Every drag and drop has a tap-to-select alternative. Subtitles can be turned on, but completion with subtitles on is recorded as assisted. This primitive does not suit learners with hearing impairment, who should use a reading task with written instructions instead.

kcSignals: the KC is about listening to instructions or classroom language (kt:en-skill-listen-and-do, kt:en-fn-classroom-language, kt:ja-fn-classroom-language, kt:zh-fn-classroom-language, kt:zh-skill-listen-basic)
route and operation KCs (kt:en-skill-listen-directions, kt:ja-fn-directions, kt:zh-fn-directions, kt:zh-fn-instructions)
notions include directive-request, space-location; itemTypes include listen-comprehend and match
commonErrors include "confusing position words", "catching only the verb", "waiting for others to act and then imitating"
learnerSignals: the child always waits until classmates have finished before moving
when asking the way, remembers only the first step
the teacher says "they can't hear the difference between on and under"
contraindications: the object names have not been learned yet
a whole-class physical TPR activity need not be moved onto a screen
learners with hearing impairment

rules: A move counts as complete only when object, attribute, position and order are all right; getting only the object right does not count (blocks an answer that is too weak).

The scene layout ensures that every instruction has at least one distractor object that differs in just one attribute or position. Object positions are randomised for every item, so tapping the most prominent object or dragging in a fixed order cannot pass (blocks gaming).
After the learner's own Step 3 instruction is executed literally, it must yield the one target state; if it is ambiguous it is judged as failed.
check.independence: The first move on each instruction is recorded separately, together with the number of replays (0, 1, 2 or more). Completion with subtitles on, and any revision made in Step 2 after seeing the segment flashing, are recorded as assisted. When a partner carries out Step 3, the partner's prompts are ticked on the record sheet.

evidence.retained: The first scene state for each instruction, the number of replays, whether subtitles were opened, the difference type the learner judged in Step 2, and, for Step 3, the instruction text and the result of executing it literally.

licensed.claim: Can understand single-step instructions containing this type of information (position or attribute)
Can carry out two- or three-step sequential instructions
Can give an instruction without ambiguity

prohibited: Counting a move made after seeing a demonstration or a peer as understanding
Inferring from a correct move that the learner can say these words
Inferring listening in a real classroom or on the street from performance on recordings in a quiet environment

hints: Replay once at normal speed
Replay slowly
Replay in segments, and let the matching object or position flash
Show the text subtitle
scaffold.fade: After 4 consecutive instructions of the same type are correct on the first attempt without replay, the replay button needs confirmation to be used and subtitles are no longer offered.

primitives.reverseHalf: Each set has at least one instruction with a part that is not to be done (Don't touch the red one／赤いのは触らないでください／不要动红色的), one "if … then …" whose condition is not met, and one position whose reference point is not the learner but a figure in the picture (on his left).
