This shows that listening to instructions is not "move whatever you hear".

failureModes.failure: The learner guesses from a fixed order of instructions (always moves the leftmost object first)
failureModes.mitigation: Object positions are randomised for each item, and the order of instructions does not follow the scene's layout
failureModes.test: Only if the first-attempt accuracy does not drop after the object positions are shuffled does it show the learner is listening

failureModes.failure: Unlimited replays or subtitles always on inflate performance
failureModes.mitigation: Replays and subtitles are both recorded as assisted conditions
failureModes.test: Check that independent and assisted completions are listed separately in the report

failureModes.failure: Young children's dragging is not precise enough and they are wrongly judged as not understanding
failureModes.mitigation: The drop area has a wide snap zone, and a tap-to-select alternative is provided
failureModes.test: In usability trials with 5–6-year-olds, operation slips and comprehension errors are recorded separately

stacksWith.how: After the positions and objects in an instruction have been carried out in the same scene, show them directly as role links, and compare them with particles / prepositions
Use the same scene the other way round: the scene after the instructions have been carried out is the picture the learner is asked to describe next
At confusion points like on/under and 四/十, pull that word out of the instruction for minimal-pair sound discrimination, then return to the same instruction

languages.en: Classroom instructions Stand up / Colour the small ball red / Put the pencil under the book; positions on/in/under/next to/between/behind/in front of; directions turn left, go past, the second on the right; traps: on/under and left/right heard as each other, catching only the verb and missing small/big
languages.ja: Classroom instructions ～てください (立ってください, 見てください, 書いてください); position nouns 上・下・中・前・後ろ・となり・横 + の + に／を; directions まっすぐ行って、二つ目の角を右に曲がって; traps: missing the negation in ～ないでください, the reference point of ここ／そこ／あそこ
languages.zh: Instructions 请坐／把书放在桌子上／拿那个红色的大球; position words 上／下／里／前边／后边／旁边／左边／右边; directions 一直走、往左拐、过两个路口; traps: tones or near-sounds such as 四／十 heard as each other, measure words and quantity as clues, position words placed after the noun

primitives.name: Functional exchange
primitives.oneLine: In a purposeful conversation, choose or say the communicative function for each turn, and the other side's reply branches according to your choice
primitives.difficulty: The learner can recite single-sentence formulas but, in a purposeful exchange, does not know what to do on this turn: apologise first or explain first, whether to give a reason when refusing, whether to give your name first on the phone. And as soon as the other side's reply departs from the textbook, the learner cannot follow. Transfer from the first language makes the function "grammatical but communicatively wrong": *Please give me your pen. (blunt to a stranger), *Who are you?, *这是马克 (on the phone), *你是谁？, ごめんなさい said to a superior, *ペンを借りてください。
primitives.object: A pre-written exchange script with a clear purpose (ordering food, borrowing something, rescheduling by phone, complaining, inviting and declining, contacting about being late). Its structure is a tree of turns: on each turn the other side says one line (a recording, with optional text), the learner chooses or says one line, and the other side's next line is pre-written according to the branch chosen. This primitive is not a chatbot: every line of the other side is a pre-written, human-checked branch. The system generates no replies and does no automatic scoring of the learner's speech. For turns where the learner speaks openly, either the learner chooses "which function I just performed" to decide the branch, or a real partner outside the page plays the other side, and the page provides only role cards and a record sheet.
primitives.requires: The learner has already been through the key words and sentences of the scene (see prim:scene-walkthrough). If the scene vocabulary is not yet known, go back first.
learnerAction: Step 1 Walk through it: on each turn choose one of 3–4 options (at beginner level, whole sentences; at intermediate and advanced level, function descriptions such as "apologise first, then explain", "make the request directly", "first confirm who the other person is"). The other side responds according to the branch, all the way to an ending (purpose achieved / partly achieved / relationship damaged).

Step 2 Review the branches: for each turn on the path walked, open another branch to see how the other side would respond. Judge each turn's choice with locked categories: achieved the purpose but hurt the relationship / did not hurt the relationship but did not achieve the purpose / both achieved / either choice would have been the same. The last is the reverse half: on some turns, saying it directly is the most appropriate.

Step 3 Say the key turns yourself: turn off the options and, on two key turns, say or write the line yourself (the recording is kept only inside the page and is not scored automatically). Then choose "which function I used" to let the branch continue. The learner can also act it out with a real partner using the role card, and the partner records it on the tick sheet on the page.
systemResponse: The branch tree in the side panel unfolds as the turns go on. The path walked is in bold, and unwalked branches stay clickable.

On reaching an ending, two pre-written scales are shown: how far the purpose was achieved, and what state the relationship between the two sides is now in, with an explanation of which turns led to this.

In Step 3 the learner first self-assesses the function used, and only then is the pre-written model for that function shown, side by side with the learner's own words. The system does not judge whether the openly spoken words are right.

ui.screen: At the top is the role card (who I am, who the other side is, what I want to achieve). On the left is the stream of conversation bubbles, where each line from the other side has a recording and text that can be switched on or off. At the bottom are the option buttons. On the right are the branch tree and the two ending scales.
interactions: Number keys choose options, Space replays the other side's recording, R starts or stops recording
Click a node on the branch tree to return to any turn and walk it again
On phones the options are fixed at the bottom
ui.childVariant: Scenes are limited to greetings, borrowing an eraser, buying ice cream, and telling the teacher "I don't understand". Options are whole sentences with pictures. Endings are shown with face emoticons, and terms such as "relationship" do not appear. In Step 3 the teacher or a parent can play the other side.
ui.adultVariant: Scenes are workplace phone calls, complaints, rescheduling, politely declining an invitation. Options are written as functional strategies, and function names can be shown (cushion – reason – request – alternative). Step 3 requires saying the lines independently on three key turns.
ui.accessibility: Every line of the other side can be shown as text. Recording is not required and typing can replace it. There is no time limit by default; timed fluency practice is optional.

kcSignals: component is functional, strategic or sociolinguistic, and notions include directive-request, social-ritual, interaction-management, politeness-register

the KC is a functional scene (kt:en-fn-requests, kt:en-fn-telephone, kt:en-fn-complaints, kt:en-fn-invitations, kt:en-fn-appointments, kt:en-fn-thanks-apologies, kt:ja-fn-ordering, kt:ja-fn-borrow-request, kt:ja-fn-lateness-contact, kt:ja-fn-telephone-ja, kt:ja-fn-thanks-apologies, kt:zh-fn-ordering, kt:zh-fn-phone-appointments, kt:zh-fn-complaints, kt:zh-fn-invite-suggest, and *-str-repair-basic)
itemTypes include role-play
learnerSignals: can recite the textbook dialogue but freezes when the other side changes one line
"What I said wasn't wrong, so why is the other person unhappy?"
in real situations can say only one sentence
contraindications: the goal is open discussion or argument, where the branches cannot be fully pre-written (use prim:discourse-map or a discussion with real people)
the vocabulary of the scene is not yet known
it cannot be used to assess pronunciation

rules: Clearing the script requires both that the purpose is achieved and that the relationship is not damaged; just getting the thing does not count (blocks an answer that is too weak).

The turn tree includes over-polite or overlong branches that leave the other side not understanding the request or feeling distant. Choosing the longest, most polite option every time cannot clear the script (blocks gaming).

The words the learner says on a key turn must contain the necessary components of that function (complaint: problem + request; refusal: cushion + reason; phone call: self-identification + purpose). This is judged by three parties, the learner's self-assessment, comparison with the model and the partner's tick sheet; the system does no automatic scoring.
check.independence: The first choice on each turn is recorded separately. Walking the same script again after seeing the unwalked branches is recorded as "ending already seen" and does not count as independent. In Step 3, only what is said before seeing the model counts as independent. If a partner is present and prompts, mark it as assisted on the tick sheet.

evidence.retained: The full path of the first walk-through, the paths of any later re-walks, the classification of each turn in Step 2, the recording or text from Step 3 and the function the learner chose, and the partner's tick sheet.

licensed.claim: In a controlled script, can pick for this scene a function sequence that both achieves the purpose and is appropriate
Can say, in the key turns of this scene, words that contain the necessary components

prohibited: Inferring that the learner can handle real conversation from clearing a script
Inferring acceptable pronunciation from the existence of a recording
Counting a clear on the second walk-through of the same script as independent
Treating the ending scales as universal facts about the target culture

hints: Show the role card again: who the other side is, what you want
Show the names of the usual functional steps for this turn (cushion → reason → request)
Play one model sentence for this turn
scaffold.fade: After two different scripts in the same scene family reach both ending scales on the first attempt, the options change to open speaking. After one more pass, the role card no longer shows function hints.

primitives.reverseHalf: More polite is not always better: in an emergency call for help, small matters between friends, and ordering at a fast-food counter, being short and direct is what fits. Using Would you mind… with a friend, or layering cushions for a shop assistant, leaves the other side unable to tell what you want. Every script has at least one turn where saying it directly is the best branch.

failureModes.failure: The learner memorises the tree and gets a high score by re-walking the same script
failureModes.mitigation: Prepare several script variants for the same function (change the other person, add an unexpected complication), and count first-attempt performance on the new script
failureModes.test: Compare the first-attempt clear rate on a new variant with the clear rate on a re-walk

failureModes.failure: The learner thinks the page "understands" what they say
failureModes.mitigation: The interface states clearly that the other side is pre-recorded and that branches are decided by the function the learner chooses
failureModes.test: Interview learners after the trial about whether they mistook it for speech recognition

failureModes.failure: The author treats one politeness style as the only correct answer
failureModes.mitigation: Every ending card states "in this setting, given this relationship between the two people", and native speakers are asked to check the branches
failureModes.test: The authoring checklist must not allow judgments of the form "people from X all …"

stacksWith.how: On the same turn, say the same function to different people (shop assistant / friend / boss) and see how the ending scales change
A badly ended script becomes a cultural incident directly; after interpreting it, return to the script and walk that turn again
In a phone rescheduling or asking-the-way turn, deliberately leave out one piece of information that the learner must ask for before the branch continues

languages.en: Function contrasts: Could you… / Could I… (*Could you borrow me your pen), Would you mind… → No, not at all, phone This is… / Who's calling, please?, complaint I'm afraid… + complain about, declining I'd love to, but…, repair Sorry? / Pardon? (not What?)
languages.ja: Function contrasts: すみません used to call someone / to thank / to apologise, ごめんなさい vs 申し訳ありません, ペンを貸してください (*借りてください), ordering and answering the number of people with 三人です (*三名様です), contacting about being late by apologising first and then giving the expected time (遅れます, *遅いです), giving the company name on the phone, ending a call with 失礼いたします, declining with あいにく／ちょっと…, not adding さん to a colleague of your own company when speaking to outsiders
languages.zh: Function contrasts: ordering 我要一碗面 (*我要面条一碗) / 来一个……, phone 我是…… / 请问您是哪位 (*这是马克, *你是谁), rescheduling 能不能改到星期五, complaint 这个有问题，能换一个吗 (*这个手机不工作), invitation without using "让我们", refusal needs a reason, replying to thanks with 不客气

primitives.name: Register calibration
primitives.oneLine: Adjust the politeness level and formality of what you say to the relationship (higher or lower rank, close or distant, setting), and spot where it gives you away
primitives.difficulty: The meaning is right but it is aimed at the wrong person. In English emails, must / have to run at full strength all the way through, and a post for a school's public account is written like a chat message. In Japanese, honorific (respectful) forms are used for one's own actions, a department head of one's own company is given さん when talking to a client, and adding です・ます is assumed to be keigo. In Chinese, a teacher is called by full name, *您们 is said to a group, "改天请你吃饭" is taken literally and a time is fixed, and "哈" and "啥" turn up in a formal notice. What is missing is not words but the step from "what is my relationship with this person, and in what setting" to a concrete form, and the awareness that "too polite gives you away just the same".
primitives.object: A passage built around one fixed matter (a request, a notice, an introduction), with 3–5 slots (address term, polite verb form, strength of request, connective, sentence-final particle), plus a set of relationship parameters that can be dialled: distance (close / distant), status (higher / equal / lower), setting (private spoken / public / written), and for Japanese also "whether the person being talked about is inside or outside the group". The whole primitive is dialling the parameters and refilling the slots again and again on this one passage.
primitives.requires: The learner can say the matter itself correctly in one register (the propositional content is already known). The learner has studied at least two levels of form in the target language (ます form and plain form, 您 and 你, must and could). If the forms themselves still cannot be produced, fall back first.
learnerAction: Step 1 Dial the parameters and refill the same passage: fill the slots at the level given by the relationship parameters, then dial to another set of parameters and refill the same passage. The content stays the same and only the way of saying it changes.

Step 2 Spot what gives it away: judge, place by place, where a passage gives itself away (locked options: wrong address term / direction of honorific reversed or inside / outside wrong / request too forceful / register mixed with another level / this place does not give it away — the reverse half: accurate information is the same whoever it is given to, formal does not mean long, and being too polite also gives you away).

Step 3 Write for a third person: given a combination of parameters that did not appear in the first two steps (for example, talking to an outsider about one's own superior, or messaging an unfamiliar elder), the learner writes the matter themselves.
systemResponse: When a parameter is dialled, any existing fill in a slot that does not fit the new parameters flashes with "gives itself away here", and the ones that fit stay as they are, so the learner sees which parameter decides which place.
The right-hand column automatically sets out a comparison table of the two versions, with identical slots marked "＝".

After the learner has judged what gives it away, the system shows "how the other side may hear this sentence" (as if giving an order / stiff, as if meeting for the first time / as if joking / as if raising one's own side).
In Japanese honorific items, an arrow shows who is doing the action; the arrow lands on inside or outside, and turns red when its direction is reversed.

ui.screen: At the top are three parameter sliders (distance, status, setting; Japanese has one more inside / outside switch). In the middle is the passage with slots. Below are the candidate forms for the current slot. The right-hand column holds the two-version comparison table. No score is shown.
interactions: Left and right arrow keys dial the parameters; on touch screens the sliders can be dragged
Tab moves between slots, and number keys choose a candidate
Step 3 can be typed, or recorded in the page
ui.childVariant: The parameters become pictures of people (mum, teacher, classmate, shop assistant), with only two levels, "someone familiar / an unfamiliar adult". Only address terms, greetings, asking and thanking are practised (ja: おはよう／おはようございます; zh: 你／您, 王老师好). No terms appear.
ui.adultVariant: Workplace emails, client phone calls, messages to a manager, leave requests. Terms are shown (尊敬語・謙譲語・丁寧語, written register, hedging). In Step 3 the learner writes a complete short email.
ui.accessibility: Give-away marks use both underline and icon. The slider state is read out in words ("Now: to a superior, written"). Levels are not distinguished by colour alone.

kcSignals: component is sociolinguistic, or notions include politeness-register
the label contains 敬語／尊敬語／謙譲語／内外／称呼／客套／谦辞／语体／formal／informal (such as kt:ja-honorifics, kt:ja-soc-uchi-soto, kt:zh-soc-address-terms, kt:zh-soc-written-style, kt:en-formal-informal-register)
commonErrors include "used for one's own action", "sounds casual to a superior", "colloquial words in formal writing", "too direct"
learnerSignals: "Is this polite to say?"
emails are all must and have to
the teacher says the Japanese is too casual or too stiff
speaks the same way to friends and to the teacher
after learning honorifics, stacks them on every sentence, producing double honorifics
contraindications: the propositional content itself still cannot be said
at the introductory stage where only one register is taught (for example young children learn only the ます form or only "你好／您好"), do not dial three parameters
an item cannot be set when both levels are natural in that context and the relationship meaning does not differ

rules: Step 3: the required markers for the target level must appear. In ja, for an outside superior there must be at least one honorific or humble form in the correct direction; in zh, the written level must not contain words from the colloquial word list; in en, no full-strength words may appear (blocks an answer that is too weak).

Excess is checked at the same time: double honorifics (*おっしゃられる) are banned, humble or courtesy phrases may not exceed the limit, and the written version may not be more than 1.5 times as long as the spoken version (blocks overcorrection).
Direction check: the agent of an honorific verb must be the other person or an outsider, and the agent of a humble verb must be oneself or someone inside one's own group.
The content slots (numbers, times, facts) must be the same in the two versions: changing register must not change the information.
check.independence: The first fill of each slot in Step 1 is recorded separately. A refill after seeing "how the other side may hear it" is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 uses a new parameter combination and does not show the comparison table.

evidence.retained: Under each set of parameters, the two versions of the fill, the first fill and refills, the give-away judgments, and the Step 3 text are all kept on the passage and its comparison table.

licensed.claim: Can choose the right politeness level and register for controlled slots under given relationship parameters
Can judge the direction and inside / outside of honorifics (whose action, which side it belongs to)
Can independently write an appropriate short text for a new combination of relationships

prohibited: Concluding from this that the learner is appropriate in real communication (there is no reaction from a real other party)
Treating "used an honorific form" as the same as using it appropriately
Using English's one-dimensional ladder of strength to infer that Japanese honorifics have been mastered
Making value judgments about the politeness practices of any culture

hints: Ask only: "Who is doing this action? What is their relationship to you? In what setting?"
Highlight on the sliders the parameter that decides this place
Give a minimal contrast between the two levels adjacent to this slot
scaffold.fade: After 4 consecutive places on the same parameter dimension are filled correctly on the first attempt, hide the sliders and describe the relationship in one sentence only (for example "writing an email to the section chief of the next department"), and let the learner work out the parameters.

primitives.reverseHalf: Too polite gives you away just like too casual. Each set has at least one place where the right answer is "no need to step up" (accurate information is the same whoever it is given to; formal does not mean long). In Japanese, when talking to an outsider about a superior in one's own company, one actually has to drop さん and use humble forms: higher status does not mean always using honorific forms. In Chinese, using "您" or written-style words between acquaintances sounds stiff or even sarcastic.

failureModes.failure: The learner takes away "the more polite the safer" and always chooses the highest level
failureModes.mitigation: Every set has items where being over-polite is wrong, and double honorifics and the length limit are checked
failureModes.test: A simulated answer that always picks the highest level fails at least one third of the items

failureModes.failure: The relationship is squashed into a single "politeness" scale, and Japanese inside / outside cannot be seen at all
failureModes.mitigation: At least half of the Japanese items involve inside / outside or the direction of the action
failureModes.test: A simulated answer that looks only at status and not at inside / outside fails all the inside / outside items

failureModes.failure: The learner chooses mechanically by marker word (sees "先生" and uses an honorific)
failureModes.mitigation: Design items where the same person belongs to a different side before different listeners (talking to a client about one's own department head)
failureModes.test: Half of the "superiors" in the adversarial examples appear in an outside-facing context

failureModes.failure: Feedback slides into cultural stereotypes
failureModes.mitigation: Explanations describe only "how the other side may hear it" and do not evaluate people or cultures
failureModes.test: Review all diagnostic text: statements such as "people of country X are more polite" must not appear

stacksWith.how: Put the contrasting forms of the same slot on one context card, with the deciding factor changed from "the meaning to be expressed" to "who you are speaking to"
When the "strength / register" spotlight is opened on the learner's own draft, this set of relationship sliders appears beside it
The sentence that caused the problem in a misunderstanding incident becomes a passage with slots directly, and when rewriting, the sliders are used to find which parameter was misjudged

languages.en: The parameters project mainly onto two dimensions: modal strength (the four-step ladder in c17: hard must / have to → firm should / need to → soft might / could → open Would you mind…?, with too soft judged wrong as well) and written register (the four give-aways in c42: generic you, colloquial connective And so, contraction can't, vague a lot of; reverse: when the information is accurate the two versions are identical, and formal does not mean long). Common for Chinese native speakers: literal translation of Chinese courtesy (kindly find attached, Dear Mr John), Teacher Wang. The existing implementations c17 and c42 do not include address terms or the distance and status parameters, so the status is partial.
languages.ja: Parameters: distance (親／疎), status (上／同／下), setting (私／公), inside / outside. Slots: register (plain form / です・ます), honorific (おVになる, Vれる・られる, いらっしゃる・召し上がる・おっしゃる), humble (おVする, 参る・伺う・拝見する), address term (さん／様／くん／ちゃん／none), request form (Vて／Vてください／Vてくださいませんか). Locked give-away types: reversed direction (honorific used for oneself, humble used for the other), inside / outside wrong (*私のお母さん, *田中さんは今いません said to a client), mixed register, excess (double honorifics, てくださいませんか to a friend), does not give it away. Key points: 丁寧語 is not 敬語; a person of high status is "lowered" in an outside-facing context.
languages.zh: Parameters: distance (familiar / unfamiliar), generation and status (elder / peer / junior, superior), setting (spoken / written notice / official document). Slots: address term (王老师, 李师傅, 小王／老李, 阿姨, 张先生, with the surname before the term), person (您／你, 各位／大家, *您们), courtesy in requests (请问, 麻烦你, 劳驾), humble phrases and replies (哪里哪里, 过奖了, 不客气), register words (啥／什么, 咱们／我们, 立即／赶紧, particles "哈" and "呗"). Give-away types: calling by full name, 您／你 misplaced, colloquial words in writing, written words in casual talk, courtesy taken literally, or courtesy missing where it is due. For English native speakers: excuse me is not always "对不起", and replying to a compliment with only "谢谢" sounds not modest enough before elders.

primitives.name: Information gap
primitives.oneLine: The learner lacks a piece of information and must ask for it to finish the task; the question itself is recorded and evaluated
primitives.difficulty: Almost all speaking practice is about answering, but in real situations it is more often the learner who lacks information and has to ask. Learners can ask only yes/no questions, and each question gets back one word; they never follow up; when nervous, they grab any question they can say to fill the silence, when the answer is actually already in their own hands. In Japanese it is common to ask outright with no lead-in, with no ～んですが opening where one is needed. In Chinese it is common to stack question forms as in *你去不去吗, and to mix up "几" and "多少".
primitives.object: An information card with gaps: one half is information the learner already knows, the other half is 3–5 gaps that only the other person knows; and the conversation record pasted back after the chat.
primitives.requires: The learner already knows the basic question forms of the language (en do / wh questions, ja か questions and question words, zh 吗 questions, affirmative-negative questions, interrogative pronouns) and has someone to talk to (a classmate, a teacher, a voice assistant). If either is missing, fall back.
learnerAction: Step 1 Take the card and ask: have a real conversation with the other person outside the page, come back, fill in the gaps, and paste the conversation record back.

Step 2 Recognise your own questions: the page extracts all the questions in the record, the learner ticks which ones they asked themselves, and classifies each (locked options: yes/no question / open question / follow-up / confirmation / asked but as good as not asked — the reverse half: the answer is on one's own card).
Step 3 Take a new card and write before speaking: given a new gap card, first write down the three questions you plan to ask, and go and talk only after passing the check.
systemResponse: After the gaps are filled, the learner links each answer to the question that got it. A gap with no question to link stays blank and is marked "not asked yet", and one the other side volunteered is marked "he gave it unasked".
After each question is classified, what this type "got back" is shown beside the question: one word / a stretch / something he had not meant to say / a confirmation / nothing.
For a question classified as "asked but as good as not asked", the matching known information on the card is highlighted at the same time.
Beside each question written in Step 3, its type and what it may get back are shown in advance.

ui.screen: On the left is the information card (two columns: known / gaps). On the right are the paste area and the list of extracted questions (each with a tick box and five type buttons). At the bottom is the Step 3 question editor.
interactions: Paste the conversation record
Space ticks "I asked this", and number keys 1–5 classify
Drag a line, or press C, to link a question to a gap
ui.childVariant: The conversation partner is a teacher or parent playing a role, and the cards use pictures (a missing price in a toy shop, where a small animal lives). There are only two types: "is it a question" and "did it get an answer". The record may be transcribed by an adult or kept as a recording.
ui.adultVariant: Booking a meeting room, viewing a flat, a hospital appointment, asking a supplier for a quote. Step 3 needs at least one follow-up. Types are shown with their terms.
ui.accessibility: The conversation record is stored only locally in the browser and is not uploaded. The list of questions can be read out sentence by sentence by a screen reader. No speech recognition is relied on.

component is functional or strategic
itemTypes include role-play or situated-production-spoken
learnerSignals: can only answer, not ask
conversations stop after one question and one answer
"I don't know what to ask"
never speaks up in speaking class
contraindications: the basic question forms still cannot be produced
no conversation partner can be found
when the learner is highly anxious about conversation with real people, rehearse first with prim:exchange-script

rules: Card validation: if the overlap between a gap question and the text in the known column exceeds the limit, report an error, because something that can be looked up on the card is not a gap.

Step 3: the three questions cannot all be yes/no questions (blocks an answer that is too narrow); at least one is a back-referring follow-up that quotes one specific word from the other person or the card (blocks an answer that is too scattered).
The model follow-up shown in Step 2 must itself pass the Step 3 check.

Type labels are checked in reverse: an open question must start with a question word, a follow-up must have a back-reference marker, a confirmation must have a checking marker; the improved version of an "asked but as good as not asked" question must really ask out the gap.
check.independence: The conversation takes place outside the page, so independence cannot be proved. Only questions that the learner ticked themselves are counted. A change of type after viewing the type explanation is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 does not show the question frames.

evidence.retained: The gap entries, the links between answers and questions, the questions the learner ticked themselves and their types, and the questions written in Step 3 are all kept on this information card.

licensed.claim: Can ask out the gap information in a real conversation
Can use a follow-up to get back information the other person had not intended to give
Can recognise ineffective questions whose answers are already in one's own hands

prohibited: Evaluating the grammar or pronunciation of the questions from the pasted record
Counting information volunteered by the other person as asked out by the learner
Evaluating how well the conversation partner spoke

hints: Ask only: "Could this answer be in your own hands?"
Show the names of the five types and what each "gets back"
Give a follow-up frame (such as "You said …, so …?")
scaffold.fade: After two consecutive cards each have at least one follow-up made without looking at a hint, the frame button is no longer offered in Step 3.

primitives.reverseHalf: "Asked but as good as not asked": a question whose answer is already on one's own card wastes a turn and makes the other side suspicious. On the other side, more open questions are not always better: key figures such as prices and times should instead be repeated back with a confirmation question.

failureModes.failure: To fill the follow-up type, the learner forces in "you said" and what follows does not refer back
failureModes.mitigation: A follow-up must quote one word that appears in the other person's record
failureModes.test: A simulated follow-up whose quoted word is not in the other person's words must be judged as failed

failureModes.failure: The learner ticks the other person's questions as their own
failureModes.mitigation: After ticking, check whether the link between question and gap holds, and show the turn position of the utterance for self-checking
failureModes.test: A simulated record that ticks in the other person's questions will have gaps that cannot be linked

failureModes.failure: The conversation partner (especially an AI assistant) pours out all the information at once, so the learner does not need to ask
failureModes.mitigation: The opening instructions require the other side to answer only what is asked; long stretches by the other side are marked "he gave it unasked"
failureModes.test: A record in which the other side speaks in monologue must not let Step 1 pass

stacksWith.how: When the gaps are numbers, times or prices, the answers asked for go into the two-cell table, and the unit cell is checked as well
The learner transcribes the conversation recording themselves, and the transcript is the record pasted back
On the same card, change the other person (classmate / shop assistant / teacher), and the polite form of the questions is adjusted by the relationship parameters

languages.en: Five locked types closed / open / probe / check / dead; back-reference markers You said… / When you say…; confirmation So … , right?; common for Chinese native speakers: statement-order questions *You can tell me…?, *Where the room is?; existing implementation c58
languages.ja: Open questions 何・どこ・いつ・どのくらい・どうして; yes/no questions ～ますか／～んですか; follow-up さっき～っておっしゃいましたけど、それは…？; confirmation ～ということですね; opening lead-in すみません、ちょっとお聞きしたいんですが (lacking the lead-in sounds abrupt, and can be stacked with register-calibrate); use the ます form to a shop assistant and the plain form to a friend
languages.zh: Yes/no questions 吗 / affirmative-negative questions (*你去不去吗 is a stacking error) / 还是 choice questions; open questions 什么、哪儿、怎么、为什么、多少、几 (use 几 for numbers up to ten); follow-up 你刚才说……，那……？; confirmation ……，对吧？／是不是……？; opening 请问、麻烦问一下; note the ambiguity of "怎么" asking about manner versus reason

primitives.name: Critical incident
primitives.oneLine: Read a short cross-cultural misunderstanding, decide where it went wrong and how the other side understood it, then rewrite what was said at the time
primitives.difficulty: Grammar and word choice are right, but communication goes wrong, and the learner cannot see why: "吃了吗" translated literally as Have you eaten?; small talk that asks straight out about salary and marital status; saying "清明节快乐" on Qingming; saying "私のお母さんは" to an outsider; hearing "改天请你吃饭" and pressing for which day and what time. In the other direction, learners also easily generalise one experience into an absolute rule, "they are all like that".
primitives.object: A short cross-cultural misunderstanding: four to eight lines of dialogue or narration, with a relationship card for the people (higher / lower, close / distant, setting). Each of the two people has an inner monologue, hidden at first and revealed later.
primitives.requires: The learner can read the language of the incident (the language of the incident is easier than the learner's level). If it cannot be read, first lower the language difficulty; language is not taught here.
learnerAction: Step 1 Find the problem point: in the incident, mark "from which sentence things start to feel wrong", and first write one sentence of one's own explanation. This explanation is saved as the first judgment.

Step 2 Judge the cause: judge item by item with locked categories: the wording itself (words or grammar) / politeness level or address term / topic or timing / understanding of courtesy formulas or implied meaning / actually no cultural misunderstanding, just personality or the circumstances of the day (the last is the reverse half). Then the inner monologues of both sides are revealed, to compare with one's own judgment.
Step 3 Rewrite what was said at the time: at the problem point, rewrite that sentence (or the other person's next response) so that both sides' intentions can be realised.
systemResponse: After the problem point is marked, a line is drawn between that sentence and the other person's reaction.
After the reveal, the two people's inner monologues appear beside their own lines. The first explanation from Step 1 stays locked, and a "current explanation" column is added beside it.

After the rewrite, the incident is played again: when the rewrite falls into the category that matches a pre-written branch, the other person's next line is replaced by the corresponding pre-written reaction; otherwise a list of features of acceptable rewrites is shown for the learner to check themselves. The system does not automatically score open rewrites.

ui.screen: At the top is the character relationship card. In the middle are comic panels or dialogue bubbles. On the right are the "My explanation" column (locked after the first judgment) and a row of category buttons. At the bottom is the rewrite input box.
interactions: Click a sentence to mark it as the problem point, and number keys choose the category
The reveal key can be pressed only after the first explanation has been written
The rewrite can be typed or recorded (only inside the page)
ui.childVariant: Small school incidents (borrowing something without saying thanks; a foreign classmate not eating the snack handed over) are shown with pictures. There are only three categories: what was said / how it was said / actually no problem. It is mainly discussion, without judging right or wrong.
ui.adultVariant: Workplace, neighbours, banquet and visiting scenes. Terms such as face, inside / outside and implied meaning can be shown. Step 3 requires two rewrites and an explanation of which relationship each suits.
ui.accessibility: Pictures and text in two channels, and the monologues can be read aloud. Category buttons carry text explanations. No reliance on colour.

kcSignals: component is sociolinguistic, or implied meaning within strategic (kt:ja-str-implicature, kt:zh-str-implicature)

the KC is a social and cultural norm (kt:en-soc-small-talk, kt:en-soc-politeness-basic, kt:en-soc-softening, kt:en-soc-varieties, kt:ja-soc-manners, kt:ja-soc-uchi-soto, kt:ja-soc-address-terms, kt:ja-soc-cushion-refusal, kt:zh-soc-face-modesty, kt:zh-soc-culture-customs, kt:zh-soc-address-terms, kt:zh-soc-politeness)
notions include social-ritual, politeness-register, reference-person; commonErrors say "grammatically correct but comes across as …"
learnerSignals: "But I didn't say anything wrong"
generalises one experience into "they are all like that"
worry about "saying the wrong thing" before studying or working abroad
contraindications: the language of the incident cannot be read by the learner
do not use when the topic cannot give an "it depends on the person" boundary and would only reinforce stereotypes
incidents involving sensitive matters such as religion or politics do not go into the children's version

rules: The category in Step 2 must match the problem point marked in Step 1. Marking the wrong sentence but happening to choose the right category does not count (blocks an answer that is too weak).

The rewrite in Step 3 must keep the original communicative purpose and cannot avoid it by "not saying this at all". The change must fall on the chosen category: if the category is address term, the address term must be changed, and just adding a "please" or "sorry" is not enough (blocks gaming).
In a set of incidents, at least one item has the answer "actually no cultural misunderstanding", so a learner who always picks "cultural difference" will be detected.
check.independence: The first explanation is locked before the monologues are revealed. A change of judgment after the reveal is recorded as after a hint. A rewrite made after viewing the list of acceptable rewrites is recorded as assisted completion.

evidence.retained: The problem point marked first and the first explanation (locked), the category choice, the changes after the monologues are revealed, and the rewritten sentence.

licensed.claim: Can recognise this kind of sociolinguistic mismatch (such as inside / outside address terms, courtesy taken as a commitment)
Can rewrite an appropriate way of saying it in a similar situation

prohibited: Inferring from correct interpretation that the learner can do it in real situations
Treating one party in an incident as representative of a whole culture and concluding that "Japanese / Chinese / Americans all …"
Treating the learner's explanation as an evaluation of their attitude toward the culture

hints: Ask only: "When the other person heard this sentence, what did they think you wanted to do?"
Show the three scales of higher / lower, close / distant and setting on the relationship card
Reveal the monologue of one side first
scaffold.fade: After 3 consecutive items of the same category are judged correctly on the first attempt, the relationship scales are no longer shown.

primitives.reverseHalf: Not every awkward moment is a cultural difference: some are personality, mood on the day, or just a language error; within the same culture there are also differences of age, region and relationship. Every set has at least one item with "no cultural misunderstanding", and every outcome states "in this kind of relationship, in this setting".

failureModes.failure: Reinforcing stereotypes
failureModes.mitigation: Every incident is accompanied by a variant of "some people would also respond this way"
failureModes.test: The authoring checklist checks whether universal statements appear in item wording and feedback

failureModes.failure: The learner notices the answer is always "a politeness issue" and chooses by habit
failureModes.mitigation: Categories are evenly distributed within a set, and include "no misunderstanding" items
failureModes.test: Check the category distribution in each set, and count whether the learner picks the same category consecutively

failureModes.failure: The rewrite just mechanically adds "please" or "sorry"
failureModes.mitigation: The check requires the change to fall on the chosen category
failureModes.test: Adversarial example: a rewrite that only adds politeness words must be judged as failed

stacksWith.how: A badly ended outcome in an exchange script is used directly as the source of an incident; after the rewrite, return to the script and walk it again from that turn
When the category is politeness level or address term, layer the politeness gradient on the same sentence and see which level is appropriate

languages.en: Incident material: small talk that asks straight out about salary, marital status, age; "吃了吗" translated literally as Have you eaten?; Would you mind… answered with Yes, sure; small talk answered only with Yes/No, which kills the conversation; British / American usage differences (first floor); over-apologising, and apologising where thanks is due
languages.ja: Incident material: calling one's own mother お母さん to an outsider, adding さん to a colleague of one's own company when speaking to a client; not saying お邪魔します when entering; the taboos on 4, 9 and white in gifts, and new versus old banknotes for weddings and funerals; the implied meaning of declining with just ちょっと…; あいにく misused for one's own wish; Chinese native speakers judging by Chinese taboos (giving a clock)
languages.zh: Incident material: "改天请你吃饭" taken as a concrete appointment; replying to a compliment with only thanks; saying "快乐" on Qingming; choosing between 师傅／阿姨／老师 as address terms; saying "一点儿小意思" when giving a gift; "您们"; English native speakers always rendering excuse me as "对不起"; note regional differences (Hong Kong and Taiwan usage) and individual differences

primitives.name: Attempt then compare
primitives.oneLine: First write or say your own first draft independently and save it, then compare it with a model to mark the gaps, then rewrite
primitives.difficulty: If learners see the model before writing, what they write is copied. After seeing the model, they still cannot say where they fall short. After this revision is done, the next one is the same. Once the order is reversed, learners have no chance to notice the gap between their own output and the target.
primitives.object: The learner's own first draft (once submitted it is sealed and cannot be changed), and a model text released sentence by sentence, one sentence of which is badly written.
primitives.requires: The learner can write coherent text of the unlock length for the task. If they cannot write even a few sentences, fall back and first grow a sentence into a paragraph.
learnerAction: Step 1 Write first, with nothing given: only the task and the information points that must be included are given, with no model and no example sentences. It can be submitted only when long enough, and after submission the first draft is sealed.

Step 2 Release the model one sentence at a time: for each sentence released, mark "what it has that I don't" (locked options: I left this information out / it says it more precisely / it links more clearly / it fits the audience's tone better / this sentence is badly written and not worth learning from — the reverse half), building up one's own list of gaps.
Step 3 Rewrite from your own list: look only at the list, not the model, and rewrite the piece.
systemResponse: After sealing, the first draft stays pinned at the top of the page, and the next two steps are done against it.
As each sentence of the model is released, the system links it to the matching part of the first draft. When the first draft has no matching content, it is marked "you have nothing here".

The labels the learner attaches go into the gap list in the right column and are counted by type. After the badly written sentence is marked correctly, the system shows why it is not worth learning from.
The rewrite is shown beside the first draft, and next to each item in the list it shows "the rewrite did it / has not done it yet".

ui.screen: At the top is the read-only first draft. In the middle are the model cards released sentence by sentence. The right column is the gap list. At the bottom is the rewrite area (with a word counter).
interactions: Enter releases the next sentence of the model
Number keys 1–5 attach a label
The rewrite area counts words live, and the model is folded away in Step 3
ui.childVariant: The task becomes speaking about a picture or writing two or three sentences (can be spoken and recorded, with an adult typing). The model has only two or three sentences, and only two types are used: "it has one more thing" and "this sentence is not good".
ui.adultVariant: Emails, notices, application paragraphs, work reports. Gap types are shown with terms. The rewrite has a word limit.
ui.accessibility: The word-count bar comes with the number. The model can be read aloud sentence by sentence. The link relationships are also listed in text.

kcSignals: itemTypes include situated-production-written or situated-production-spoken
component is activity (writing, presenting), such as kt:ja-skill-write-paragraph, kt:en-skill-write-formal-correspondence
mastery is written at the "use in context" level
learnerSignals: "I can't write it", asking to see a model first
copies once the model has been seen
does not know where they fall short
teacher: "after this revision, next time is the same"
contraindications: cannot write even the unlock length (do prim:grow-text first)
there is no reliable model equivalent in information to the task
the task is pure form practice with no communicative purpose

rules: If the first draft has not reached the unlock length, no model is released, and it must cover at least half of the required information points (blocks padding to reach the count).
Step 2: the badly written sentence must be marked "not worth learning from" to pass; the list must have at least two types, and each item must point to a specific sentence in the model.

Step 3: at least two items in the list must be carried out in the rewrite (for example, missing information points filled in) (blocks an answer that is too weak); the longest continuous overlap with the model must not exceed the limit (blocks copying).
check.independence: The first draft is sealed before any example appears and is the only independent evidence. The rewrite is always recorded as output "after seeing the model". The first label for each sentence in Step 2 is recorded separately.

evidence.retained: The sealed first draft, the gap label for each model sentence, the gap list, the rewrite and its differences from the first draft are all kept on the same page.

licensed.claim: Can notice the gap between own output and the model in a given category
Can carry out in a rewrite the gaps one has noticed
This category of gap disappears in the independent first draft of the next task

prohibited: Judging writing level from the quality of the rewrite
Treating the number of gap labels as progress
Treating the model as the only correct answer

hints: Step 1 asks only a question and gives no sentences: "Did you put in all the information you must include? Count them."
Step 2: highlight this model sentence and the matching part of the first draft side by side
Give the name of the most likely gap category for this sentence
scaffold.fade: Once a category of gap from the previous list no longer appears in the independent first draft of the next task, Step 2 no longer gives hints for that category.

primitives.reverseHalf: One sentence in the model is badly written (made-up data, off topic, over-polite) and must be recognised as not worth learning from: a model is not a text where every sentence can be copied.

failureModes.failure: The first draft repeats the same sentence to reach the unlock length
failureModes.mitigation: Unlocking checks information-point coverage and repeated sentences at the same time
failureModes.test: A first draft with one sentence repeated five times cannot unlock

failureModes.failure: The rewrite copies whole sentences from the model
failureModes.mitigation: Limit the longest continuous overlap with the model
failureModes.test: A rewrite with a whole sentence of the model pasted in is blocked

failureModes.failure: Every sentence gets the same label
failureModes.mitigation: The list must have at least two types and the badly written sentence must be identified
failureModes.test: A simulated answer labelling everything "says it more precisely" does not pass

failureModes.failure: The model is far above the learner's level, so the list cannot be carried out
failureModes.mitigation: Keep the model one level above the learner's current level
failureModes.test: No more than two sentences in the model go beyond the knowledge points of the current level

stacksWith.how: The categories in the gap list directly become the order of the spotlight, applied to the same first draft
For items in the list marked "wrong form chosen", go back and practise a set on the contrasting forms, then return to revise the same sentence in the first draft
The same "yourself first, comparison afterwards" logic applied at sentence level: for the sentence one is stuck on, first bring up the wording oneself and only then reveal

languages.en: Common gaps: information points left out, missing links (As a result), strength too hard (must → could), vagueness (a lot of → about twenty). Chinese native speakers' first drafts commonly have one information point per sentence with no linking, and a Chinese-style opening As we all know. Existing implementation c37
languages.ja: Common gaps: inconsistent sentence-final register (だ／です mixed), a single connective (そして overused, lacking ので・ため・ただし), は／が, direction of honorifics. The amount of kanji used is not made a gap category, so that learners do not turn to copying kanji. The overlap limit is counted in kana and kanji characters.
languages.zh: Common gaps (English native speakers): measure words, position of 了, paired connectives (虽然……但是), time and place placed first. Younger learners or those who cannot yet read characters may write the first draft in pinyin. The overlap limit is counted in Chinese characters (for example 8 consecutive characters).

primitives.name: One-fix revision
primitives.oneLine: Deal with only one category of problem at a time on your own draft, finish one category before moving to the next, and take away one action
primitives.difficulty: The marked work comes back and not one place has been changed. Ten problems are pointed out at once and the learner forgets them all. The same mistakes are made again and again. Having just learned one rule, the learner overcorrects (every sentence made as polite as possible, concession and transition sentences deleted along with the padding). The core of revising is "does this place need changing, and what action finds it", and when facing all the problems at once this judgment cannot be made at all.
primitives.object: One draft with many faults (preferably the learner's own), the same draft from start to finish, revised category by category.
primitives.requires: The single-point knowledge for each category of the spotlight has already been learned elsewhere (such as subject-verb agreement, tense, linking, strength). Do not turn on the spotlight for a category that has not been learned; if necessary fall back.
learnerAction: Step 1 Spotlight: light up a few places of only one category of problem at a time, with the rest greyed out and unclickable. For each place, choose a fix from the options, and the options always include "no change needed". The next category appears only after this one is done. (Cutting version: cut the draft to below the word-budget line, but not one of the required facts in the right column may be lost.)

Step 2 The action to take away: several items share the same set of checking actions (cover the middle and read the skeleton, scan the verbs on their own, ask between every two sentences what the relationship is, read it aloud to the recipient), and the learner judges which action would find each problem.
Step 3 Revise a paragraph yourself: a new draft with no spotlight, where the learner uses the actions just learned to find and fix problems on their own.
systemResponse: Once a fix is chosen, that place is replaced on the spot and the count for this category goes from 0/2 to 1/2. The next category lights up only after this one is complete.

When "no change needed" is chosen at a place that should be changed, the system shows how a reader would understand this place. When a place that should not be changed is changed, it shows where the changed version reads as too much.

In the cutting version, striking out a sentence makes the paragraph close up automatically and the word-count bar falls live. Struck sentences are labelled as padding and placed below. Clicking a sentence that is doing work (a concession, a transition) makes it bounce back and explains what work it does.
After all categories are done, a ledger is laid out: how many places were changed and how many were left alone.

ui.screen: At the top is a strip of category tabs (the current category highlighted). In the middle is the draft (everything not in this category greyed out), and a small option card pops up at the lit places. The right column is the ledger or the word-budget bar.
interactions: Tab jumps only between the lit places of this category
Number keys choose the fix, and 0 is "no change needed"
In the cutting version, clicking a sentence strikes it out and clicking again restores it
ui.childVariant: Only one category is opened (such as capital letter and full stop at the start and end of a sentence, Japanese は／を written wrongly, wrong characters in kanji). The draft is three or four sentences, stickers replace the options, and no terms appear.
ui.adultVariant: Uses the learner's own real email or report paragraph, the order of the spotlight can be set by the learner, and in Step 3 the learner revises another draft of their own.
ui.accessibility: The greyed-out parts can still be read by a screen reader but are marked "not handled in this round". The word-count bar comes with the number.

kcSignals: itemTypes include error-correct
commonErrors has many entries that appear together in production
component is discourse, sociolinguistic or activity (writing)
learnerSignals: "the marked work came back and not one place was changed"
ten problems are mentioned at once and all forgotten
the same type of mistake is made again and again
after learning to soften, every sentence is softened; after learning to cut, cuts too much
contraindications: the single-point knowledge of the focus category has not been learned yet
the draft has fewer than two places in a category, so it cannot form a category
the draft has already been revised by someone else and is no longer the learner's own output, so it is not counted as independent evidence

rules: A category needs at least two places to count as a category (one place shows no pattern).
Every place has a "no change needed" option; at least one place has "no change needed" as the correct answer, but not more than one third of the total (checked from both ends).
Step 3: the flagged problems must be fixed (blocks an answer that is too weak); no more than two unflagged sentences may be changed (blocks rewriting the whole paragraph and overcorrection).
In the cutting version, three conditions apply at once: the word upper limit (must cut), all required facts present (must not cut useful material), the word lower limit (must not cut too far).
check.independence: The first choice at each place in Step 1 is recorded separately. A changed choice after seeing the diagnosis is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 has no spotlight and is the only independent evidence.

evidence.retained: The first choice at each place, the final fix, the "no change needed" judgments, the ledgers for each category, and the changes in Step 3 are all kept on this draft.

licensed.claim: Can find and correct this category of problem once the category has been named
Can judge that a place does not need changing
Without the spotlight, can locate this category of problem in a new draft by oneself

prohibited: Inferring from correct revisions that the learner no longer makes the mistake when writing a first draft
Counting errors left unchanged in the greyed-out area as the learner's oversights
Equating a reduced word count with better writing

hints: Give only the category name and "this paragraph has two places"
Narrow down to the specific sentence
Give the checking action for this category (such as "cover the part between subject and verb and read it again")
scaffold.fade: After a category is found in full independently in Step 3 on two consecutive occasions, the next draft no longer turns on the spotlight for this category and keeps only its name on the category strip.

primitives.reverseHalf: Not every fault is worth changing: at least one place has "no change needed" as the right answer (the strength is just right, the concession sentence is doing work, an omitted subject is natural anyway). Changing too much is as wrong as not changing.

failureModes.failure: Always choosing "no change needed", or always changing
failureModes.mitigation: The proportion of correct "no change needed" answers has a lower and an upper limit
failureModes.test: Two simulated answers, one choosing "no change needed" every time and one choosing to change every time, must both fail

failureModes.failure: The spotlight is made into a "suggestion" and the learner clicks everywhere anyway
failureModes.mitigation: Areas outside this category must really be unclickable
failureModes.test: Automated clicks on areas outside this category produce no edit events

failureModes.failure: Each item in Step 2 has different options, so the learner need not compare the actions
failureModes.mitigation: All items share the same set of checking actions
failureModes.test: Count that the number of different actions appearing in Step 2 equals the number of categories

failureModes.failure: In cutting, necessary facts are deleted along with the rest
failureModes.mitigation: The required-facts check and the word upper limit both apply
failureModes.test: A simulated answer that keeps only the first two sentences fails for missing facts

stacksWith.how: The order of categories in the gap list directly becomes the order of the spotlight, applied to the same sealed first draft
When the "strength / register" category lights up, the relationship sliders appear beside it, and whether to change is decided by the slider parameters
The checking action for the subject-verb agreement category is to fold away modifiers to find the main skeleton, carried out on the same sentence

languages.en: c36 has four focuses agree / tense / link / force (corresponding to the single-point practice in c22, c35, c33, and c34 / c17 respectively). c40 has four padding labels: saying what you are going to say, empty remarks everyone agrees with, only adjectives and no facts, saying it again in other words; what cannot be cut are concessions and transitions. Existing implementations c36, c40
languages.ja: Suggested focuses: consistent style (です・ます mixed with だ・である), particles (は／が, に／で, を), conjugation (sound changes in the て form, potential form), linking (そして・それから overused → ので・ため・ただし), direction of honorifics. "No change needed" often falls on: plain form to a friend, a subject omission that is natural anyway (no need to add "私は"). Padding types: ～と思います stacked on every sentence, repeated synonyms.
languages.zh: Suggested focuses (English native speakers): word order (time and place first), position and redundancy of 了, measure words, matching of connectives, colloquial words in writing. For Japanese native speakers add character shapes (Japanese forms → standard forms). "No change needed" often falls on: natural subject omission, "吧／呢" in spoken settings. Padding types: 众所周知, 随着社会的发展, repeated synonymous four-character phrases.

primitives.name: Picture description
primitives.oneLine: Speak or write about a picture, then check against the picture's elements what was covered and whether positions and numbers are right
primitives.difficulty: Describing a picture, learners only list nouns (a dog, a tree), or mention only the one or two most prominent things. Existence, position and state structures are forced into first-language templates (*The park has a dog, *There is two cats, *A boy running, *桌子有一本书, *有一本书在桌子上, *她正在戴眼镜, *机の上で本があります). After speaking, there is no way to check whether everything was covered and whether it was said correctly.
primitives.object: A scene picture whose elements (people, objects, positions, numbers, actions in progress, continuing states) are pre-marked as a checkable element list (which the learner cannot see). The first draft, the linking and the added description all happen on this picture.
primitives.requires: The learner knows the names of most objects in the picture and can say the basic form of an existence sentence. If names are not known, first do prim:listen-and-do on the same picture.
learnerAction: Step 1 Say or write first: describe the picture (three sentences for children, six to eight for adults), and the first draft is saved.

Step 2 Check against the picture: drag each of your own sentences onto the matching element in the picture. Then judge sentence by sentence: is the position right / is the number right / is it an action or a state / is this actually in the picture (the last is the reverse half: some sentences are reasonable inferences rather than things visible in the picture (he seems tired), and must be marked as inferences and not stated as fact).

Step 3 Add to it: from the elements not mentioned, choose three and describe them using structures not used in the first draft; or describe to a party who cannot see the picture (a real partner, or the page's "blind canvas"), who arranges things according to the description, and then compare with the original picture.
systemResponse: After a sentence is linked to an element, the element lights up, and those not mentioned stay grey. The coverage bar shows "mentioned x / y elements" and gives no score.
When the position or number in a sentence does not match the picture, a translucent copy appears "where it should be according to your words", side by side with the real position.

The blind canvas parses written sentences deterministically only against a controlled word list (position words, number words, colours, object names) and places objects accordingly. It does no open-ended understanding and no automatic scoring of spoken descriptions.

ui.screen: On the left is the picture, and on the right is the learner's text, each sentence being a draggable card. At the bottom are the coverage bar and a row of judgment-category buttons.
interactions: Drag a sentence card onto an element in the picture, or select a sentence and then click an element
Keyboard: Tab selects a sentence, arrow keys move between elements in the picture, and Enter makes the link
Step 1 can be recorded (only inside the page) or typed
ui.childVariant: The picture has only 4–6 elements. The oral description is recorded by the learner, who then taps icons to show "which things I mentioned". Writing is not required. In Step 3, the teacher or a parent arranges stickers on paper according to the child's description.
ui.adultVariant: Complex scenes such as a street scene, an office or a kitchen, requiring a distinction between states and actions and adding "inference" sentences. Scenes converted from charts may be chosen.
ui.accessibility: The picture comes with a text description. Visually impaired learners can use the read-aloud version of the element list, but then the task becomes going from the list to a description, and is recorded as a different task condition. Judgments do not rely on colour.

kcSignals: the KC is picture description (kt:en-skill-describe-picture, kt:zh-skill-describe-picture) or description of places and space (kt:en-fn-places, kt:ja-fn-describe-places, kt:ja-location-existence, kt:ja-spatial-nouns, kt:zh-zai-location, kt:zh-zhe-durative, kt:en-prepositions-place)
notions include existence, space-location, aspect-progress
itemTypes include situated-production-spoken or situated-production-written
learnerSignals: only lists nouns
does not know what to write when asked to write about a picture
always uses have／有 at the start of existence sentences
contraindications: most of the vocabulary for the objects in the picture has not been learned
when a plot across several pictures is to be told, use prim:sequence-retell
when describing trends in charts, use prim:grow-text

rules: Coverage: at least the required number of elements must be mentioned, of which at least two sentences contain a position, one contains a number, and one contains an action or state (blocks an answer that is too weak).

Accuracy: the element each sentence is linked to must agree with the position, number and action in the sentence. If one sentence pattern (There is a X. There is a Y.) takes up more than half, or one sentence is linked to several elements to pad out coverage, prompt a change of structure (blocks gaming).
Inference sentences must be marked as inferences; stating as fact something not in the picture is judged as failed.
check.independence: The first draft is locked before the elements light up. In the adding stage, if the learner has seen the highlighting of unmentioned elements or the sentence-pattern frame, it is recorded as completed after a hint. In the children's version, anything an adult writes or says on the child's behalf is recorded as assisted.

evidence.retained: The first draft, the first link between sentences and elements, the element coverage map, the sentences added, and the arrangement result on the blind canvas.

licensed.claim: Can describe a visible scene with existence and position structures
When describing, takes in the whole picture and not only the prominent spots

prohibited: Inferring grammatical accuracy from high coverage
Inferring the ability to narrate from the ability to describe a single picture
Counting what an adult said or wrote on the child's behalf as the child's independent output

hints: Point only to an area: "What else is on the left / at the top?"
Make one unmentioned area flash
Give a sentence-pattern frame (There is/are … on/under …; NにNがあります; 桌子上有／放着……)
scaffold.fade: After the first drafts for two consecutive pictures meet both coverage and accuracy, the sentence-pattern frame is no longer offered.

primitives.reverseHalf: More is not always better: what is not in the picture cannot be stated as fact (inferences must be marked with maybe, 好像, ようです). States and actions must be kept apart (她戴着眼镜 ≠ 她正在戴眼镜; 窓が開いている ≠ 窓を開けている). Left and right are taken from the viewpoint of the person looking at the picture, and the left and right of a figure in the picture must be stated.

failureModes.failure: The learner piles up elements with one sentence pattern to gain coverage
failureModes.mitigation: Check structural variety and prompt when one pattern takes more than half
failureModes.test: Adversarial example: a draft entirely in There is a X cannot pass

failureModes.failure: The position or number in the picture is ambiguous
failureModes.mitigation: Two people independently list the elements for each picture, and elements on which they disagree do not go into the list
failureModes.test: Record of author agreement

failureModes.failure: While linking, the learner links a wrong sentence to an element that happens to fit, and so changes their story
failureModes.mitigation: The first link is locked and recorded separately
failureModes.test: Check that the first link and the final link are listed separately in the record

stacksWith.how: On the same picture, first link the roles and then describe, and check the particles or prepositions of position sentences directly with the role links
For each action or state in the picture, first judge whether it is in progress or a resulting state, then choose 着／在, ている, -ing
The first draft is saved as the initial draft, then compared with a model description, the gaps are marked, and it is rewritten

languages.en: Structures: There is/are + prepositional phrase of position, present continuous A boy is running, have used only for possession. Traps for Chinese native speakers: *The park has a dog, *There is two cats, *A boy running
languages.ja: Structures: NにNがあります／います (いる for people and animals), Nの上・下・中・となり, ている for progress and resulting state (窓が開いています). Traps: *机の上で本があります, *かばん中に, saying 壁に and not 壁の上に for something stuck on a wall
languages.zh: Structures: place + 有／V着 + number + noun (桌子上放着一本书), noun + 在 + place, the distinction between 正在 and 着, measure words. Traps for English native speakers: *桌子有一本书, *有一本书在桌子上, *书在桌子, *她正在戴眼镜

primitives.name: Sequence & retell
primitives.oneLine: Put the pictures or sentences of a story or process in order, then retell it using linking devices
primitives.difficulty: When retelling or narrating, the order gets muddled, or everything is strung together with "then"; tense stays flat or is all present (*Then the rabbit see a carrot., *Yesterday I go to the park); the devices for before and after are used wrongly (*昨天我先吃饭，再看电影, *以后下课, and *When I arrived, she left when meaning she left first); when listening to a story, order words are ignored and the learner gives up the whole stretch at the first unknown word.
primitives.object: A short story or process (4–6 pictures or 4–6 sentence cards) in which, in one place, the order of telling differs from the order of happening (flashback or added background). Ordering, linking and retelling all happen on this same set of cards.
primitives.requires: The learner can understand, by listening or reading, each single sentence on the cards; for English, can recognise past-tense verbs. If the learner cannot describe even a single picture, use prim:picture-describe first.
learnerAction: Step 1 Put in order: arrange the shuffled cards in the order the events happened (not the order of telling).

Step 2 Add links: between each pair of neighbouring cards put a linking device, judging place by place with locked categories: before-after / at the same time / cause / contrast (the last is the reverse half: the order of telling is not the order of happening, and here a back-reference device must be used (had done, 之前已经……了, ～ていた)).

Step 3 Retell: the text on the cards is hidden and only the pictures remain, and the learner says or writes a retelling (a recording stays only inside the page), then drags each of their own sentences back to the matching card.
systemResponse: After ordering, a timeline of the order of happening is shown below. Where the order of telling differs from the order of happening, the two lines cross and are highlighted.
After the linking devices are placed, the arrows between cards change to the matching type (single arrow = before-after, parallel lines = at the same time, thick arrow = cause).

After the sentences of the retelling are dragged back to the cards, cards not covered turn grey. Where the retelling's order is the reverse of the order of happening without using a back-reference device, a crossing mark is shown.

ui.screen: The top half is a row of cards that can be rearranged horizontally, with linking slots between cards. The bottom half is the timeline. In the retelling stage the cards shrink to thumbnails and the retelling text is on the right.
interactions: Drag cards to put them in order; with the keyboard, select a card and move it with ←/→
Click a linking slot and use number keys to choose a device
The retelling can be typed or recorded
ui.childVariant: Four picture-book pictures; listen to the story first, then order. Linking devices are only three: "first, then, finally" or first/then/finally. When retelling, the child may point at the pictures while speaking, with an adult present.
ui.adultVariant: Cooking, handling paperwork, a news event or a personal experience, including flashback and simultaneous events. The retelling must use at least three different linking devices and include one flashback.
ui.accessibility: Each card has a text description. Ordering has a keyboard alternative. The crossing points on the timeline are marked with both a shape and text.

kcSignals: notions include sequence

the KC is narration, retelling or explanation of steps (kt:en-skill-listen-stories, kt:en-fn-past-experience, kt:en-fn-events, kt:en-skill-write-narrative, kt:en-past-perfect, kt:ja-tekara, kt:ja-fn-weekend-past, kt:ja-fn-travel-story, kt:zh-xian-zai, kt:zh-fn-instructions, kt:zh-fn-past-experience)
itemTypes include order-words and situated-production-spoken
learnerSignals: the retelling is all "then"
verbs do not change when talking about the past
after hearing a story, cannot say what came first
contraindications: cannot describe even a single picture
the material has no clear time order (pure description or argument)
cannot be used when the order is given away entirely by picture numbers

rules: The ordering matches the order of happening; the retelling covers all the key cards and its order can be traced (blocks an answer that is too weak).

The retelling must use at least two different linking devices and cannot be all then／然后. If the word-for-word overlap with the original exceeds a certain proportion, prompt "use your own words" (blocks gaming).
Tense and aspect markers agree with the narration: English uses the past tense, with the past perfect for background; in Chinese, something already happened does not use "再".
check.independence: The first ordering is recorded separately. A retelling made after listening again or looking at the original again is recorded as assisted completion. Changes made after seeing a linking-device hint are recorded as after a hint.

evidence.retained: The first ordering, the first choice of linking devices, the retelling text or recording, and the links between retelling sentences and cards.

licensed.claim: Can rebuild the order of events from material heard or read
When retelling, can mark before and after with linking devices and tense/aspect

prohibited: Inferring the ability to retell from correct ordering
Inferring understanding of cause and effect from a fluent retelling
Scoring the retelling recording automatically or judging pronunciation from it

hints: Ask: "When this happened, had that other thing already happened?"
Mark on the timeline the place where the order of telling and the order of happening cross
Give a list of linking devices
scaffold.fade: After two consecutive stories are ordered correctly on the first attempt and a back-reference device is used in the retelling, the list of linking devices is no longer offered.

primitives.reverseHalf: The order of telling is not necessarily the order of happening (flashbacks and added background are marked with had done, 之前已经……了, ～ていた). And "then" is not a universal device: something already happened does not take "再", and things happening at the same time use while, 一边……一边, ながら, not then／然后.

failureModes.failure: The learner orders by the default position or numbering of the cards
failureModes.mitigation: Shuffle randomly every time, and put no numbers on the cards
failureModes.test: Check the correlation between the first ordering and the initial arrangement

failureModes.failure: The learner orders only by the linking words and not the content
failureModes.mitigation: In each set at least one story has the linking words removed, so that before and after can be judged only from the content
failureModes.test: Compare the accuracy of the version without linking words with that of the version with them

failureModes.failure: The retelling copies the original
failureModes.mitigation: Hide the original in the retelling stage, and prompt with the word-for-word overlap rate
failureModes.test: Adversarial example: a retelling that copies the original must receive the prompt

stacksWith.how: Put the same set of event cards directly onto the timeline, and at the flashback also require a choice of past perfect or 已经……了
