A wrong choice is not marked wrong. The system shows "this reading appears in these words ..." and lists the word family the reading belongs to, and the learner chooses again in the original text.

Characters for which the basis "must be remembered separately" was chosen are collected into the learner's exception cards. When exception cards pile up, the system prompts "these may follow a rule" and guides the learner back to review the bases.

ui.screen: The short passage is in the middle, with marked spots underlined and carrying a reading slot. Below are the candidate reading buttons (2–4) for the current spot and a row of basis buttons. The narrow right column holds the exception cards.
interactions: Tab jumps between marked spots; number keys choose a reading and letter keys choose a basis
Tap a reading slot to play the audio (counts as viewing, not as asking for help)
Step 3 is typed, and readings can be entered in kana, pinyin or stress marks (capital letters)
ui.childVariant: For primary-school children who can read characters: handle only the two readings of one character at a time (长 cháng/zhǎng, 大人 おとな), distinguished by pictures of the meaning. No basis terminology; only ask "Does it mean 'long/short' or 'grow up'?"
ui.adultVariant: Materials come from news headlines, station names, menus and personal names. The bases show terms (音読み/訓読み, 熟字訓, rendaku, variant readings, stress shift). Step 3 asks the learner to explain the basis for each of the two readings.
ui.accessibility: Readings are shown in both text and audio. Underlines carry added numbers. A screen reader reads "spot 3, candidates: ぎょう, こう". Autoplay can be turned off.

kcSignals: The KC involves reading characters, on and kun readings, rendaku, jukujikun, polyphonic characters or word stress (kt:ja-kanji-system, kt:ja-kanji-joyo, kt:ja-sound-rendaku, kt:ja-counters, kt:zh-hanzi-l3, kt:en-phon-word-stress)
commonErrors include "thinking a character has only one reading", "reading jukujikun character by character", "misreading a polyphonic character" and "putting the stress on the wrong syllable"
itemTypes include script-reading or read-aloud
learnerSignals: Always reads the same character with one sound when reading aloud
"Why did this character turn into another reading again?"
Looks only at the first reading in a dictionary
contraindications: The learner does not recognize any reading of the character yet; use prim:oral-to-print or prim:character-anatomy first
When the difference in reading is only connected-speech change (third-tone sandhi, 一/不 tone change), use prim:contour-match
Do not set items where both readings are standard with no difference in meaning

rules: The reading and the basis must agree: a correct reading with a wrong basis is not recorded as passed (blocks gaming: hitting the right reading by luck)

In each set, the most frequent reading of the character is the correct answer on at most half of the items. Always choosing the most frequent reading fails on more than half of the items (blocks gaming).
The two readings in Step 3 must differ, and the basis for each must hold. Changing only the meaning and not the reading does not count (blocks an answer that is too weak).
check.independence: The first reading and first basis in Step 1 are recorded separately. Changing a choice after seeing the word-family list is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 does not show the word-family list.

evidence.retained: For each marked spot: the first reading, the first basis, any change, and the learner's exception cards, plus the Step 3 self-made sentence and its marked readings, all kept on the same short passage

licensed.claim: Can choose the right reading for this set of same-form characters or words by word formation or context
Can state the type of basis for a reading choice
Can correctly extend the reading by analogy in words not seen before

prohibited: Inferring accurate pronunciation from a correct reading choice (no pronunciation scoring)
Inferring that a whole class of polyphonic characters or rendaku is mastered from performance on one character
Counting a correct choice after seeing the word-family list as independent
Treating memorized jukujikun as mastery of the rule for analogy

hints: Only ask "Which word is this character part of here? What part of speech is it?"
Highlight the context relevant to the reading (the number before, the okurigana after, the whole compound)
Show one minimal contrast example for each of the two readings
scaffold.fade: After the same written form is first-attempt correct in two different contexts, the basis buttons are no longer shown for that character and only the reading is required

primitives.reverseHalf: Not every variant reading can be inferred from context. Jukujikun (今日, 大人, 土産) must be remembered separately. For 今日, both きょう and こんにち are correct and differ in register. Rendaku has many exceptions and cannot be applied as a rule everywhere. Some Chinese variant readings coexist in speech and writing (血 xuè/xiě). In English, "stress on the first syllable of a two-syllable noun and on the second of a verb" is only a tendency, and hotel and develop do not follow it.

failureModes.failure: The learner always chooses the most common reading
failureModes.mitigation: Control the proportion of the high-frequency reading under the check rules
failureModes.test: Count the score of the strategy "always choose the high-frequency reading" on the adversarial set; it should be below half

failureModes.failure: Treats the basis as a guessing game and taps any one
failureModes.mitigation: Items whose basis does not agree with the reading do not pass, and overuse of "must be remembered separately" is exposed on the exception cards
failureModes.test: Check whether the distribution of chosen bases is concentrated on a single option

failureModes.failure: Chinese learners deduce Japanese on-readings from the Mandarin sound (学校→*がこう)
failureModes.mitigation: Add to the Japanese items characters whose on-reading differs greatly from the Mandarin sound, and on-readings with geminate or long-vowel forms
failureModes.test: The adversarial set includes on-reading change words such as 学校, 一緒 and 発表

stacksWith.how: When phonetic aid is removed from the same material, polyphonic spots are removed last, and after removal this primitive takes over the reading choice
A compound is first cut into morphemes, then rendaku or the compound's reading is judged on that same segmentation
English stress contrasts (REcord/reCORD) layer a stress contour on the same word

languages.en: Contrast sets: heteronyms read (present/past), lead, live, wind, tear; stress-shift words REcord/reCORD, PREsent/preSENT, OBject/obJECT. Traps: equal stress on every syllable, putting stress on the first syllable (*HOtel)
languages.ja: Contrast sets: on/kun readings (生, 行, 上), rendaku (手紙 てがみ, 本棚 ほんだな), jukujikun (今日, 大人, 土産, 一人), special counter readings (一人, 二人, 三本, 六本, 一回). Traps: deducing on-readings from the Mandarin sound, reading jukujikun character by character, applying rendaku everywhere
languages.zh: Contrast sets: polyphonic characters 行 (xíng/háng), 长 (cháng/zhǎng), 还 (hái/huán), 了 (le/liǎo), 得 (de/dé/děi), 重 (zhòng/chóng). Traps: reading "还书" as hái, always reading "得" as de, expectations of meaning shaped by Japanese kun readings

primitives.name: False-friend check
primitives.oneLine: First write down the meaning guessed from the mother tongue, then check it against real usage and mark it as same, shifted or completely different
primitives.difficulty: When a character or word shape looks transparent, learners interpret it with confidence through their mother tongue. Chinese speakers learning Japanese take 大家 as "大家", 手紙 as "手纸", 勉強 as "勉强" and 留守 as "留守". Harder to notice are words whose meaning has shifted (研究生, 検討, 意見). Katakana English (マンション, テンション, スマート) is taken to have its original English meaning. Learners of Chinese with a Japanese or Korean background read 手纸, 汽车, 新闻 and 工夫 through their mother tongue. Chinese speakers learning English always translate "宣传" as propaganda and take eventually to mean "possibly". The problem is not that the word is unknown but that it is too familiar.
primitives.object: A same-form word comparison card. The left column holds the learner's guess written from the literal mother-tongue meaning. The right column holds 2–3 real example sentences in the target language. In the middle is a three-level marker (same / shifted / completely different). A set of cards builds into the learner's own false-friend table.
primitives.requires: Can understand the gist of the example sentences in the right column. If the sentences cannot be read, fall back to prim:context-guess first.
learnerAction: Step 1 Guess first: look only at the word shape, write down the meaning guessed from the mother tongue, and save this first guess

Step 2 Compare and judge the level: read the real example sentences in the right column and mark the word as same, shifted or completely different. For shifted, choose where it shifts (locked options: range wider or narrower / different praise or blame coloring / different register / different collocation. There is also a kind that "looks like a trap but in fact means the same", and this is the reverse half).
Step 3 Use it yourself: write a sentence with the target word that makes sense only if it is understood in its real meaning
systemResponse: After the level is judged, the line between the two columns changes color (one color plus text for each of same, shifted and completely different), and for shifted words the difference is highlighted in the example sentences
The learner's first guess always stays in the left column, is never rewritten, and is labeled "what I thought before"
After a set is finished, the cards are filed into the learner's false-friend table by level. The "same" level is also kept, showing the positive transfer from the mother tongue.

ui.screen: A horizontal comparison card: left column (what I thought before), the three-level marker in the middle, right column (real example sentences). Below the card are the shift-dimension buttons. On the right are the progress for this set and the entry to the personal false-friend table.
interactions: Step 1 is typed; the right column cannot be expanded before submitting
Click or press number keys 1–3 to judge the level, and letter keys to choose the shift dimension
Step 3 is typed; the false-friend table can be filtered by level
ui.childVariant: For primary-school children who can read: only 3 words per set, with pictures for the two meanings (手紙 paired with a letter and a roll of paper). The three levels become the faces "the same / a bit different / completely different". Writing the shift dimension is not required.
ui.adultVariant: Example sentences come from news, business email and rental contracts. The shift dimensions show terms. Add katakana loanwords and register problems of Chinese-origin words. Step 3 asks for two sentences in one work or life scene.
ui.accessibility: The three levels are shown by color, icon and text together. A screen reader reads in the order "what I thought before / marker / example sentences". All buttons work by keyboard.

kcSignals: The KC is a Chinese-character word, a loanword or morpheme-based guessing (kt:ja-str-guess-kanji, kt:ja-lex-word-origin, kt:ja-kanji-system, kt:zh-str-guess-morphemes, kt:en-false-friends)

commonErrors include "applying the Chinese character meaning to a same-form word with a different meaning", "thinking a loanword has the same meaning as the English original", and "Japanese speakers understanding same-form words by Japanese meaning"
itemTypes include translate-zh-target or match, and the error comes from the literal mother-tongue meaning
learnerSignals: Reads Chinese-character words quickly but understands them wrongly with confidence
"This word exists in Chinese too, so isn't it just ...?"
Literally translated same-form words appear in compositions
contraindications: When the learner's mother tongue and the target language share no written forms or loanwords (most words for English-background learners of Chinese), this primitive has no object; use prim:context-guess
When a word has the same meaning in both languages with no difference in collocation or register, do not set it as an item; place it only in reverse-half items
The learner still cannot understand the example sentences

rules: The Step 3 sentence must make no sense under the literal meaning and make sense only under the real meaning (example: 大家さんに家賃を払う). A sentence that works under both readings does not pass (blocks gaming).
A word marked shifted must have its shift dimension chosen, otherwise the level judgment is not recorded as complete (blocks an answer that is too weak)
At least one third of each set are truly synonymous words. If the learner marks these as "completely different" too, show "You may be over-cautious" and do not record it as passed.
check.independence: The Step 1 guess is locked before the example sentences are expanded and cannot be changed. The first level judgment in Step 2 is recorded separately, and changing the level after seeing the difference highlight is recorded as after a hint. Step 3 does not show the example sentences.

evidence.retained: For each word: the first guess, the first level judgment and any change, the shift dimension and the Step 3 sentence, all kept on the same comparison card and summarized into the learner's false-friend table

licensed.claim: Can tell same, shifted and completely different apart for this set of same-form words
Uses these words in production by their real meaning in the target language
When meeting a new same-form word, suspects it first and then checks

prohibited: Treating a wrong guess in Step 1 as an error or deducting points (a wrong guess is expected and is the starting point of this primitive)
Inferring that all same-form words are mastered from getting one set right
Inferring that the learner will avoid them in writing from being able to identify them
Counting a correct judgment after seeing the difference highlight as independent

hints: Only ask "In the example sentence, can this word be replaced by the meaning you guessed?"
Highlight the context in the example sentence that conflicts with the literal meaning
Show side by side one typical sentence using this word in the mother tongue and one in the target language
scaffold.fade: After 4 words in a row at the same level are judged correctly on first attempt, the conflict highlight in the example sentences is no longer provided

primitives.reverseHalf: Most same-form Chinese-character words in fact mean the same or nearly the same (学生, 問題, 経済, 電話), which is the biggest advantage for Chinese speakers learning Japanese. Treating every Chinese-character word as a trap makes learners give up positive transfer and read more slowly. Even when the meaning is the same, register and collocation may differ (Chinese-origin words in Japanese are often more formal than native Japanese ones, and *そろそろ帰宅します sounds stiff to a friend). These should be judged as shifted, not completely different.

failureModes.failure: To avoid mistakes the learner deliberately writes nothing or "don't know" in Step 1
failureModes.mitigation: Step 1 requires a literal guess to be written, and an empty answer cannot go to the next step
failureModes.test: Count the proportion of empty answers and "don't know"

failureModes.failure: After learning this, overcorrects and judges every Chinese-character word "completely different"
failureModes.mitigation: Fix the proportion of reverse-half items and record misjudgments of synonymous words separately
failureModes.test: One third of the adversarial set are true synonyms

failureModes.failure: Memorizes only the Chinese equivalents of this batch of words and does not form the habit of guessing first and checking after
failureModes.mitigation: Bury unlearned same-form words in later reading materials and see whether the learner marks them on their own
failureModes.test: In the transfer test, the first-time marking rate of unlearned same-form words

stacksWith.how: Words at the shifted level go straight into usage judgment, deciding one by one on the same card whether it can be said this way
When a same-form word is met in reading, write the literal guess first on the same passage, then revise it as the word is met again
Words at the completely different level go to the dictionary with their example sentences, and the correct sense is chosen on the same card

languages.en: Target: common correspondence pitfalls for Chinese speakers (宣传/propaganda, eventually/可能, sensitive/sensible, actually, treating advice as countable) and differences between English loanwords in Chinese and the English original. Trap: the first translation in a dictionary is taken as the only equivalent
languages.ja: Target: same-form kanji words (大家, 手紙, 勉強, 留守, 娘, 汽車, 研究生, 検討, 意見) and katakana loanwords (マンション, テンション, スマート, クレーム). Traps: completely different words are easy to remember, while shifted words are the hardest to notice. Reverse-half items use true synonyms such as 学生, 問題 and 図書館.
languages.zh: Target: same-form words for learners with a Japanese or Korean background (手纸, 汽车, 新闻, 工夫, 走, 老婆, 东西). For English-background learners there are no written forms to work with, so this primitive is not used and only loanwords such as "酷" and "粉丝" are handled. Trap: Japanese speakers treating a Japanese character form as the same character (単/单) is a character-shape problem, handed to prim:character-anatomy

primitives.name: Cross-language alignment
primitives.oneLine: Align the source text and the translation by meaning block, mark where things are added, deleted or re-expressed, then relay it for a specified reader
primitives.difficulty: In translating and relaying, learners match word by word. They copy passives as they are (*这本书被一位年轻作家写了), fill Chinese with pronouns and "当……的时候", and carry same-form words straight over (勉強→*勉强, 手紙→*手纸). When relaying, they drop deadlines and exception conditions and mix in their own opinions. What is missing is not vocabulary but the judgment "first align by meaning block, then decide where to add, delete or re-express, and finally say it again to a specific listener".
primitives.object: A short source text (a notice, dialogue or explanation of three to six sentences), plus the meaning-block alignment table and the relay draft for a specified listener that the learner builds step by step on the same page
primitives.requires: Can already read or hear the gist of the source (no more than about 5% unknown words when understanding the source alone). If the source cannot be understood, go back first; do not try to solve comprehension and conversion here at the same time.
learnerAction: Step 1 Cut and align: cut the source into meaning blocks (who, does what, condition, deadline, tone) and, in the right column, write or drag in the matching translation block for each block. The system pre-fills a word-for-word literal draft, and the learner must change at least one unnatural block in it.

Step 2 Mark the treatment: for each aligned block, judge it one by one (locked options: direct correspondence / re-expressed / added implied information / deleted redundancy / deleted content that should not have been deleted. The last is the reverse half).

Step 3 Relay for a specified listener: given one concrete listener (a parent who does not know the foreign language, a colleague in a hurry, a client at a formal occasion), write or say a relay. It must keep every block of the source marked "key" and adjust the register to the listener.
systemResponse: In Step 1, each time a block is aligned, the matching parts of the source and the translation are joined by a line of the same color. Source blocks with no line stay gray, showing at a glance which information has not been handled.

When the learner marks a block "deleted redundancy" and it belongs to a deadline, number, negation or exception condition, a "key information" marker appears on that block in the source, the deletion is not accepted, and the learner needs to change the judgment

After Step 3 is submitted, each place in the relay draft that covers a key block is joined to the source by a line of the same color. A missed key block flashes an empty slot on the source, and the learner can write it in. Writing it in is recorded as a revision.

Shown side by side with the word-for-word literal draft: blocks the learner changed are colored, and blocks that were not changed and are still word for word stay as they are. This is not judged right or wrong; the system only shows "this is still one-to-one here".

ui.screen: The left column is the source (strips colored by block), the middle column holds the alignment lines, and the right column holds the translation blocks. Below is the relay area, headed by "who are you speaking to" and the listener card. A narrow sidebar lists the key blocks, ticking those already covered.
interactions: Drag a source block to a translation slot to align, or select a source block and press Enter to jump to the matching translation input box
Number keys 1–5 choose the treatment
The relay area accepts typing or recording (recordings stay inside the page and are not scored automatically)
Ctrl+Z undoes the most recent alignment
ui.childVariant: The source is a picture with two or three simple sentences, and the learner only does a relay such as "help the little child tell mom". No add/delete terminology; only ask "What is the one thing mom must know in this sentence?" and mark key information with stickers.
ui.adultVariant: Sources come from work email, contract clauses, meeting remarks or news clips. The treatment names show terms (addition, omission, transposition). Step 3 can specify a written or an interpreting channel, and in the interpreting channel the learner restates under a time limit and then transcribes it themselves.
ui.accessibility: Alignment does not rely on line color alone; blocks are also matched by number. Every drag has an equivalent keyboard action. A long source can be read aloud block by block.

kcSignals: The KC's notions include reported-speech and its itemTypes include translate-zh-target (kt:zh-skill-translate-mid, kt:zh-skill-translate-advanced)
KCs for mediation and relay skills (kt:ja-skill-mediate-ja, kt:en-skill-relay-information)
commonErrors include "word-for-word translation", "missing a condition or deadline" and "mixing in own opinion"
learnerSignals: Every word of the translation matches but it does not read like real language
When relaying, reads the source as it is or picks only the parts of interest
The teacher's own words: "You translated too rigidly", "You left out the most important sentence"
contraindications: The source itself cannot be read or heard yet
The aim is to practice the correspondence of single words (use prim:false-friend-check or prim:recall-before-reveal)
The source is a legal or medical text that must not be altered and is to be actually used; the learner's practice translation must not go out directly

rules: The Step 3 relay draft must cover all blocks of the source marked key (deadline, number, negation, exception condition, the person addressed by a request). Missing any one block means it is not passed (blocks an answer that is too weak).

If the block-level overlap between the relay draft and the word-for-word literal draft is too high (for example, more than 80% of blocks left unadjusted), it does not pass and shows "still one-to-one". Also, if the relay draft contains facts or evaluations not in the source (such as "I think", "should"), it is marked "added opinion not in the source" and does not pass (blocks gaming).
The treatment marks must agree with the alignment: for a block marked "added implied information", the added content must be traceable to the source context
check.independence: The first alignment in Step 1 and the first relay in Step 3 are saved separately. Parts written in after seeing a key-block hint or a flashing empty slot are recorded as completed after a hint. No reference translation is provided. The reference translation can be viewed only after Step 3 is submitted, and a rewrite after viewing is recorded as revision after comparison.

evidence.retained: The alignment lines, the treatment mark for each block, the first relay draft in Step 3, the missed blocks that flashed and the text written in for them, and the listener card, all kept on the same source page

licensed.claim: Can align by meaning block rather than by word in this kind of text
Can keep key information (deadline, number, condition) when relaying
Can adjust the register and level of detail of a relay for different listeners

prohibited: Judging from practice with this primitive that the learner can do professional translation or interpreting
Treating a grammatically correct relay draft as an accurate relay
Treating wording close to the reference translation as high translation quality
Automatically scoring the speech in the interpreting channel's recordings

hints: Only ask "Which things must the listener know?"
Mark all key blocks on the source (without giving the wording)
Give an alignment example of a source of the same kind, showing one re-expression and one addition
scaffold.fade: After 3 sources in a row where the first relay covers all key blocks and is not judged word-for-word, the key-block markers are no longer shown and only the level 1 question remains

primitives.reverseHalf: Every set has at least one source with a block that must be kept word for word (a proper name, number, legal term, or quoted original words), where re-expressing or "paraphrasing" it is the mistake. There is also a block that looks redundant but serves politeness or cushioning (恐れ入りますが, 麻烦您) and must not be deleted for the specified listener.

failureModes.failure: To avoid the "word-for-word" judgment, the learner rewrites at random, losing the original meaning or adding content
failureModes.mitigation: The word-for-word overlap check, the key-block coverage check and the added-opinion check all apply at once
failureModes.test: Adversarial samples: a fluent relay that changes the deadline and a fluent relay that adds an evaluation must both fail

failureModes.failure: The learner works out the rule for judging key blocks (keep whenever there is a number) and deletes all other information
failureModes.mitigation: Rotate the key-block types, including negation, condition and the person addressed by a request, not only numbers
failureModes.test: Check that number-type blocks are no more than half of the key blocks in each set

failureModes.failure: The listener card is a formality and the relay is the same for everyone
failureModes.mitigation: In later rounds, relay the same source again to a different listener and compare the two drafts
failureModes.test: When the register marks in the two drafts are exactly the same, show "Are these two listeners the same?"

stacksWith.how: When a Chinese-Japanese same-form word or an English-Chinese false-friend block comes up during alignment, add a "literal guess vs. real usage" check on the spot, and write the result directly into that block's treatment
The relay draft in Step 3 is calibrated on the same page for the politeness level that fits the listener's relationship, and where it slips is marked on the relay draft
For quantity blocks in the source such as 万/亿 and 三成, number-place conversion is called during alignment, and the conversion result becomes that block's translation

languages.en: Chinese→English and English→Chinese relay. Traps: Chinese sentences with no subject need a subject added, the Chinese "被" does not equal the passive, culture-loaded words translated literally as in *mutual benefit and common winning; person and tense adjustment when relaying (He said he would come). Corresponds to kt:en-skill-relay-information.
languages.ja: Japanese→Chinese mediation and Japanese→Japanese relay of key points. Traps: same-form words and softened expressions such as 勉強になりました, 手紙 and 検討します; dropped subjects leading to the wrong actor; missed deadlines and exception conditions. Corresponds to kt:ja-skill-mediate-ja.
languages.zh: Foreign language→Chinese and Chinese→foreign language translation, and interpreting. Traps: English speakers translating passives and "当……的时候" word by word and using too many pronouns; Japanese speakers carrying over Japanese kanji words. The advanced stage includes contract register and conversion of "三成" and "万/亿". Corresponds to kt:zh-skill-translate-mid and kt:zh-skill-translate-advanced.

primitives.name: Number-system mapping
primitives.oneLine: Convert between different digit-grouping systems such as 万/亿 and thousand/million: estimate first, then calculate, then read it out
primitives.difficulty: Chinese and Japanese group numbers in fours (万, 亿), while English groups them in threes (thousand, million, billion). Learners make errors when converting between the two groupings. They say 15 万 as *fifteen ten thousand or 1.5 million, English speakers say 100,000 as *一百千, the いち of 一万 is dropped in Japanese, and "三成" is translated as three percent. The error is not in counting but in converting character by character without first estimating the order of magnitude.
primitives.object: A fixed quantity card: one large number, approximate number or sum of money in a real context (population, house price, budget), shown in three forms at once: Arabic digits, the target-language reading and a digit-grouping bar. The learner estimates, calculates and reads on the same card.
primitives.requires: Can already read and write numbers up to 9999 (see kt:zh-numerals, kt:ja-numerals-system, kt:en-fn-numbers). If numbers below 万 are not yet fluent, go back first.
learnerAction: Step 1 Estimate the magnitude first: on seeing a number said in the source language (such as "十五万"), first mark on a number line roughly which level it is (thousands / ten-thousands / hundred-thousands / millions). No calculator is allowed.

Step 2 Drag the grouping: on the digit-grouping bar, drag the comma or the 万 line to the right place (150,000 ↔ 15|0000) and judge what the number reads as under each of the two groupings (locked options: corresponds to the thousand level / corresponds to the million level / contains "万" and needs conversion / an approximate-number word shifts the position. The last is the reverse half, e.g. the "多" in "三万多人" and "about 150,000").

Step 3 Read it out: say or write the number in the target language as a full quantity phrase (with a measure word or unit and an approximate-number word). Then take a number from your own life (your hometown's population, the price of something you want to buy), convert it and read it out.
systemResponse: After the Step 1 mark is placed, the true position lights up on the number line, and a gap arrow is drawn between it and the learner's estimate. When the gap is one order of magnitude or more, the arrow turns red.
When the grouping line is dragged, the comma positions of the Arabic digits and the 万/亿 positions in Chinese or Japanese characters move in sync, and the two readings below are rewritten in real time

After Step 3 is submitted, the learner's reading is split back onto the digit-grouping bar, and the system shows on the bar what number the learner actually said. When they differ, it shows side by side "You said 1,500,000; the original number is 150,000".

ui.screen: At the top is the context sentence (containing a number). In the middle is the draggable digit-grouping bar (showing the three-digit commas and the four-digit 万 line at once). Below are the number line and the reading input box. A small column on the right records each card's estimation error, with no score shown.
interactions: Left and right arrow keys move the grouping line, and Enter confirms
Click on the number line or use arrow keys to choose the magnitude
The reading can be typed, or recorded and then transcribed by the learner (no automatic recognition or scoring)
ui.childVariant: Numbers are kept within ten thousand, and pictures of blocks or coins show the conversion of thousands and ten-thousands. "一万 is ten 一千" is demonstrated with ten stacked blocks, and million does not appear.
ui.adultVariant: Contexts come from news, financial reports, house prices and population statistics. Includes 亿/billion, percentages, 成数, decimals and currency units. Step 3 asks for a complete sentence with an approximate number.
ui.accessibility: Each cell of the digit-grouping bar can be read by a screen reader as "ten-thousands place", "hundred-thousands place". Besides color, separator lines of different thickness distinguish the three-digit and four-digit groupings.

kcSignals: notions include quantity and involve large numbers, approximate numbers or sums of money (kt:en-lex-numbers-data, kt:zh-numbers-large-approx, kt:ja-numerals-system, kt:en-fn-numbers)
commonErrors include "error in converting by 万" and "converting by three-digit groups"
A translation KC has an error in converting number units (kt:zh-skill-translate-advanced)
learnerSignals: On hearing a large number, pauses for a long time and then converts character by character
Confuses 十万 and 一百万
The teacher's own words: "This number is off by ten times"
contraindications: Only discriminating single digits by ear (13/30) or reading a phone number digit by digit; use prim:sound-contrast or prim:listen-for-data
The learner cannot yet read numbers below 万

rules: The reading in Step 3, converted back to Arabic digits, must equal the original number (for approximate-number items, within the range the approximate word specifies). An error in the order of magnitude means it is not passed (blocks an answer that is too weak).

The reading must follow the target language's number-word form: in English, no -s on million/thousand or hundred after a specific number; in Chinese, the position of "多"; in Japanese, the いち of 一万; the use of 二 and 两. Simply writing Arabic digits does not pass (blocks gaming).

A card whose Step 1 estimate differs from the true value by one order of magnitude or more is marked "calculated right but no sense of magnitude" and goes into the review queue, even if it is read correctly in Step 3
check.independence: The Step 1 estimate is locked before the digit-grouping bar is seen. A re-reading after seeing the linked grouping bar or the "you said ..." echo is recorded as completed after a hint. No example is given for the conversion of self-chosen numbers.

evidence.retained: On each quantity card are kept the first estimate point, the end point of the grouping-line drag, the first reading, the echo comparison and the revised reading

licensed.claim: Can convert correctly between 万/亿 and thousand/million in controlled contexts
Has a sense of magnitude for large numbers (estimation error within one order of magnitude)
Can handle large numbers on the spot in listening and speaking

prohibited: Judging that the learner can read the number from correct Arabic digits alone
Treating correct written conversion as equal to understanding large numbers said aloud
Automatically scoring speech in recordings

hints: Only ask "Is this thousands, ten-thousands, or hundreds of thousands?"
Show on the grouping bar the matching positions of the four-digit 万 line and the three-digit comma
Give anchor conversions: 一万 = ten thousand, 十万 = one hundred thousand, 一百万 = one million
scaffold.fade: After 5 cards in a row where the first estimate error is within one order of magnitude and the first reading is correct, remove the synced display of the grouping bar and keep only the context sentence and the input box

primitives.reverseHalf: Every set has at least one card that needs no conversion or cannot be converted by rule: numbers below 一万, phone numbers and years that are read digit by digit or in pairs, "三成" meaning 30% and not three units, Japanese 四千 (よんせん) and 九千 that cannot be read literally, and English dozens of / millions of with no specific number, where -s is added

failureModes.failure: The learner practices only a few round anchors (十万, 一百万) and still errs on non-round numbers (15 万, 2.3 亿)
failureModes.mitigation: More than half of the cards in each set are non-round numbers or carry approximate words
failureModes.test: Adversarial samples: at least one card each of 1.5 million, 23 亿, 三万多人 and about 150,000

failureModes.failure: The learner works the answer out on scratch paper before estimating in Step 1, so the estimate loses its meaning
failureModes.mitigation: Step 1 is timed and gives only the source-language reading, not Arabic digits
failureModes.test: Check the answer-time distribution in Step 1 and mark abnormally long times separately

stacksWith.how: The same quantity card becomes a listening task: first listen to a large number read in the source language and fill the cells, then convert on the grouping bar, and record the error type (magnitude, grouping, unit) on the same card
The quantity cards come from real documents (price lists, statistics tables), and the numbers found by scanning go straight into estimate-calculate-read
When reading out the quantity phrase in Step 3, the measure word or counter is chosen at the same place (三万多个人, 二万人), and the classifier and the digit places are checked together

languages.en: Contrast: thousand/million/billion in three-digit groups vs. Chinese 万/亿. Traps: *fifteen ten thousand, *three millions people, adding -s to hundred, reading digits after the decimal point as a whole number, writing percent as *percents. Corresponds to kt:en-lex-numbers-data and kt:en-fn-numbers.
languages.ja: Groups numbers in fours like Chinese, but the reading has traps: 一万 must be said いちまん, いち is not added before 百 and 千, 二万 is not *りょうまん, and sound changes such as 三百 (さんびゃく). Converting to English is the same as for Chinese. Corresponds to kt:ja-numerals-system and kt:ja-numerals-variants.
languages.zh: For English speakers: *一百千 and *三十千 must become 十万 and 三万; the position of "多" and "左右" (三万多人), the word order of fractions (三分之一), 二/两 (两万), the "零" in 一百零五, and 成数. Corresponds to kt:zh-numbers-large-approx and kt:zh-numerals.

primitives.name: Variety mapping
primitives.oneLine: Set the variants of one meaning (regional, dialect, traditional/simplified) side by side and judge which to use on which occasion
primitives.difficulty: Learners recognize only one variety and treat the others as mistakes. They think Did you eat yet? must be wrong, hear the Kansai ～へん as a past tense, or call Hong Kong and Taiwan usage "wrong Chinese". Or the reverse happens: British and American spellings are mixed in one text, a dialect is imitated on a formal occasion, and one-to-many conversions go wrong in simplified-to-traditional conversion (头发→*頭發). What is missing is a map of "which variety each of these expressions belongs to and which to use on which occasion", and the ability to recognize first and decide afterward whether to produce.
primitives.object: A set of parallel expressions with the same meaning (British and American versions of one sentence, Mandarin and Hong Kong/Taiwan usage, simplified and traditional, standard language and Kansai dialect), laid out as a variety comparison table, with a swappable occasion of use
primitives.requires: Already knows the meaning of the sentence in one of the varieties (usually the standard variety). If even the standard form is not understood, go back first.
learnerAction: Step 1 Recognize: listen to or read a set of parallel expressions and drag each one to the variety column it belongs to (British/American, mainland/Taiwan/Hong Kong, simplified/traditional, standard/Kansai). At least one needs to be judged from a spelling, word or sound cue, not from the label on the item.

Step 2 Fix the occasion: given an occasion (writing an email to a British company, eating at a friend's home in Osaka, making a poster for Taiwanese readers), judge each expression one by one (locked options: the best fit here / also acceptable, the other side will understand / would seem inappropriate or confusing / not another variety but a real error. The last is the reverse half).
Step 3 Choose and stay consistent: write two or three sentences for the specified occasion (or convert a passage from simplified to traditional). The whole passage must stay in one variety.
systemResponse: After an item is dragged in Step 1, the part of the expression that decides the variety is marked (the -our of colour, the words in 出租车/計程車/的士, ～へん, 髮/發), and the system does not only show right or wrong

After the choice in Step 2, a listener's reaction appears on the occasion card (understands but notices a slight foreign accent / cannot understand at all / thinks you are joking), and the learner can change the judgment

After Step 3 is submitted, forms in the same passage that belong to different varieties are colored differently, so mixing is visible at a glance. In simplified-to-traditional conversion items, one-to-many characters (发/髮/發, 后/後) are circled separately.

ui.screen: On the left is the column of parallel-expression cards. On the right are the variety columns (2–4, with small regional icons). Below are the occasion card and the writing area. Cards with the same meaning are aligned horizontally across the variety columns.
interactions: Drag, or use number keys, to put a card into a variety column
Space plays a recording (dialect and accent items)
The writing area colors forms in real time, and Tab jumps between the marked forms
ui.childVariant: Only the two steps "recognize" and "where would you hear it", with cartoon characters standing for regions (for example a British child and an American child saying biscuit / cookie). Children are not asked to produce varieties from regions other than the one they are learning.
ui.adultVariant: Adds business and publishing scenes (a product manual for the Taiwan market, British official correspondence, a Kansai client) and discusses why a text should stay consistent. Step 3 includes converting a whole passage between simplified and traditional and unifying spelling.
ui.accessibility: Variety columns have text labels as well as colors. All recordings come with transcripts. Dialect recordings can be played slowly.

kcSignals: KCs in the sociolinguistic category involving regional or dialect varieties (kt:en-soc-varieties, kt:zh-soc-varieties, kt:ja-soc-dialects)
itemTypes include script-reading (traditional/simplified) or listen-discriminate (dialect, accent)
commonErrors include "treating the other side's variety as an error", "mixing" and "one-to-many conversion errors"
learnerSignals: Corrects other people's usage as "not standard"
Both colour and color appear in the same composition
Asks before going to Taiwan or Osaka, "Will what I learned work there?"
contraindications: The learner does not yet know this expression even in the standard variety
Do not teach social class or accent ranking as "variety choice", to avoid marking some accents as inferior
Children and beginners are not asked to produce dialects outside the target region

rules: The whole passage in Step 3 may contain marked forms from only one variety. Mixing two spellings or two regions' usage means it is not passed (blocks an answer that is too weak).

In Step 1, at least half of the cards have obvious labels removed (such as the word "British:") and must be judged from spelling, wording or sound. Guessing from a place-name word on the card does not count as recognition (blocks gaming).
In conversion items, one-to-many characters must be chosen correctly by context (頭髮/發展, 皇后/之後). A mechanical conversion of the whole passage does not pass.
check.independence: The first sorting in Step 1 is recorded separately. A change of judgment after seeing the highlight on the deciding part is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 does not show the variety comparison table, which can be viewed only after submission if the learner chooses.

evidence.retained: On the variety comparison table are kept each card's first sorting and any change, the occasion judgments, the variety coloring result of the Step 3 passage and the choices on one-to-many characters

licensed.claim: Can recognize which variety each expression in this set belongs to
Can keep one variety without mixing in a specified occasion
Can recognize another variety as "different" and not "wrong"

prohibited: Judging from this practice that the learner can understand real, natural conversation in a dialect
Judging a variety other than the "standard" form as an error
Making any ranking evaluation of the learner's accent on this basis

hints: Only ask "Which word or character in this sentence tells you where it is said?"
Highlight the part that decides the variety
Show a small comparison table of that word across the varieties
scaffold.fade: After 5 cards in a row of the same variety set are sorted correctly on first attempt, and Step 3 passes the consistency check at one go, the small comparison table is no longer provided

primitives.reverseHalf: Every set includes one expression that "looks like a variety but is in fact an error" (*頭發, *colourful written as *colorfull, *行かへんかった in an ungrammatical position), and one expression common to all varieties that need not be distinguished, to prevent learners from attributing all differences to variety or all to error

failureModes.failure: The learner learns the variety comparison as a wrong hierarchy such as "British = formal, American = casual"
failureModes.mitigation: The occasion cards include both formal and informal scenes for both varieties
failureModes.test: Adversarial samples: one American formal official document and one British informal chat; register must not be inferred from variety

failureModes.failure: Traditional/simplified conversion relies on a one-to-one table, and one-to-many characters are converted correctly only by chance
failureModes.mitigation: One-to-many characters appear in pairs in the same passage (头发/发展)
failureModes.test: When the same simplified character in one passage must be converted to two different traditional characters, converting only one correctly does not pass

failureModes.failure: Dialect items rely on one high-frequency marker (～へん, ～はる) and cannot be recognized when the marker is absent
failureModes.mitigation: Add sentences judged by intonation or other word forms
failureModes.test: One third of the dialect items drop the highest-frequency marker form

stacksWith.how: The occasion judgment in Step 2 and politeness-level calibration are done on the same occasion card: both the variety and the degree of formality are chosen
A small incident caused by a variety misunderstanding (correcting the other side's usage as wrong, Kansai dialect misunderstood) is placed in front of the same comparison table as a starting point
In accent items, the difference in how the same word is pronounced across varieties (/ɑː/ vs. /æ/, Kansai pitch accent) is first discriminated by ear as a minimal contrast

languages.en: Contrast sets: British/American spelling (colour/color, -ise/-ize), word choice (flat/apartment, biscuit/cookie), grammar (Did you eat yet? / Have you eaten yet?), accent. Traps: mixing in one text, treating the other variety as an error. Corresponds to kt:en-soc-varieties.
languages.ja: Contrast sets: standard language / Kansai dialect (～へん/～ない, ～はる, ～や/～だ). Mainly recognition and comprehension; dialect is not required in formal settings. Traps: taking ～へん as a past tense, taking ～はる as excessive honorific. Corresponds to kt:ja-soc-dialects.
languages.zh: Contrast sets: simplified/traditional (one-to-many: 发/髮/發, 后/後, 干/乾/幹), mainland/Taiwan/Hong Kong usage (软件/軟體, 出租车/計程車/的士), Mandarin/dialects. Trap: Japanese speakers treating Japanese shinjitai as simplified or traditional (気, 対). Corresponds to kt:zh-soc-varieties.

primitives.name: Figurative & implied meaning
primitives.oneLine: First write the literal meaning, then work out the metaphor, idiom, irony or implied meaning and point to the evidence
primitives.difficulty: Learners either read metaphors, idioms, set phrases, irony and implied meaning completely literally (马马虎虎 has something to do with horses and tigers; 「ちょっと…」 is "a little"; the exaggerated "said it ten thousand times" is taken as an exact count; the narrator's irony cannot be read) or, the other way round, force their mother tongue's figures onto the target language (*add legs to a snake, *一箭双雕 in place of 一石二鳥, *顔が大きい for having wide connections). What is missing is the process of first writing the literal meaning clearly, then stating the gap between the two meanings and the cues that point to it.
primitives.object: A context containing one figurative or implied expression (a line of dialogue from a novel, a conversation, a sentence that holds an idiom). On the same context the learner first writes the literal layer, then the implied layer, then marks the cues.
primitives.requires: The basic meaning of each word in the expression is already known. If even the literal meaning cannot be read, go back and deal with vocabulary first.
learnerAction: Step 1 Write the literal meaning: write only what the sentence "says literally", using the original meaning of each word. Writing an extended meaning directly is not allowed.

Step 2 Judge the gap: against the context, judge the relation between the literal meaning and what the speaker really means (locked options: metaphor / exaggeration / irony or saying the opposite / polite refusal or hint / fixed idiom whose meaning has nothing to do with the literal meaning / just the literal meaning, no implied meaning. The last is the reverse half), and write what is really meant.

Step 3 Point to the cues: in the context, mark the cues that support your judgment (intonation marking, contradiction with what comes before or after, the occasion, the relationship between the speakers, a fixed collocation that cannot be altered). Then use the expression once, appropriately, in the target language in a new situation, or explain why it should not be used.
systemResponse: After Step 1 is written, the literal layer is shown one line above the original sentence and the Step 2 meaning one line below it. The gap between the two lines is drawn as a labeled line (metaphor, irony, euphemism ...).

The cues marked in Step 3 are boxed in the context and linked to the Step 2 judgment. When a position unrelated to the judgment is marked, the cue box turns dashed and shows "This spot does not support this judgment".

If the learner judges "just the literal meaning" in Step 2 when there is in fact an implied meaning, the system does not mark it wrong. It shows a follow-up reaction from the listener (the other person did not ask again, the other person laughed) so the learner judges again.

ui.screen: The context passage is in the middle, with the sentence containing the target expression enlarged. Above the sentence is the "literal layer" input box and below is the "what is really meant" input box, with a row of gap-type buttons in between. A narrow right column is the list of cues.
interactions: Number keys 1–6 choose the gap type
Drag to select text in the context as a cue and press Enter to confirm
Tab switches among the literal layer, the meaning layer and the cues
ui.childVariant: Pictures show the literal meaning (a real picture of "raining cats and dogs", a real picture of "drawing legs on a snake"). The child first laughs at the literal picture, then chooses another picture for the real meaning. Only metaphors and idioms are done, not irony.
ui.adultVariant: Contexts come from novels, commentary and business conversation (「検討します」「前向きに考えます」), including narrator irony, the distinction between narrator and author, and polite refusal. Step 3 asks the learner to explain whether it should be used in formal writing.
ui.accessibility: The gap line is also read out through its text label. Picture items have text alternatives. Cues can be selected sentence by sentence by keyboard.

kcSignals: KCs for idioms, set phrases and proverbs (kt:zh-lex-chengyu-basic, kt:zh-lex-chengyu-advanced, kt:ja-lex-yojijukugo-idioms, kt:en-idiomatic-expressions)
Rhetoric and implied meaning (kt:zh-rhetoric, kt:zh-rhetorical-questions, kt:zh-str-implicature, kt:ja-str-implicature, kt:en-str-infer-attitude)
Literary reading (kt:en-skill-read-literature, kt:ja-skill-read-literature-ja), and commonErrors include "understanding literally" and "missing irony"
learnerSignals: Keeps asking "What time would suit you?" after a polite refusal
Can only retell the plot after reading a novel
Translates mother-tongue idioms literally into the target language
contraindications: The basic vocabulary in the expression is not yet known
Do not set an item when the context is not enough to judge the speaker's intent (isolated single-sentence irony)
Do not make culturally contested or offensive figures the target of practice production

rules: The meaning in Step 2 must differ from the literal layer (unless judged "just the literal meaning") and be compatible with the context. Merely restating the literal meaning or writing only "this is a metaphor" does not pass (blocks an answer that is too weak).

Step 3 must mark at least one cue that really exists in the context and agrees with the judgment. Marking no context cue and relying only on the expression "sounding like an idiom" does not count as passed (blocks gaming).
In production items the fixed parts of a fixed expression must not be altered (*on the same pages, *很一模一样), and register is checked: using a colloquial saying in a formal text does not pass
check.independence: The first answers in Steps 1 and 2 are locked before any hint. A changed judgment after seeing the listener's follow-up reaction or a cue hint is recorded as completed after a hint. No idiom glossary is provided; the explanation can be viewed only after submission.

evidence.retained: On each context are kept the literal layer, the gap type of the first judgment, the real meaning, the cue boxes the learner marked and later changes of judgment

licensed.claim: Can distinguish literal meaning from implied meaning for this kind of expression
Can support their judgment of implied meaning with context cues
Can use this kind of set phrase appropriately on the right occasion

prohibited: Judging that the learner understands implied meaning in context from memorizing idiom glosses alone
Judging one reasonable reading of a literary work by the learner as the only correct answer
Equating recognizing a metaphor with being able to use it appropriately

hints: Only ask "If it really happened literally, would this scene make sense?"
Highlight one key cue in the context (without giving the conclusion)
Give a parallel example of the same type with a transparent meaning
scaffold.fade: After 4 passages in a row of the same kind of gap (such as polite refusal) are judged correctly on first attempt with valid cues, hints above level 2 are no longer shown

primitives.reverseHalf: Every set has at least one passage whose expression looks figurative but is simply literal ("他像他爸爸" is a comparison and not a metaphor, it's pouring said while it is really pouring), and one passage whose expression could be literal or figurative and context decides (the case where 「ちょっと…」 really is just "a little"), to prevent learners from pushing every set phrase they meet toward an implied meaning

failureModes.failure: The learner memorizes the fixed gloss of every idiom and fills it in directly, skipping the context
failureModes.mitigation: The same idiom appears in different contexts, including positive or negative coloring and ironic reversal
failureModes.test: Adversarial sample: a positive idiom used ironically (他真是“聪明绝顶”) must be judged by context

failureModes.failure: The learner over-interprets and reads an implied meaning into every sentence
failureModes.mitigation: About a quarter of the items in each set are "just the literal meaning"
failureModes.test: Check the learner's misjudgment rate on literal items and prompt when it is too high

failureModes.failure: The cue marking is guessed (always marking the last sentence)
failureModes.mitigation: The position of the cue rotates among the beginning, middle and end of the context, and the cue must match the type of judgment
failureModes.test: Check that the correct cue positions are evenly distributed

stacksWith.how: When reading literature or commentary, first separate the voices of narrator, character and author on the same passage, then judge who is being ironic

For Chinese-Japanese same-form idioms or similar Chinese-English set phrases (一石二鳥/一箭双雕), first write the literal guess from the mother tongue, then compare it with the literal layer of this primitive
A misunderstanding incident around a polite refusal or social courtesy serves as the context; after the judgment, rewrite the response made at the time on the same incident

languages.en: Target: idioms (under the weather, break the ice), literary irony, narrator voice, understatement. Traps: altering fixed parts (*on the same pages), translating Chinese idioms literally (*add legs to a snake), taking a first-person narrator for the author, missing ironic tone. Corresponds to kt:en-idiomatic-expressions, kt:en-skill-read-literature, kt:en-str-infer-attitude.
languages.ja: Target: 慣用句 (顔が広い/顔が大きい), 四字熟語, euphemism (ちょっと…, 検討します, 考えておきます), 察し. Traps: substituting Chinese idioms (*一箭双雕), taking 八方美人 as praise, taking 検討します as agreement. Corresponds to kt:ja-lex-yojijukugo-idioms, kt:ja-str-implicature, kt:ja-skill-read-literature-ja.
languages.zh: Target: rhetoric (metaphor, hyperbole, parallelism, antithesis), rhetorical questions, chengyu, proverbs, xiehouyu, implied meaning (我再考虑考虑, 时间不早了). Traps: treating comparison as metaphor, modifying a chengyu with a degree adverb or giving it an object, confusing praise and blame (差强人意), register mismatch. Corresponds to kt:zh-rhetoric, kt:zh-rhetorical-questions, kt:zh-lex-chengyu-basic, kt:zh-lex-chengyu-advanced, kt:zh-str-implicature.

primitives.name: Dictionary sense picking
primitives.oneLine: Take a sentence in context to the dictionary, pick the right sense among several, and give the reason
primitives.difficulty: The learner finds the word but uses it wrongly. They look only at the first sense or remember only the Chinese gloss (taking every light as "光"), look up an inflected form and find nothing (looking up *studied, looking up 食べた), pick a synonym that does not fit the context in a Chinese-English dictionary (*sky hot), or cannot locate a character by radical or pinyin. What is missing is not the willingness to look things up but the whole set of operations: go back to the dictionary form, rule out among several senses by context, and say the reason.
primitives.object: A real sentence containing one target word, plus a corresponding multi-sense dictionary entry (a simplified learner's dictionary entry with 3–6 senses, example sentences and collocations). The learner works back and forth between the sentence and the entry.
primitives.requires: The rest of the sentence apart from the target word can be mostly read. Can already recognize the basic inflected forms of the target word (see prim:paradigm-apply). If the learner cannot restore an inflected form to its base form, go back first.
learnerAction: Step 1 Find the entry: starting from the form in the sentence, write the dictionary form to look up (studied→study, 食べた→食べる, locate the character by radical or pinyin). If the lookup is wrong, the entry does not open.

Step 2 Pick the sense: among the entry's several senses, choose the one that best fits the sentence, and for each of the other senses judge the reason to exclude it (locked options: wrong part of speech / wrong collocation / wrong register / the meaning does not work here / this one also works. The last is the reverse half).

Step 3 Take it away: rewrite the chosen sense in your own words and put it back into the original sentence to test whether it can replace the word. Then, in the vocabulary notebook, record the original sentence, the sense and one collocation, and write a new sentence of your own using the same sense.
systemResponse: After the dictionary form is entered in Step 1, a restoration chain is drawn between the inflected form in the sentence and the entry headword (studied ← study + -ed), showing the basis for each step. When a wrong base form is entered, the system shows "This form is not in the dictionary" and not the answer.

After a sense is selected in Step 2, that sense's gloss is substituted into the original sentence and displayed, so the learner can read directly what the sentence means after substitution. The exclusion reasons are highlighted in sync with the part-of-speech and collocation labels on the senses.

When written into the vocabulary notebook in Step 3, the record automatically carries the original sentence and the sense number, and when the same word later appears in other sentences it links back to this record

ui.screen: At the top is the original sentence containing the target word (the word is tappable). In the middle is the dictionary entry card (senses laid out by number, each with part of speech, collocations and an example sentence). Below are the "substitute into the sentence" preview strip and the vocabulary-notebook record box.
interactions: Click the target word to start Step 1 and type the dictionary form or pinyin/radical in the input box
Up and down arrows move between senses, Space selects, and number keys choose the exclusion reason
Enter substitutes the selected sense into the original sentence preview
ui.childVariant: Uses a picture dictionary: each of a word's two or three senses has a picture (the racket and the animal for bat), and the child taps the picture according to the sentence. Step 1 covers only the most common plural and -ing restorations, and character lookup uses only radical icons.
ui.adultVariant: Uses full learner's dictionary entries (with register labels, collocation boxes and usage notes), including phrasal verbs and polysemous function words. Step 3 asks the learner to export the record to a personal chunk notebook.
ui.accessibility: Sense entries can be read aloud one by one. When the preview strip sits beside the original sentence, the replaced part is underlined. The radical selector has text names (三点水, 木字旁).

kcSignals: KC for dictionary look-up and vocabulary recording in learning strategies (kt:en-str-dictionary-learning)
KCs that require restoring an inflected form to the dictionary form (restoring the dictionary form in kt:ja-verb-groups, kt:en-orth-inflection-spelling)
Character look-up and polysemous words (radicals in kt:zh-hanzi-components, radicals in kt:ja-kanji-system)
commonErrors include "looking only at the first sense" and "cannot find the inflected word"
learnerSignals: Still misunderstands the sentence after looking in the dictionary
The vocabulary notebook has only the word and the Chinese gloss
The teacher's own words: "You looked up another meaning"
contraindications: The target word can be guessed directly from context and looking it up would break the reading (use prim:context-guess to decide whether to look up or skip)
The target word has only one sense in this dictionary, so there is no choice to make
The learner cannot yet do basic morphological restoration

rules: The sense chosen in Step 2, substituted into the original sentence, must read sensibly and agree with the reference judgment. The dictionary form in Step 1 must be accurate (blocks an answer that is too weak).

An exclusion reason must be given for each excluded sense, and at least one reason must cite a specific cue in the original sentence (object, collocating word, register). If the learner always picks the first sense and the accuracy is lower than expected from the sense distribution, show "You may be choosing in order" (blocks gaming).
In the new sentence in Step 3 the target word must be used in the same sense, and using it in another sense does not pass
check.independence: The first dictionary form entered in Step 1 and the first sense chosen in Step 2 are recorded separately. A changed choice after seeing the substitution preview is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 does not show the example sentences in the entry.

evidence.retained: On the original sentence are kept the restoration chain, the first sense chosen, the exclusion reasons, changes of choice in the substitution preview, and the vocabulary-notebook record carrying the original sentence and sense number

licensed.claim: Can restore this kind of inflected form to the dictionary form and find the entry
Can choose the right sense among several according to context
Has formed the habit of comparing several senses when looking up a dictionary

prohibited: Judging that the learner can actively use a sense because they chose it correctly
Equating looking up the dictionary correctly with mastering the word
Treating the number of records in the learner's vocabulary notebook as evidence of vocabulary size

hints: Only ask "Is this word a noun or a verb in the sentence? What follows it?"
In the entry, gray out senses whose part of speech does not match the original sentence
Show the two closest senses side by side in the substitution preview
scaffold.fade: After 5 items in a row where the sense is chosen correctly on first attempt without opening the preview, the part-of-speech filter is no longer shown automatically and is provided only on request

primitives.reverseHalf: Every set has at least one item where two senses both work in this sentence, so a larger context is needed or the ambiguity must be admitted. There is also one item where the target word is part of a fixed phrase or idiom (take off, 気がする, 打招呼), where none of the senses of the single word is right and the learner must turn to a phrase entry.

failureModes.failure: The learner always picks the first or the longest sense
failureModes.mitigation: The correct sense is evenly distributed across positions in the entry, and common words whose correct sense is not the first are included
failureModes.test: In the adversarial set, the correct sense is in position 1 in no more than one third of items

failureModes.failure: The learner looks only at the Chinese gloss and skips part of speech and collocation
failureModes.mitigation: In some items the entry hides the Chinese gloss and keeps only the English or Japanese definition and the example sentences
failureModes.test: Compare accuracy between the items with and without Chinese glosses, and prompt when the gap is too large

failureModes.failure: The learner completes morphological restoration by exhaustive trial and error
failureModes.mitigation: After more than 3 entries in Step 1, the item switches to completed after a hint and is recorded as such
failureModes.test: Check the distribution of the number of entries in Step 1

stacksWith.how: First guess a meaning on the original sentence and save it, then look up the dictionary to pick a sense, and compare the gap between the guess and the chosen sense
The restoration chain in Step 1 calls the inflection rules to derive it, and the learner works back from the inflected form to the dictionary form on the same word
In Step 3, the chosen sense and the collocation in the original sentence are collected into the chunk notebook as a chunk

languages.en: Target: polysemous words (light, run, fair), phrasal verbs, restoring inflected forms (studied→study, children→child). Traps: looking only at the first sense, remembering only the Chinese, choosing the wrong synonym in a Chinese-English dictionary (*sky hot). Corresponds to kt:en-str-dictionary-learning.
languages.ja: Target: restoring from the ます form, て form, た form and ない form to the 辞書形 and then looking up (食べた→食べる, 行って→行く), polysemous verbs (かける, とる), looking up kanji by radical or reading. Traps: wrong restorations such as *飲みる and *起きく, same kun reading with different characters. Corresponds to kt:ja-verb-groups and kt:ja-kanji-system.
languages.zh: Target: looking up characters by pinyin or radical, readings and senses of polyphonic characters (还 huán/hái, 行 xíng/háng), choosing the sense of polysemous words (打, 开). Traps: taking the phonetic component as the pronunciation, looking only at the first sense. Corresponds to kt:zh-hanzi-components and the character KCs at each level.

primitives.name: Input-method conversion
primitives.oneLine: Type in pinyin or romaji, choose the right character or kana from the candidate list by context, and catch homophone mistakes
primitives.difficulty: When typing with an input method, the reading is typed correctly but the wrong homophone or near-homophone is chosen from the candidates. In Chinese: *我明天在来 (should be 再), *以後 (in a simplified-character environment it should be 以后). In Japanese: 帰る/変える, *げにん (for 原因, where only one n was typed for ん), typing を as o and getting 「お」, and typing simplified character forms with a Chinese input method. A character the learner can write by hand is chosen wrongly when typing, because they "pick the first one" or "it looks right", and the learner usually cannot see the mistake themselves.
primitives.object: A sentence the learner types with an input method, either to a given meaning or from dictation. The whole conversion process, from the romaji/pinyin typed, through the candidate choice, to the final text, stays on the same input strip.
primitives.requires: Can already spell the target word correctly in pinyin or romaji (see prim:sound-spelling-blend) and can recognize the target character. If the pinyin or romaji itself is still spelled wrongly, go back first.
learnerAction: Step 1 Type it: for a given meaning or a sentence heard, type in pinyin or romaji, convert in segments, and choose characters from the candidate list. The system keeps every keystroke and every candidate choice.

Step 2 Find the homophone error: in a set of already typed sentences (some the learner's own, some supplied by the system), judge each spot (locked options: correct, the reading and meaning both fit / a homophone was chosen wrongly / the reading was typed wrongly, producing a wrong character / the character form belongs to another writing system, such as simplified mixed into Japanese or Japanese shinjitai mixed into Chinese / both candidates are acceptable here. The last is the reverse half).

Step 3 Type again without the candidate hints: for a new sentence on the same set of meanings, turn off the frequency ranking of candidates (candidates are arranged in random order by reading) and complete one input independently.
systemResponse: After each character is chosen in Step 1, a line of the trail "typed → candidates → chosen" is kept below the input strip. The chosen character is displayed side by side with its homophone candidates, so the learner can see the ones that were skipped.

When Step 2 is judged a homophone error, a line is drawn between that character in the sentence and the word in the context that decides the character (明天 + 再, 家 + 帰る, 样子 + 変える), showing that the choice of character is decided by context
When the reading was typed wrongly (ん, を, pinyin initial or final), the wrong keystroke is marked in the trail line, and the result the correct key sequence would give is shown
After Step 3 is finished, it is compared side by side with the choices at similar positions in Step 1, showing "With no frequency ranking, you chose ..."

ui.screen: At the top is the meaning prompt or the dictation play button. In the middle is a simulated input strip and candidate window (switchable between Chinese pinyin and Japanese romaji). Below are the trail line and the list of completed sentences. A narrow right column shows how many times homophone errors and reading errors have occurred, with no score shown.
interactions: Normal keyboard input: Space converts, number keys or arrow keys choose a candidate, Enter confirms (same as a real input method)
Step 2 uses number keys 1–5 to choose the judgment
On touch devices the candidate window is a tappable horizontal list
ui.childVariant: Uses only common homophone pairs (在/再, 他/她/它), with at most three candidates and a picture for each. The child is not asked to complete a whole sentence independently, only to choose the character.
ui.adultVariant: Uses real-scene sentences (email, chat, forms), including proper nouns, multi-segment conversion, the okurigana boundary in Japanese (変える/替える) and mixing of Chinese and Japanese character forms. Step 3 is timed.
ui.accessibility: A screen reader can read out the candidates one by one with a sample word (再: 再见的再). The trail line also states in text which key was wrong. Font size can be enlarged to tell similar-looking characters apart.

kcSignals: KC for input methods (kt:ja-orth-input)
commonErrors of the character KCs include homophone substitution (kt:zh-hanzi-l1 to kt:zh-hanzi-l6: *我在说一遍, *在见, *即然, *治定)
itemTypes include script-writing and the production is done by typing
learnerSignals: Writes correctly by hand but wrongly when typing
Homophone errors recur in chat and compositions
Simplified character forms are mixed into Japanese text
contraindications: The learner cannot yet spell in pinyin or romaji
The target is handwritten character shape and stroke order (use prim:character-anatomy)
Not used with children who have not started using a keyboard

rules: The final text in Steps 1 and 3 must match the target sentence character by character (including okurigana and character-form system). A correct reading with a wrong character means it is not passed (blocks an answer that is too weak).

In Step 3 the candidate order is shuffled, so "choose the first" or remembering a candidate position cannot pass. If in Step 1 the learner always chooses the first candidate and the errors are concentrated on targets not in first place, show "You may be choosing in order" (blocks gaming).
When Step 2 is judged "homophone chosen wrongly", the word in the context that decides the character must be pointed out
check.independence: The first result of each candidate choice in Step 1 is recorded separately, and deleting and rechoosing is recorded as a revision. A correction made after seeing the context line is recorded as completed after a hint. Step 3 provides no lines or trail hints until it is submitted.

evidence.retained: For each sentence: the keystroke trail, the candidate list and the first choice, deletion and rechoice, the Step 2 judgment and the context word pointed out, and the result in Step 3 with shuffled candidates, all kept on that sentence's input strip

licensed.claim: Can choose the right character by context among this set of homophone candidates
Can find and correct homophone errors in their own input
The romaji or pinyin typing rules (typing of ん, を, ü) are stable

prohibited: Judging that the learner can handwrite these characters from correct typing
Equating choosing the right candidate with understanding the word meaning
Judging the learner's overall writing level from one dictation input

hints: Only ask "Does this mean 'once more' or 'at a place'?"
Highlight in the context the word that decides the character
Show one common word next to each candidate (再见, 在家)
scaffold.fade: After 5 times in a row on the same homophone group with the first choice correct, remove the sample words beside the candidates and keep only the read-aloud available to a screen reader

primitives.reverseHalf: Every set has at least one spot where both candidates are right (Japanese 分かる/わかる can be written in kanji or kana, Chinese variant forms such as 唯一/惟一), and one spot where the default first choice of a real input method is the correct character, to prevent the learner from forming the opposite bias "the first choice is always wrong" or "I must always change it"

failureModes.failure: The learner remembers positions in the candidate list and not the characters
failureModes.mitigation: Shuffle the candidate order in Step 3 and in some Step 1 items
failureModes.test: Compare accuracy with fixed and with shuffled candidate order

failureModes.failure: The simulated input method behaves very differently from the one the learner actually uses, so the learned operations do not transfer
failureModes.mitigation: Keep key rules and conversion units as close as possible to mainstream input methods, and state the differences
failureModes.test: Spot-check that the input methods for ん/nn, xn and ü match mainstream input methods

failureModes.failure: Only high-frequency homophone pairs are practiced, and the learner still picks the first candidate for a new homophone group
failureModes.mitigation: Add one unpracticed homophone group to each set
failureModes.test: Count first-attempt accuracy on new homophone groups separately

stacksWith.how: Before typing in Step 1, do the pinyin or romaji spelling of the same word, and tell reading errors from character-choice errors on the same trail
For polyphonic characters or same-form heteronyms (行, 生), the reading must be decided before typing, and the reading choice is recorded on the same input strip
On the learner's own composition draft, do a dedicated round of "homophone error" revision, checking spot by spot with the Step 2 judgment categories

languages.en: English has no character conversion and is not the main binding for English. It can be used only by analogy, as a check on wrong homophones chosen by phone autocomplete or autocorrect (their/there/they're, your/you're).
languages.ja: Romaji input and kana-kanji conversion: typing ん as nn (げんいん/*げにん), typing the particle を as wo, long vowels and geminates, homophones with different characters (帰る/変える/替える, 会う/合う, 暑い/熱い/厚い), okurigana boundaries, typing simplified forms with a Chinese input method. Corresponds to kt:ja-orth-input.
languages.zh: Pinyin input: homophones (再/在, 以后/以後 as a character-form system issue, 即然/既然, 做/作, 治定/制定), typing ü as v, wrong initials or finals producing wrong words, word-segmentation errors when entering a whole sentence. Corresponds to the homophone-substitution errors in kt:zh-hanzi-l1 to kt:zh-hanzi-l6.

primitives.name: Repair & backchannel
primitives.oneLine: Handle the moments in a conversation when you did not understand, cannot say it, or must take up the conversation: ask for repetition, confirm, restate, back-channel, take the turn back
primitives.difficulty: When trouble comes up in a conversation, the learner cannot handle it on the spot. When they do not understand, they stay silent or say only Yes / はい / 嗯, and the other person takes this as understood or agreed. When asking for repetition they sound abrupt (*What?, *Please repeat, *Again, a falling-tone え？なに？) or get the word order wrong (*请说再一遍, *请一点儿慢说, *请又说一遍). When asking a word's meaning they say *What is mean…?. While thinking of a word they fill the gap with Chinese "那个、就是". To cut in they say *Wait, I want to say… or "等等！" directly. A follow-up question comes out as an interrogation (*你是什么意思？). Textbook dialogues contain no trouble, so these moves have never been practiced.
primitives.object: A purposeful exchange (a script from prim:exchange-script, or a conversation with a live partner following a role card) in which "trouble moments" are inserted at pre-marked positions: the other person speaks too fast, a word the learner does not know appears, a string of numbers is given, the other person stops and waits for the learner to take over, the other person speaks at length without checking, the topic drifts and must be pulled back, or a remark must be inserted.
